item.title: GameWM 把分工定死了：引擎守规则/状态/相机/布局，视频模型只管「长相」与交互细节 ｜ GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games with Interaction-Centric World Models
item.description:
一句话：现有系统把视频模型当渲染器，只重绘引擎已经写好的运动——生成能力大半被浪费。

要点：

  • 现状诊断很准：神经网络已经在已发售游戏里画出「大多数像素」，而近期的世界模型让**轻量引擎守世界状态、视频模型把引擎的粗代理视频变成最终帧**——但这些系统把视频模型当渲染器，只重绘引擎已写好的运动，于是生成能力大半没用上，游戏的多样性也被限住
  • GameWM 的分工：**GameWM-engine 保留必须精确的东西**（规则、状态、相机与世界的布局），这同时免除了视频模型去记忆这些东西的负担；**GameWM-VM 生成手工做起来很贵的东西**（世界的观感、玩家交互的细节）
  • 结果是：同一个玩法机制可以被实现成许多**视觉与物理上都不同**的样子，而结果仍严格等于引擎算出的那个；论文还给出配套的数据引擎（以交互而非探索为中心）、让角色设定图/场景美术/技能描述进入模型的接口，以及 5B–33B 的模型族

为什么值得看：这是本周「分工」主线最完整的一篇：它不只主张拆，还给出了拆完之后引擎侧保留什么、模型侧生成什么、以及「机制可复用、结果必须精确」这条验收标准。做 AI NPC 或生成式关卡时，这基本就是可直接照抄的接口划分。

中文摘要：半个世纪以来，电子游戏一直在追求更好的画面、更自然的交互与更有趣的玩法，而生成式视频模型如今同时关系到这三件事：神经网络已经在已发售游戏中绘制了大多数像素，近期的世界模型也让轻量引擎保留世界状态、由视频模型把引擎的粗代理视频转成最终帧。但作者指出，这些系统把视频模型当成「只重绘引擎已写好的运动」的渲染器，于是生成能力大半被闲置，也限制了游戏能提供的多样性。GameWM 因此提出一种明确分工：GameWM-engine 保留必须精确的规则、状态、相机与世界布局（同时免除视频模型记忆这些内容的负担），GameWM-VM 负责生成手工制作代价高昂的部分——世界的观感与玩家交互的细节。这样同一个玩法机制可以被实现成许多视觉与物理上都不同的样子，而结果仍严格等于引擎计算出的那个。系统层面还包括以交互（而非探索）为中心的数据引擎、让角色设定图与场景美术及技能描述进入模型的接口，以及 5B 到 33B 的模型族。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-18

GameWM: Toward Next-Generation Video Games
with Interaction-Centric World Models

Abstract

For more than half a century, video games have pursued better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay. Generative video models (VMs) now bear on all three. Neural networks already draw most of the pixels in shipped games, and recent world models let a lightweight game engine keep the world state while a VM turns the engine’s coarse proxy video into final frames. These systems, however, treat the VM as a renderer that only restyles motion the engine has already authored, which leaves most of its generative capacity unused and limits the diversity a game can offer. We present GameWM, a design for next-generation games built on a clear division of labor. The GameWM-engine keeps what must be exact: rules, state, camera, and the layout of the world, which also spares the video model from having to remember it. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author by hand: the look of the world and the detail of the player’s interactions. One game mechanic can then be realized in many visually and physically distinct ways, while its outcome stays exactly as the engine computed it. To realize this division of labor, we build GameWM as a complete system: a data engine centered on interactions rather than exploration, an interface through which authored character sheets, scene art, and skill descriptions enter the model, and a model family from 5B to 33B parameters with a real-time causal variant for play. Together they give every player a fresh version of the same game: each player’s own character, world, and skills turn the same engine mechanics into a new experience, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed.

1 Introduction

“A game is a series of interesting choices.” — Sid Meier

Video games began as laboratory curiosities, Tennis for Two in 1958 and Spacewar! in 1962, and became an industry with Pong and the Magnavox Odyssey in 1972. Today 3.6B people play them [Newzoo, 2025]. Across these seven decades, successive generations of hardware and software have pursued the same three goals: better graphics, more natural interaction, and more engaging gameplay (Section 2). Progress on one axis has repeatedly opened the others. Hardware 3D acceleration made first-person shooters and open worlds possible. Networking turned games into persistent shared worlds. Accessible creation tools let players build and share worlds of their own.

Generative video models are the newest technology to touch all three axes. On graphics, neural networks already produce most of the pixels in shipped games, although not yet through video generation: DLSS 4 upscales and interpolates frames so that 15 of every 16 displayed pixels are generated [NVIDIA, 2025c], DLSS 4.5 raises that to 23 of 24, and DLSS 5, released in September 2026, adds a neural rendering stage that infuses engine frames with photoreal lighting and materials [NVIDIA, 2026b; NVIDIA, 2026a]. In parallel, open video models have grown from Wan2.1 (1.3B and 14B, February 2025) [Wan Team, 2025] to MiniMax H3 (33B, August 2026) [MiniMax, 2026], and their visual quality now approaches that of film footage. The open question is therefore no longer whether generated pixels belong in games, but how much of the game a VM should be responsible for.

On interaction, we distinguish two levels of semantic granularity. Coarse-grained interaction moves the camera and the protagonist through the world: where to look and where to go. Fine-grained interaction is what the protagonist does to an object or another character and how: opening a car door and getting in, striking an opponent, casting a spell.

World models have gone through two generations, and both have centered on the coarse level (Section 3). The first is driven by low-dimensional action signals, camera poses or a handful of keys [Valevski et al., 2024; Bruce and others, 2024; He and others, 2025; Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025], and does not yet deliver even coarse-grained control: a key says which way to go, but how fast the protagonist moves and how fast the camera turns are left to the model, so the same input yields different motion from one sample to the next. Because the world state lives only in generated frames, control degrades further under fast viewpoint changes and revisited places drift [Xiao and others, 2025; Ye et al., 2026]. A game built this way cannot be steered reliably, let alone played with immersive control. The second generation conditions the VM on a proxy video: an engine, increasingly one written by a coding agent, keeps the state and renders a coarse proxy, and the VM turns it into the final frames [Chen et al., 2026; Zhan and others, 2026; Matrix-Game Team, 2026; Huang et al., 2026c; Lu et al., 2026b]. Because the proxy fixes layout and camera frame by frame and is re-rendered whenever the player returns, this route makes coarse-grained interaction exact and alleviates the memory problem, and it is becoming the mainstream for playable worlds.

Fine-grained interaction, where new gameplay lies, has remained largely unexplored. Second-generation world models cast the VM as a renderer: they pair each proxy with frames that a game engine rendered or a camera recorded [Zhan and others, 2026; Matrix-Game Team, 2026; Huang et al., 2026c; Chen et al., 2026], so a proxy has exactly one correct output, and none of these systems treats protagonist interaction as the objective of data curation. Appearance may be restyled, but what happens and how it moves is fixed by the pair, which leaves most of the VM’s generative capacity unused. Consider a ranged attack. The engine resolves the mechanic exactly: who attacks, which target is hit at which frame, and how much damage is dealt; how the attack looks is not part of the mechanic. A VM could realize the same event as a fireball, an ice lance, or a bolt of lightning, or as a pistol shot or a rifle burst, with the attacker’s motion following the weapon: a staff is raised and swung, a bow is drawn and released, a rifle is shouldered and recoils. A renderer cannot, because its data never pairs one proxy event with more than one realization. This is the increment a VM can bring to a game: not a restyled copy of the engine’s frames, but fine-grained interactions that the engine never animated, played out on outcomes that the engine still computes. Because the realization follows the player’s own character, world, and skills, the same mechanics unfold as different interactions for every player, and each player meets their own version of the game.

On gameplay, existing work is even less concrete. A position paper proposes interactive generative video as the basis of a generative game engine and outlines a five-level maturity roadmap [Yu et al., 2025]. Matrix-Game 4.0 [Matrix-Game Team, 2026] lets a coding agent create gameplay from natural language, Magpie [Zhan and others, 2026] targets the prototyping stage of game development, and Project Genie [Google, 2026] offers 60-second explorable worlds but, by Google’s own account, is not a game engine [Vigliarolo, 2026]. These works describe what generative games could be, but not what a VM adds to a game that its engine cannot: a session is specified by a prompt, a first frame, or an engine scene, and who the protagonist is, what world it lives in, and what it can do are left unspecified.

We present GameWM, a system design for next-generation games in which the VM is a first-class component with a defined responsibility. Building on the engine–VM split of proxy-conditioned systems [Chen et al., 2026], GameWM names the two sides the GameWM-engine and the GameWM-VM and designs every part of the system around the contract between them: a division of labor, an authoring interface through which a game supplies its characters, scenes, and skills, a data engine curated for interactions, a model family that implements the GameWM-VM for offline content and real-time play, and an evaluation that sets every output beside the proxy that drove it and the event timing. The GameWM-engine is defined by this contract rather than by an implementation: any engine, hand-written or produced by a coding agent, fills the role if it supplies what it computes exactly and cheaply, namely rules, state, camera, layout, and the coarse kinematics of the protagonist and the objects it interacts with, as a proxy video and a log of events. The GameWM-VM generates what is expensive to author: the appearance of the world and the articulated detail of protagonist interactions, and it may realize one engine event in many ways as long as the event’s semantics are preserved. A game is then authored as rules in the GameWM-engine plus a character sheet, scene concept art, and skill descriptions that the GameWM-VM renders.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    A system design that assigns the VM a responsibility. The design splits a game into a GameWM-engine, specified by the contract it must meet, and a GameWM-VM, and turns the VM from a renderer into the source of a fresh, personal experience for every player: the same mechanics, played as the player’s own character, in the player’s own world, with the player’s own skills, while every event keeps the timing and outcome the GameWM-engine computed. This places GameWM between proxy renderers, which only restyle the motion the engine authored, and pure world models, which fail to maintain a stable world.

  • •

    An interaction-centric data engine. It mines interaction-rich clips from unpacked game buffers and from screen recordings of many titles, and turns them into aligned pairs with four proxy modalities, stylized targets, interaction-centric captions, and VLM-based quality control. Proxies of screen recordings come from monocular estimates rather than engine access, so any footage can enter and target appearance is not bounded by any one engine.

  • •

    A model family from 5B to 33B that implements the GameWM-VM. All members share one proxy-reference interface trained with LoRA or full fine-tuning, without extra control modules, and are mapped to deployment tiers: GameWM-H3-33B for offline content and as the distillation teacher, GameWM-Wan2.2-14B as a low-cost offline model, and a causal GameWM-Wan2.2-5B for real-time play; GameWM-H3-33B is also distilled into a four-step causal model that generates chunk by chunk. We evaluate them visually on held-out interaction clips, with every output shown beside the proxy that drove it and the recorded event times marked.

    • 2 Seven Decades of Video Games along Three Axes

    Across the eras of Figure 1, one cycle repeats in three steps, and it tells us where a VM should sit in a game.

    A machine takes over one stage of authoring.

    Real-time 3D replaced hand-drawn sprites, shaders and ray tracing compute lighting that artists once baked, physics middleware and motion matching move the objects and bodies once scripted or keyed, and DLSS reconstructs most of the pixels the engine once shaded. Coarse-grained control has needed no new takeover since the mid-1990s. Fine-grained interaction is still authored per character: every action the protagonist can perform on an object or a character, and how it looks, is designed in advance. This is the stage a VM can take over.

    The machine joins the engine under a contract.

    None of these steps replaced the engine. Each came with a contract, such as middleware interfaces, or for DLSS 5 an engine frame that defines “what must remain” [NVIDIA, 2026a], and the engine stayed authoritative over content and rules. Pure world models instead ask the industry to replace the engine, its rules, and its tools at once; a Google spokesperson has said that Genie “is not a game engine and can’t create a full game experience” [Vigliarolo, 2026]. GameWM keeps the engine and makes the contract explicit: the GameWM-engine computes every event, and the GameWM-VM decides how it plays out.

    The new capacity becomes new gameplay.

    Real-time 3D brought open worlds, physics brought puzzles and combat built on objects, and systemic objects brought the emergent play of Breath of the Wild. DLSS makes games look better but leaves their play unchanged, and so does a VM used only as a renderer. Because fine-grained interaction is authored once per character, every player sees the same actions; a VM that takes over this stage can realize them anew for each player, as the player’s own character with the player’s own skills (Section 4.3).

    3 Related Work

    Interactive video world models.

    Single-game simulators [Valevski et al., 2024; Alonso and others, 2024; Decart and Etched, 2024; Kanervisto and others, 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025] and latent-action models learned from gameplay video [Bruce and others, 2024] were followed by open-domain models driven by keyboard and camera [He and others, 2025; Li and others, 2025; Mao et al., 2025; Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Riemann Dynamics, 2026; DreamX Team et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a; AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026a] and by recent real-time, long-horizon systems on consumer hardware [ABot-World Team, 2026; Overworld, 2026]; open full-stack frameworks now cover the path from a bidirectional video model to a few-step autoregressive world model [Zhao et al., 2026a; Rui et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a]. Interaction-oriented variants widen the action vocabulary with object interactions, character actions such as combat and spell-casting, and text events [Xiong and others, 2026; Robbyant, 2026], and ActWorld builds a dedicated interaction dataset for this setting; the results nonetheless remain coarse in both control precision and visual quality. Revisit consistency is addressed with explicit memory [Xiao and others, 2025; Huang et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2026], and memory, interaction adherence, and persistent state are measured by dedicated benchmarks [Ye et al., 2026; Ying et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026a]; [Kong et al. [2025]] survey the wider field. These models form the first generation of interactive world models: control is limited to what a few keys can express, results stay coarse, and the state lives in the generated frames, so rules and outcomes are visual guesses (top of Table 1).

    Engine-conditioned world models and neural renderers.

    CWM introduced a coding agent that keeps state in code, a compiler that renders a proxy video, and H3 as the renderer [Chen et al., 2026]. Magpie, Matrix-Game 4.0, EdenLive, and StreamRender-H3 [Zhan and others, 2026; Matrix-Game Team, 2026; Huang et al., 2026c; Lu et al., 2026b] build real-time systems on the same separation within three months of 2026, from industry labs (Skywork, Mogo AI, VAST, NVIDIA) and academic groups, which makes engine- or agent-supplied proxies the emerging mainstream for playable worlds; DLSS 5 brings neural enhancement of engine frames to shipped games [NVIDIA, 2026a]. All of them train the VM to render a proxy as one fixed output; CWM leaves local motion to the VM’s prior, but still learns one realization per proxy. Table 1 places their designs between the first generation and GameWM. On the state side, agents and programs increasingly maintain the world that a neural model renders [Liao and Liu, 2026; Huang et al., 2026d; Liang et al., 2026; Chi et al., 2026].

    Spatially controlled video generation.

    ControlNet-style and reference-based control [Zhang et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2025; Jiang and others, 2025; Ju et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2025a; NVIDIA, 2025b], 3D- and motion-aware conditioning [Gu et al., 2025; Burgert et al., 2025], and photorealism enhancement of synthetic or G-buffer renders [Richter et al., 2023; Liang and others, 2025; Wang et al., 2025b] condition a video model on depth, edges, poses, motion, or G-buffers. Concurrent generative renderers start from G-buffers [Huang et al., 2026e; Zeng et al., 2026], coarse 3D simulations or lightweight proxies [Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026], or structured states exported from physics engines [Lin et al., 2026], and SolarRenderer follows arbitrary control videos through H3’s reference pathway with frame-aligned positions [Fang et al., 2026]. These methods treat the control signal as a complete description to be preserved, most of them through an added control branch. GameWM’s proxy need not carry the protagonist’s limb motion or the effects of an interaction, which the model adds, and it enters through the backbone’s own reference pathway as a prefix with its own temporal coordinates (Section 6).

    Causal generation and few-step distillation.

    Real-time world models generate chunk by chunk with an autoregressive video diffusion model. Diffusion forcing [Chen et al., 2024] trains causal generation with per-frame noise levels, and CausVid [Yin et al., 2025] distills a bidirectional teacher into a causal student; Self Forcing [Huang et al., 2025b] trains the student on its own rollouts to close the gap between clean training history and generated inference history, and later work refines this recipe and bounds error accumulation over long rollouts [Zhu et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026c; Zhuang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b]. Distribution matching [Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a] and flow-map distillation [Gu et al., 2026] reduce sampling to a few steps. GameWM follows the SolarWM pipeline [Huang et al., 2026a] built from these components and conditions both teacher and student on the proxy.

    Data for world models.

    Datasets for world modeling pair video with actions in games [Guss et al., 2019; Yu and others, 2025; Li et al., 2026b], with camera trajectories and spatial annotations in real and rendered footage [Li et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2026], or with simulator buffers [Dosovitskiy et al., 2017; Zhong et al., 2025], and SolarWM unifies ten such sources into one frame-aligned format with metric camera geometry [Huang et al., 2026a]. They are organized around exploration, camera motion, or action labels; GameWM’s corpus is instead cut around protagonist interactions, and each proxy is paired with several targets rather than one (Section 5).

    4 GameWM System Design

    GameWM is designed for one experience: an immersive game in which the player’s own character, weapons, and skills look the same and change the world in the same way in every clip, scene, and session, while every rule and outcome stays exact. This section derives the system from that goal. Section 4.1 places GameWM between engine-bound graphics and pure world models, Section 4.2 divides each frame between the GameWM-engine and the GameWM-VM, and Section 4.3 shows how a game is authored once so that what the GameWM-VM generates stays consistent. The models that take these assets as input, and the deployment tiers they serve, follow in Section 6.

    4.1 Where GameWM Sits: Stability and Generative Capability

    From traditional graphics to a pure world model, each design hands one more module of the frame to a neural network (Figure 2). DLSS takes over the final pixels and refines what the engine rendered [NVIDIA, 2025c; NVIDIA, 2026a]. Proxy renderers, the engine-conditioned world models such as CWM, Magpie, PWM, and Matrix-Game 4.0, take over appearance and render it from a coarse proxy video rather than from finished engine frames [Chen et al., 2026; Zhan and others, 2026; Huang et al., 2026d; Matrix-Game Team, 2026]. GameWM also hands over interaction detail: how each interaction plays out. Pure world models such as Genie 3 and LingBot-World hand over the rest, namely layout, motion, rules, and state [Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Robbyant Team et al., 2026]. Each step adds generative capability, the range of content the network produces without being authored, and gives up some game stability, the guarantee that rules, state, and outcomes are exact and replayable. Stability declines slowly while the engine keeps the world state, because a visual error cannot change an outcome; it collapses once the state moves into the generated frames and outcomes become visual guesses. GameWM takes the last step before that collapse: it maximizes generative capability subject to game stability, with the network deciding how interactions look and the engine still deciding where everything is and what happens.

    4.2 Division of Labor

    The GameWM-engine keeps everything a designer must be able to inspect, replay, and balance: rules, scores, health, collisions, quest state, and the positions and coarse poses of all entities. It renders a proxy video from the player’s camera. The proxy determines where things are and when an interaction happens, for example that the protagonist reaches the driver’s door at second 2.1 and the car departs at second 3.4. The GameWM-VM determines how the interaction looks: the hand on the handle, the body folding into the seat, the door closing, and the appearance of the protagonist, the car, and the street. A visual error can therefore make the feedback less clear, but it cannot change an outcome, because outcomes are computed before the GameWM-VM runs.

    This division follows from cost. The quantities on the GameWM-engine side are cheap to compute exactly and expensive for a VM to infer: a rule is a line of code, and a revisit is a re-render. The quantities on the GameWM-VM side are expensive to author and cheap to sample from a strong prior: a new interaction costs an animator weeks, but a VM trained on interaction footage has seen thousands of examples of people entering cars.

    One event, many realizations.

    Because outcomes live in the GameWM-engine, the GameWM-VM is free to vary everything that does not change them. An engine event fixes its semantics, such as the event type, the participants, and the hit frame, together with the coarse kinematics of the bodies involved; any realization that keeps these is valid, so one ranged attack can appear as a fire spell, an ice spell, or a rifle shot. The proxy therefore has to carry event semantics rather than a fully posed animation, and the data has to pair one event type with many realizations (Section 5.2). Section 4.3 uses this freedom to give every character its own skills.

    4.3 Authored Once: Consistency for an Immersive Game

    What GameWM offers the player is immersion, and immersion rests on consistency. A player who plays a fire mage expects the same face and costume in every scene, the same fire in every attack, and the same scorch where that fire lands; if any of these changes from one clip to the next, the game stops feeling like one world. Game world models so far set up each session from a prompt, a first frame, or an engine scene, and nothing in the system carries the protagonist’s identity or abilities from one session to the next. GameWM makes them assets that are authored once and reused by every clip: the mechanics of the GameWM-engine, the character and its world, and the skills that join the two (Figure 3).

    Mechanics from the GameWM-engine.

    The game framework defines a small set of mechanics, for example a melee attack, a ranged attack, and a dash. Each is code with exact rules: what can be targeted, when the hit lands, and how much damage it does. The designer writes each mechanic once, every character shares it, and it is what the proxy shows: coarse bodies in motion and an event in the engine’s log.

    The character and its world.

    A character sheet shows the protagonist from the front, the side, and the back. In conventional production a character is a textured, rigged 3D model with an animation set. Under the division of labor this asset splits in two: the GameWM-engine keeps a coarse body, a capsule or low-poly mesh that it simulates, collides, and renders into the proxy, and the sheet carries everything the player sees, at the cost of an image instead of modeling, rigging, and animation. The first frame, scene concept art aligned with the GameWM-engine’s opening view, sets the look of the world. The two are generated to agree with each other, starting from whichever the player provides. From a sheet, an image model paints the first frame from that opening view with the character in it; this is the step that restyles first frames in the data engine, so the anchor relates to the proxy at inference as it did in training. From a first frame, the image model draws a sheet of its protagonist. The sheet slot is trained with exact supervision, because each stylized target in the data engine was rendered from its sheet (Section 5.3), and the sheet is dropped for a fifth of those samples, so the first frame alone can also set both the world and the protagonist.

    Skills: mechanic × attribute.

    A character also implies how it fights. High-level attributes are read from the sheet, such as an element, a weapon, and a palette, and each attribute is fused with each engine mechanic into one entry of the character’s skill tree. For the fire mage, the melee attack becomes Flame Fist, the ranged attack Fireball, and the dash Ember Dash; an ice mage on the same mechanics gets frost versions of all three. Each entry is text that describes the skill’s look, including what it does to the scene, such as the burst on impact or the embers left on the ground. A designer thus writes each mechanic once and obtains a family of skills across characters, and a player can wield skills that no artist animated.

    From assets to frames.

    At run time the GameWM-engine turns the player’s input into proxy frames and resolves each event exactly. When an event uses a mechanic, the character’s entry for that mechanic is added to the caption of the chunk in which it occurs, and the first frame, the sheet, the proxy chunk, and the caption enter the GameWM-VM together as in-context references (Section 6.2): motion, framing, and positions follow the proxy, the world’s look follows the first frame, the protagonist’s identity follows the sheet, and the caption describes the event. The GameWM-engine still decides the target, the hit frame, and the damage; the entry decides only how the skill looks, and the GameWM-VM generates the attacker’s motion, the projectile, the impact, and the target’s reaction in step with the hit frame.

    Together these assets make the experience consistent across a game rather than within a clip: the same protagonist appears in every scene, each scene opens with its authored look, every use of a skill draws on the same description, and its timing and outcome come from the same engine rule. Figure 9 places four characters in four scenes each, and Figure 8 gives eight characters their own skills on a ranged and a melee mechanic (Section 7).

    5 Interaction-Centric Data Engine

    Figure 4 summarizes the data engine. A clip comes from one of two sources: a game recording whose depth, semantics, player state, and event tags are read from engine buffers, or a screen recording of another title, whose depth and semantics are estimated by monocular models [Kong et al., 2026; Ravi et al., 2025] and whose events are tagged by a VLM. Clips are cut around interactions and reduced to three proxy modalities (DUV, depth, and semantics) and a window-scoped event caption. H3’s reference-to-video-and-audio mode (Ref2VA) then renders each clip again from its semantic video and event text: m low-poly versions, which stand in for the proxy frames a GameWM-engine would render, such as a simple engine or one written by a coding agent, and serve as further proxies, and n high-fidelity versions, which take their look from a restyled first frame and an optional character sheet and serve, with the source recording, as targets.

    5.1 Sources and the Appearance Ceiling

    Paired data captured inside an engine has an appearance ceiling: the target is itself an engine render, so a model trained on it learns to look like that engine. GameWM therefore does not tie its data to one engine. Any footage from which per-frame depth and semantics can be obtained, either read from engine buffers or estimated by monocular models, enters the same pipeline and is reduced to the same proxy interface: per-frame depth and semantics, also packed into a single RGB video (DUV), and low-poly re-renders in four styles (amateur low-poly, capsules, Blender primitives, and MagicaVoxel), which show the structure of a scene without the engine’s appearance. Appendix A gives the encoding. Adding a source requires only an extractor; the training interface does not change. Figure 5 shows the sources currently converted and the events their clips carry, divided by granularity.

    5.2 Fine-Grained Curation and Coarse Expansion

    The sources play two roles, and they are curated differently.

    Fine-grained events teach interactions.

    Where the source reports what happens, clips are cut around events rather than sampled uniformly. In the GTA V recordings the engine reports each event, such as enter_vehicle or shoot, with its frame, and the event times enter the proxy and the caption. Fine-grained events have a participant and a key frame that decides the outcome: entering or exiting a vehicle, a melee hit, a shot. They are what the GameWM-VM cannot infer from motion alone and what the GameWM-engine’s clock must time. Coarse events are locomotion modes, such as driving, swimming, or climbing, which the proxy already describes almost completely. Of the 1,460 GTA V clips in the snapshot, 1,018 (70%) are fine-grained (Figure 5, right); Figure 6 shows one training pair per event.

    Coarse and untagged clips broaden appearance.

    ABot-World, Magpie, and CARLA tag only locomotion or nothing, so their clips cannot be cut around events, but they reduce to the same proxy interface and are rendered into the same target styles. With the coarse GTA V clips they make up 84% of the corpus and supply far more scenes, layouts, and camera paths than one game offers, from which the model learns to take structure from the proxy and appearance from the anchor (Section 4.3). Interactions are thus learned from the fine-grained part, and appearance transfer from all of it.

    One event can also look many ways. Captions name the realization (weapon, element, vehicle class) so that text can select it, but recorded realizations are still few: melee is bare-handed, and the vehicles are cars and a helicopter. Others, such as spell elements and melee weapons, are supplied at inference by the character sheet and the skill text (Figure 8).

    5.3 Diverse Targets and Verified Captions

    A proxy describes structure; the target and the caption decide what the model learns to put on top of it. A clip’s targets are its source recording and its high-fidelity renders. Each render takes the semantic proxy, a first frame restyled by an image model, and, for many renditions, a character sheet showing the protagonist or the driven vehicle from the front, the side, and the back. The render’s subject is drawn from that sheet, so the sheet is an exact identity reference for it and is kept with the pair; the source recording has none. Pairing one proxy with targets of different looks forces the model to take structure from the proxy and appearance from the anchor and the sheet.

    Each 5.17 s training window gets its own caption with timestamp prefixes. Because captioners describe objects that a scene usually contains, the per-second content of the proxy is given to the captioner as a prior and used to check its reply: a caption that mentions a car in a second without vehicle pixels fails (Appendix A).

    5.4 Quality Control Follows Provenance

    Proxies are checked only where they are estimated. Depth and semantics read from engine buffers or from a simulator (GTA V, CARLA, Magpie) are exact; those estimated from screen recordings can flicker or mislabel over time, so these clips are reviewed by a VLM for the temporal stability and accuracy of depth and semantics. Every rendered video, low-poly or high-fidelity, is generated and is therefore screened: a VLM compares it with its source clip on camera, motion and timing, spatial relations, style, and, with a sheet, identity, and a human reviewer can override any decision. Acceptance tracks the proxy (Table 6): 94% of the GTA V low-poly renders and 70% of its high-fidelity renders pass, against about half or less for renders built on estimated (ABot-World) or sparse gray-box (Magpie) proxies. Exact proxies thus pay twice: they need no screening themselves, and the targets built on them are more reliable. Appendix A gives the review panels, the axes, the decision rules, and the rates per source.

    6 The GameWM Model Family

    6.1 Deployment Tiers

    A model’s scale decides where it can run, and where it runs decides what it can serve. GameWM is therefore a family of three models, one per deployment tier, rather than one model.

    The offline tier, GameWM-H3-33B, has the highest quality. It renders cutscenes, trailers, player replays, and user-generated videos, produces training data, and serves as the teacher for distillation. A single H3 stream currently takes several datacenter GPUs, so this tier is not for live play. The player tier, a causal GameWM-Wan2.2-5B, is distilled to few-step chunk-wise generation for real-time play. Matrix-Game 4.0 shows that a 5B renderer can reach 60 FPS at 480p on one RTX 5090 [Matrix-Game Team, 2026], so this is the tier that can follow DLSS onto consumer hardware.

    GameWM-Wan2.2-14B sits between the two as a low-cost offline model. It serves offline content that does not need the quality of the 33B model at a fraction of its cost, and it is the platform on which data and design choices are screened before they are run at 33B.

    6.2 Interface and Backbones

    All GameWM models share one interface. The inputs enter through the backbone’s existing reference pathway rather than a new control branch: the proxy video as

    The models differ in backbone and in how the proxy enters it. GameWM-H3-33B places the proxy in H3’s native Ref2VA reference rows and trains a rank-128 LoRA on the attention projections; the audio rows are kept but receive zero loss. GameWM-Wan2.2-14B is built on the high-noise expert of Wan2.2-I2V-A14B, which runs every denoising step (the low-noise expert is not used), and trains a rank-128 LoRA on the attention projections at 832×480 and 81 frames at 16 fps. GameWM-Wan2.2-5B is built on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and is fully fine-tuned at 1280×704 and 121 frames at 24 fps. Wan2.2 has no reference slot, so the inputs of the shared interface are laid out as one token sequence for its self-attention: the pictures (first frame, then the sheet), the proxy, and the target, each patchified on its own spatial grid. The proxy is encoded at half the target’s spatial resolution and placed as a temporal prefix, i.e. its latent frames take the time coordinates after the pictures and before the target. Table 2 summarizes the three models.

    6.3 Long Rollout and Real-Time Distillation

    Long sessions are generated in windows: the first window receives one latent frame of context, and later windows receive ten. CWM uses a similar 34-frame overlap, so we only report the setting. All three models are distilled in the three stages of SolarWM [Huang et al., 2026a]: bidirectional adaptation, teacher-forced AnyFlow causal initialization, and DMD with self-gradient forcing, which yields a four-step causal student per backbone. In the causal stages each chunk reads only its own proxy chunk and the five before it (Eq. (2)). Section 7.3 compares the three students on one clip.

    7 Experiments

    We examine two stages of GameWM-H3-33B on held-out interaction clips: the bidirectional model, which generates a whole clip at once, and the distilled causal model, which generates it chunk by chunk in four denoising steps. The causal students of the two Wan2.2 backbones are compared with it at the end of Section 7.3. Both receive only a proxy, the first frame, a caption, and, for the Sheet variants, a character sheet. The proxies stand in for the output of a GameWM-engine: they are derived from held-out recordings, and their event times come from the recorded game’s engine log or are read off the proxy. Evaluation is visual: every figure shows the proxy above the output it drives, with these event times marked, so that adherence and timing can be judged directly (Appendix B). Because proxy-conditioned systems differ in proxy format, interface, and availability, and text prompts cannot be aligned fairly across them, we do not rank GameWM against other systems and show only our own models.

    7.1 Setup

    Inputs.

    Each sample is a 5.17 s clip (124 frames at 24 fps) rendered at 1280×704. The condition c=(y,a,s,p) consists of the caption y with a modality tag and time-window prefixes, the appearance anchor a (the first frame), the character sheet s (Sheet variants only), and the proxy video p in one of four modalities at 640×352. Held-out clips are split by source recording (Appendix B).

    Bidirectional stage.

    Let z₀ be the target latent and zₜ its noisy version at time t. The proxy enters H3’s native reference rows, and a rank-128 LoRA on the attention projections is trained with the backbone’s flow-matching objective [Lipman et al., 2023]

    L_BD=𝔼_z₀,t,ε∥f_θ(zₜ,t,c)-uₜ∥₂²,

    		(1)

    where uₜ is the native velocity target. The loss covers only the video rows; the audio rows of H3 are kept and receive zero loss.

    Causal stage.

    The latent sequence is split into chunks zᵏ of five latent frames. The causal model factorizes the clip as

    p_ψ(z^1:K|c)=∏ₖ₌₁^Kp_ψ(zᵏ|z^

    		(2)

    so chunk k reads its own proxy chunk and the five before it, never a later one. This is what the GameWM-engine can supply during play: the proxy of the current moment, not of the future. Following SolarWM [Huang et al., 2026a], the causal model is initialized with teacher-forced AnyFlow [Gu et al., 2026] and then trained by distribution matching [Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2025] on its own rollouts [Huang et al., 2025b], with self-gradient forcing [Zhuang et al., 2026] for gradients through the key–value cache:

    ∇_ψL_DMD=𝔼[J_G_ψ^⊤ w(t)(s_fake(zₜ,t,c)-sᵣₑₐₗ(zₜ,t,c))],

    		(3)

    where G_ψ is the causal generator, sᵣₑₐₗ is the score of the frozen bidirectional model of Eq. (1), and s_fake is a critic trained on the student’s rollouts. The proxy therefore conditions both the teacher and the student, so distillation matches proxy-conditioned distributions rather than unconditional video statistics.

    Checkpoints.

    Table 3 lists the GameWM-H3-33B checkpoints of this section. The two AR models are listed because they initialize the DMD students; their own few-step outputs are not shown.

    7.2 Bidirectional Model

    One interaction, every proxy.

    Figure 7 drives one held-out vehicle entry with six proxies and a static control. Under the three engine buffers the camera, the street, and the parked cars follow the proxy, and the protagonist reaches the door and is seated at the engine’s frames. The three coarse re-renders carry no limb motion, and under the capsules the protagonist is a rigid body, yet in all three he runs to the car, the door opens, and the car pulls away on the engine’s schedule: the model decides how the interaction plays out (Figure 2). Under the static control the model still stages an entry, but the camera keeps its heading and the car arrives where the model chooses, so the model reads the proxy rather than continuing the first frame.

    One mechanic, many realizations.

    Figure 8 gives eight characters their own sheet, first frame, and skill on two capsule proxies: a shooting clip, reused in later figures, in which the protagonist attacks an opponent from a distance, and a melee clip with a single strike. In every row the opponent falls on the proxy’s schedule, while everything the proxy lacks comes from the model: the capsule has no arms, so every casting pose is generated, and the melee proxy throws a bare elbow, so the flames, staffs, claws, and hammer are too. Each character keeps its costume, colors, and build in both scenes. One mechanic thus becomes eight characters’ skills with nothing changed on the GameWM-engine side.

    One character across scenes.

    Figure 9 places four characters in four scenes each, with first frames made from the sheet. The protagonist keeps the costume, colors, and silhouette of its sheet in all sixteen pairs, while the scene, the opponent, and the interaction follow each clip. Measured by DINOv2 similarity to the sheets (Table 4; Appendix B), the protagonist is closer to its own sheet than to the other three in every pair, by 0.03 to 0.20. Removing the sheet but keeping the first frame lowers similarity by only 0.024 for BD-Sheet and 0.014 for DMD-Sheet, less than the 0.039 between two seeds, so in these clips identity is carried mainly by the first frame; isolating the sheet needs clips in which the protagonist enters later.
