Existing strategies share a common limitation: all assume that a single fixed policy suffices to reach the target budget. At aggressive budgets this assumption fails—every preservation-contract decimator we test eventually melts on fragmented inputs, manifested as part deletion, wall welding, or tolerance violation. Existing theory neither predicts where melting must occur—its budget results cover smooth convex bodies [10, 12] and plane curves [10] but not fragmented piecewise-smooth surfaces—nor addresses whether a self-improving decimator converges or how much validation evidence suffices to certify improvement. The absence of theoretical guidance is consequential: each mesh shatters differently, rendering run-once policies inadequate; manual orchestration of the cleaning-simplification-verification loop is prohibitively tedious; and unguided agent-based approaches are unstable, as erroneous early decisions propagate irrecoverably. Furthermore, once the decimation process is governed by a strict validation gate, it becomes a drift process whose convergence can be quantified.

Our central insight is that the melting point is not an algorithmic artifact but a geometric property of the input itself, and therefore a theory-mandated strategy can be derived from measured geometry rather than discovered through blind search. We therefore present RemeshingAgent, an agent for repair-based decimation of generated building meshes that combines a frozen geometry engine with a validation-gated evolution discipline [35]. The agent operationalizes the decimation craft as a validated Clean–Execute–Verify–Reflect loop (Figure 1, center–right): it cleans the fragmented input, executes decimation pipelines on the frozen engine, verifies candidates against held-out geometric scores and visual inspection, and reflects on the trajectory to refine its skill document and operator vocabulary, accepting modifications only when they strictly improve held-out validation.

Empirically, trained on 24 commercial high-poly building meshes with 19 held-out validation meshes, the agent improves its gate score monotonically from 8.8358 to 8.9811 across five accepted updates; deployed inference replays the retrieved pipelines on CPU in 11.7 s per mesh without LLM or VLM calls.

1.1 Contributions

  • •

    We present RemeshingAgent, the first agent for repair-based decimation of generated building meshes, turning fragment clouds of thousands of components into single clean components (Figure 2, right).

  • •

    We give the agent a self-evolving discipline that tunes the skill document and the operator vocabulary along the theory’s direction chain under a strict held-out validation gate, improving by +0.145 gate score without a single regressed update.

  • •

    We prove the theory behind both, a budget decomposition prescribing the clean-first direction, and a component threshold below which no output satisfies the repair contract.

    • First, the triangle budget admits a decomposition into a curvature term A_curv/ε, a crease term A_crease/√ε, and a component floor 4n_sig, with the maximum determining the active constraint (Theorem 3.1). Second, below the component threshold, no output satisfying the repair contract exists, transforming melting from an empirical observation into a prediction with a precise location, and establishing cleaning as the theory-mandated response (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3). Third, under an explicit improvement assumption, the gated evolution admits an additive-drift hitting-time bound together with a resolution law characterizing the validation-set size required to resolve improvements (He–Yao [14], Eq. (6)), with all parameters estimated from the agent’s training trace.

    2 Related Work

    LLM Agents for 3D. LLM-based agents have been applied to 3D generation [27] and procedural modeling. ReAct [37] and Voyager [30] establish observation-action loops; PhotoAgent [36], aDSL [31], and CADDesigner [8] couple LLM planning with graphics tools—none evolves its own operator vocabulary under validation discipline, establishes convergence guarantees, or addresses repair-based decimation at aggressive budgets. Our approach treats the entire remeshing policy as a trainable object, with convergence analyzed in Section 3.2.

    Level of Detail and Decimation. Classical approximation theory characterizes the triangulation complexity of smooth surfaces: the Θ(∫√|K| dA/ε) face-count bound for convex surfaces [10, 12], Fejes Tóth’s optimal polygonal curves [10], and Erickson’s sampling complexity [7]—but none of these addresses the repair-contract minimum face count of fragmented piecewise-smooth surfaces; field reports [21] document such failures without a theoretical account. Preservation-based decimators maintain input connectivity (quadric error metrics [11], progressive meshes [15], vertex clustering, recent variants for weak features and artist quad topology [3, 18]; surveys [6, 5, 24]), whereas reconstruction rebuilds the surface from samples (voxel hulls, alpha wrap, cell cuts [34], generative remeshers [22]). City-scale LOD frameworks [4] prescribe level contents but not decimation limits; our budget law supplies this missing quantitative layer. Head-to-head comparisons with these robust baselines appear in the supplementary (S11–S12). Our two-contract analysis (supplementary, S10) predicts when each family prevails; learned representations [25, 26, 13, 19] need training sets incompatible with our single-mesh setting.

    Self-Evolving Agents. Self-improving frameworks (Reflexion [29], Gödel Agent [38]) update task and meta policies; prompt optimizers (DSPy [17], TextGrad [39], GEPA [1]) refine instructions. SkillOpt [35] contributes the discipline we adopt—rollout batches, bounded edits, validation gating, a rejected-edit buffer—for a frozen geometry engine. RE-TRAC [40] addresses cross-trajectory state compression, and complementary work distills skills from multimodal resources [9] and evaluates them via checklists [20]. E-value gating [33, 28] and validation-gated skill evolution [32] provide error-control guarantees but leave open the power analysis behind our resolution law (Eq. (6)) and our planner’s multi-candidate selection; our convergence analysis builds on the additive-drift theorem [14] and hitting-time bounds [2].

    3 The Geometry of Decimation

    Section 3.1 derives the agent’s direction from measured geometry, and Section 3.2 adds a self-evolving loop that verifies every candidate against held-out scores.

    3.1 The Minimal Triangle Budget

    A generated building’s mesh arrives shattered into 10³–10⁴ components (Figure 2, left); the objective is repair-based decimation—consolidating 8,223 components into one at 0.87% of the input faces (right).

    3.1.1 The Topology-Preserving Contract

    We model the input S as piecewise-smooth with n components of total genus g; a mesh T is an ε-approximation if δ_H(S,T)≤ε diag(S). Topology is measured against the intended surfaceS^∗, the welding closure of S at the seam scale δ₀: the intended building parts, pairwise separated well beyond ε diag(S) at our budgets. S^∗ is a declared reference computed from S alone—generated assets carry no pre-fragmentation ground truth—so preservation is always relative to S^∗: welding and dust removal repair S toward S^∗ by definition; Section 4.9 audits this structure component-wise. Under the preservation contract (A), T must satisfy the tolerance and T≅S^∗ (homeomorphic)—welding is repair, not a topology change (raw-input preservation would force F≥4n if every component were a closed shell—a floor no budget meets). In the agent the welding threshold defaults to this seam scale, 0.1% of the diagonal, and adopted pipelines kept it throughout. Under the reconstruction contract (B), the output is rebuilt from samples (voxel hulls, alpha wrap, generative remeshers [22]); its budget law differs. A component is ε-significant if its diameter exceeds 2ε diag(S); deleting it violates the approximation. Significant components are closed shells (thin-walled solids); boundary components admit lower floors (supplementary, S10).

    3.1.2 The Budget Law

    Theorem 3.1(Minimal triangle budget, decomposition).

    Under the preservation contract, as the absolute tolerance ε_abs=ε diag(S)→0,

    F_\min \asymp \max (c₁A_curv/ε_abs, c₂A_crease/√ε_abs, 4 n_sig, c₄g),

    		(1)

    where A_curv=∫_Sₛₘₒₒₜₕ√|K| dA and A_crease=∑ⱼ∫_Cⱼ√κ ds, and c₁,c₂,c₄ depend only on the smoothness constants; \asymp is two-sided asymptotic equivalence.

    Each term is classical [10, 12, 23, 16]. Developable patches (K=0)—cylindrical towers—cost Θ(ε_abs^-1/2) and fold into the crease term (prism bound π√R/(2ε_abs)); the distinct exponents (ε_abs⁻¹, ε_abs^-1/2, ε_abs⁰) make the decomposition identifiable. For predominantly planar, low-genus buildings, Eq. (1) reduces to

    F_\min \asymp \max (c₂ (A_crease)/(√ε_abs), 4 n_sig),

    		(2)

    so classical analysis alone predicts near-free decimation—and the missed component floor 4n_sig is what makes every practical decimator we test melt on generated ones; the operational reading—clean first, weld, then decimate—follows (Figure 2, right).

    Theorem 3.1 is asymptotic; at 0.5–1% budgets we claim only the regional structure as evidence, validated in Section 4.3.

    3.1.3 The Operational Limit

    Fitted per algorithm family with a calibration factor ĉ,

    F̂(S,ε)=ĉ₁(A_curv)/(ε diag)+ĉ₂(A_crease)/(√ε diag)+4n_sig,

    		(3)

    Equations (1), (2), and (4) use the absolute tolerance ε_abs defined above; ε elsewhere is the contract’s dimensionless relative tolerance, so every term is a face count. n_sig is measured on the post-cleaning, welded estimate of S^∗ (the surface the contract references), with the 0.1% area threshold (rank-consistent with the diameter caliber, ρ=0.68–0.89). Fitting QEM and clustering sweeps gives ĉ∈[1.1×,2.4×] (Section 4.3): an additive working form, its max-to-sum gap absorbed by ĉ—calibrated on the sweep corpus, not predicted beyond it; the tested content is the exponent structure and the cliff shift, and a split-half probe predicts held-out error floors rank-consistently (Spearman ρ=0.83 median; supplementary, S6).

    Theorem 3.2(Component cliff).

    Let S^∗ have n_sigε-significant components, pairwise separated by more than 2ε diag(S)—true of intended building parts at our budgets—and take a budget

    F

    		(4)

    Then no mesh T with at most F triangles satisfies both δ_H(S^∗,T)≤ε diag(S) and T≅S^∗: the separation keeps the components’ ε diag(S)-neighborhoods disjoint, so no triangle serves two components, and the piece of T standing for each closed shell Sⱼ pays its own floor,

    F ≥ ∑ₖ₌₁^n_sig\max (4, c₁A_curv(Sₖ)/ε_abs) = F_comp > F,

    		(5)

    The bound is combinatorial, not statistical; it holds for every algorithm (Figure 3; proof and breaking-mode classification in the supplementary, S10).

    Corollary 3.3(The value of cleaning).

    A component is ε-deletable if every point of it lies within ε diag(S) of the retained surface; deleting such components preserves the ε-approximation. Dust is deletable by construction—shards of the intended shell—so cleaning lowers n_sig from n to n_sig≪n and F_comp accordingly. Cleaning before decimation is the theory-mandated first move (supplementary, S7).

    From fragments to one component. Three theory-licensed moves: delete dust (Corollary 3.3), weld vertices closer than δ≤ε diag (perturbs by at most δ), then pay the budget law at the reduced n_sig—realized by the agent’s clean_repair (conservative cleanup, or aggressive welding plus small-component removal), stopping before the threshold rather than melting (Section 4.4); the operators’ own perturbation is 0.0009–0.0017 normalized Chamfer, within tolerance.

    3.2 Convergence of Validation-Gated Skill Evolution

    Figure 4 illustrates the loop: the direction of Section 3.1 fixes what to do but not its parameters, which the agent tunes by evolving a skill document s through reflect-and-gate cycles. With selection set Dₛₑₗ and deterministic reward r(s,m), the empirical potential is V(s)=target-(1)/(|Dₛₑₗ|)∑ₘr(s,m), with hitting time T_ε=\min{t:V(sₜ)≤ε}. If the reflect kernel Q(s→s^′) satisfies condition (H1)—improving V by at least Δ with probability ≥p_\min (supplementary, S10)—and the gate uses strict acceptance with elite retention, the additive-drift bound of He–Yao [14] yields 𝔼[ T_ε|s₀ ]≤V(s₀)/(p_\minΔ); calibrated on our system, it agrees in order of magnitude with the observed trajectory—a consistency check, not an independent prediction. The per-group law pΔ is the testable content.

    3.2.1 The Validation Gate

    The reward is a scalarized score G(M;M₀)=∑ᵢ₌₁⁶wᵢ gᵢ with w=(0.30,0.15,0.20,0.05,0.20,0.10) over face-count, manifold, shape-preservation, planarity, sharp-edge, and compactness dimensions (calibrated in Section 4.2; supplementary S9). The gate’s statistical power limits the smallest per-step improvement it can resolve—the sub-Gaussian resolution scale

    Δ_\min(n) = σ̂√(2\ln(1/α))/(n),

    		(6)

    with σ̂ the cross-mesh std of paired differences.

    3.2.2 Forward and Backward Passes

    The harness returns scored trajectories (τ,r)=h(M_geo,M₀,s); at round k the planner samples B candidates and submodular selection picks a diverse subset. A pipeline template in s is the parameterized chain of Section 3.1 made executable. An LLM reflector proposes discrete text edits over the success/failure split, guided by a cross-trial parameter→reward contrast table; accepted edits are capped by Lₖ (the “learning rate”), yielding candidate s̃ₖ, gated on the held-out set:

    sₖ₊₁=s̃ₖ\iffrₛₑₗ(s̃ₖ)>rₛₑₗ(sₖ);

    		(7)

    otherwise sₖ₊₁=sₖ (elite retention); a pre-check skips “inert” candidates. Candidates run in an isolated read-only copy, so rejections never enter the deployed skill; the best score is non-decreasing and the initial skill is a safe lower bound (supplementary, S10). Because Dₛₑₗ is reused, the deployed skill is re-scored on a test set it never touches (Section 4.9): test numbers measure transfer, not gate fitness.

    3.2.3 The Rejected-Edit Buffer and the Tool Tier

    Rejected edits are retained as negative feedback; at epoch boundaries a meta-reflector writes longitudinal guidance into a protected slow-update region. Skill training optimizes what the agent knows but cannot escape its operator vocabulary; the tool tier removes that ceiling—an LLM proposes new operators, each passing a feasibility probe, with adoption adjudicated by the ordinary gate (Section 4.11)—and no gate is ever relaxed.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Datasets and Baselines

    The training set comprises 24 high-poly Hunyuan3D building meshes (0.9M–1.5M faces, 7,000–21,000 components), each decimated to three budgets (1%, 0.75%, 0.5%); the validation set holds 19 landmark meshes (∼740K faces) for gate evaluation; and the theory corpus covers the same 43 meshes, 12 of which also run QEM/clustering sweeps at eight budgets (10%–0.1%). We evaluate on every mesh in each split: failed epochs are scored, all 19 validation meshes enter every gate round, no mesh is added, removed, or re-weighted after results, and group order follows a pre-registered seed.

    Five method families are compared. Direct QEM is quadric-error decimation (pymeshlab, preserve-topology enabled); vertex clustering is meshing_decimation_clustering; the zoo additionally reports QEM with preserve-topology disabled (the only configuration reaching aggressive budgets). LATO.2 [22] is a learned generative remesher served on its released inference server with the vertex budget specified directly; our pipeline and all preservation baselines are CPU-only. The reconstruction pipeline chains voxel shell → nvdiff deformation → alpha wrap → refined QEM as the contract-B representative. RemeshingAgent runs zero-shot (S₀) and trained (S_K, K=24 groups).

    All experiments run on CPU (pymeshlab, trimesh, Open3D); the LLM planner and reflector employ MiniMax-M3, and the VLM bonus is disabled in training for deterministic evaluation. Reward weights derive from a calibration episode (an initial planarity weight admitted degenerate slivers); recalibration (shape/sharp reweighting, a non-linear cap >7.0, a degenerate-face penalty) aligned gate decisions with perceptual quality, robust under ±50% and 100 in-band perturbations (supplementary, S9).

    4.2 Self-Evolution of the Agent

    Figure 5 shows the gate score over 24 groups: S₀=8.8358→8.9811 (+0.145) through 5 accepted updates; all 19 validation meshes improve (supplementary, S1b), the smallest gain +0.021. The drift law predicts 24 pΔ≈0.115 vs. observed +0.145.

    4.3 The Two-Regime Structure

    QEM and clustering sweeps (12 meshes × 8 budgets) exhibit a two-regime structure (Figure 6). On clean meshes, error follows a power law with exponent 0.13–0.40 (corr(\logA,\logbudget)=0.95); on fragmented meshes, error exhibits a floor regime with exponent ≈0 for the melting families, decreasing only until the component term 4n_sig of Theorem 3.1 becomes dominant. The cliff position shifts with the predicted F_comp, consistent with component-dominated breaking. Both algorithm families exhibit identical behavior, indicating that the regional structure is a geometric property rather than an algorithmic artifact.

    4.4 The Five-Family Zoo

    All five families target the same 0.5% budget on identical fragmented meshes, measured by normalized Chamfer (50k area-weighted samples, symmetric bidirectional mean, normalized by the output diagonal). Reached face counts differ and are part of the comparison: preservation-enabled QEM cannot reach the target, whereas melting configurations reach it by deleting and welding. The agent achieves the best fidelity at 0.0015 (24/24); the reconstruction pipeline 0.005–0.009 (watertight); LATO.2 0.003–0.011, floored at low budgets by its generative prior; bare QEM and clustering 0.05–0.18, melting. An equal-cleaning control separates recipe from adaptation: conservative clean-then-QEM reaches the budget on 1/24, the fixed aggressive recipe on 19/24 (0.0014 median Chamfer on hits, clean topology)—cleaning carries most of the effect; the rest is per-mesh variation fixed parameters miss and selection covers (the agent: 24/24; supplementary, S7). The topology metrics and Section 4.5 carry the preservation verdict. Figure 7 shows the same separation per mesh.

    A regime-conditional stress test makes the scope explicit (Table 1): on Hunyuan-style shattered inputs the method is necessary, while on the independently-sourced test buildings every arm completes at the same relative budgets—and aggressive cleaning induces its own melt, stalling QEM on 2/20 meshes with 760k/660k faces remaining; per-mesh selection avoids both failure modes. The Think-stage fragmentation statistics identify the regime before any run.

    The ordering matches the two-contract prediction (supplementary, S10): preservation methods pay the component tax or melt, and the agent’s cleaning reduces n_sig to the preservation side. The epoch-3 cliff-avoidance response (face-count dimension -4 at 0.5% budget, Chamfer holding at 0.0015) and PolyFit’s contract-B verdict (18/20 test meshes complete, immaculate topology, median Chamfer 0.029 vs. ours 0.001; supplementary, S7) complete the picture.

    4.5 Isolating the Component Term

    Controlled fragmentation is applied to a clean constant-curvature mesh (∫√|K|dA≈26.2; N=1,13,35,90 pieces). At the most aggressive budget (0.1%), normalized Chamfer error rises 0.0030→0.0069 (2.3×) while curvature stays fixed. The component term is independent and identifiable (Figure 8; supplementary S6). Against known truth the lesson repeats: shattering 19 clean landmarks into hundreds of pieces, the fixed clean-then-QEM recipe recovers the true component count to a median error of 1.5 parts on ≤20-part buildings but loses 16 on more complex ones, while preservation-QEM leaves component clouds in the hundreds (supplementary, S6).

    4.6 Gate Statistics

    Each accept is a paired difference over the 19 validation meshes; Bernstein bounds (S5) put only the first two accepts above the resolution floor. Eq. (6) prices one paired comparison; under candidate multiplicity and validation reuse it is a resolution scale, not an anytime-valid certificate—the strict gate and the untouched test set carry the endpoint claim. Trajectory-level evidence escapes the per-step floor (all 19 meshes improve; supplementary S1b).

    p̂=5/21≈0.24 (95% CI [0.08,0.47], Clopper–Pearson), Δ̂≈0.02, σ̂≈0.04; regression candidates: 0 of 21 groups (95% upper bound 0.143 by the Rule of Three). The predicted 24-group gain 24p̂Δ̂≈0.115 matches the observed 0.145.

    4.7 Component Ablation

    Table 3 reports the six single-factor arms (reflector, gate, retriever, selector) against the canonical configuration. The canonical run (same shuffle seed 44) is an independent rerun of the main campaign—6/24 accepted here vs. 5/24 there; its higher endpoint reflects single-run seed variance. Every arm starts from S₀=8.8358 under the identical 24-group protocol and 19-mesh held-out gate.

    Removing the gate is the only intervention that degrades the final score (-0.086): 17/24 proposals are accepted, including negative-gain edits, and the population drifts below its start—without selection pressure, edit frequency is not learning. Thresholding (ε=0.01, +0.141) sits just under canonical. Random-attribute edits still improve (the gate filters noise) but trail LLM attribution by 0.031; uniform retrieval (+0.103) and random selection (+0.124) fall below canonical—weighting and selection each contribute, neither load-bearing alone. Removing retrieval entirely stops evolution (all 24 groups inert). Across three shuffle seeds the canonical configuration ends at 8.983±0.011—every seed above baseline, zero regressed updates in 72 groups. Attribution’s 0.031 edge exceeds this spread, and equal-budget search lands below the deployed state: random, Bayesian, and evolutionary search over sixteen clean–QEM configurations peak at 8.67/8.59/8.69, a per-mesh oracle 8.75, deployed 8.83 (supplementary, S7).

    Per-arm details are in the supplementary (S4); sensitivity orders: gating removal (the unique degradation, -0.086 vs. S₀), retrieval removal (no learning), then, against the canonical endpoint, weighting ≈ selection ≈ reflection.

    4.8 Comparison with Vendor Baseline

    The commercial comparator is the Hunyuan3D vendor remesher (the low-poly output of the same pipeline that generated our training inputs), evaluated as released. Under the face-aligned verdict protocol (20 meshes scored at the vendor’s own face counts; supplementary, S2b), our outputs win 5, tie 13, and lose 2. The protocols answer different questions: verdict ties mean both outputs meet the spec, whereas the discriminative comparison is the budget-aligned composite (17 wins to 3 losses, p=0.001).

    Budget band: 1% with -50% tolerance; per-mesh metrics for any caliber are in the supplementary (S2b).

    A blind human study corroborates the verdict: the 24 training buildings are rendered as white-model blue-wireframe images, left/right randomized, and 9 independent participants (one session each, on a single workstation) pick the mesh that “looks cleaner and more regular, with fewer tiny or stretched triangles.” Aggregating 216 paired judgments: ours 168, vendor 48, tie 0; 8 of 9 subjects prefer ours (one prefers the vendor, 11–13); the one-sided sign test on the 8-to-1 split gives p=0.0195 (Wilcoxon p=0.0039). A test-set counterpart is not informative: the 20 unseen buildings are simple block-like geometry with visually indistinguishable outputs, so preference is reported on the training geometry where triangle quality is discriminable.

    4.9 Test-Set Evaluation

    On 20 unseen German city buildings (110k–800k faces, independently sourced; supplementary S2b), the trained skill keeps zero non-manifold edges on all 20 and consolidates each into a single dominant component (gate towers or residual dust aside, ≤195 faces, against main bodies of 800–7,400), leading the composite (mean 8.82 vs. 7.83; paired n=20: p=0.001, Wilcoxon p=0.0005, 17 wins 3 losses; bootstrap 95% CI of the mean gap [0.51,1.48]). The vendor trails on planarity (3.56 vs. 3.22), sharp edges (5.79 vs. 5.67) despite 1.5× our median faces, and worst-case distance (one-sided Hausdorff median 0.0105 vs. 0.0081); AutoRemesher fails on 45% of inputs. These medians are the delivered approximation scale: the contract’s ε fixes the significance scale (Section 3.1.1), not a per-output bound—at aggressive budgets the binding side is topology, which the outputs hold (zero non-manifold edges, single dominant component, all 20)—with full manifold metrics agreeing: self-intersections 1.5 vs. 14.5 median, degenerate faces 0/20 vs. 12/20, boundary edges 3/20 vs. 13/20 (supplementary, S2b). The zero-non-manifold transfer is direct evidence that “clean before decimating” generalizes (Figure 11).

    Retrieval-only inference (KNN replay, no LLM calls) is zero-non-manifold on 19/20 of the same meshes and trails the full loop (20/20) but beats the vendor—transferable knowledge lives in the experience database itself. The evolution claim is tested directly on this untouched set: the zero-shot baseline S₀ (empty database, full loop; 16/20 buildings completed before a runner fault) reaches a median composite of 8.61 against the trained skill’s 8.85—paired n=16, the trained skill wins 15 (Wilcoxon p=0.0001)—while S₀ itself holds zero non-manifold edges on 15/16, locating the evolution gain on held-out data in quality beyond topology.

    4.10 Cross-Domain Transfer

    We evaluate the same trained database (13 per-mesh records, all of Paris buildings) on nine non-architectural meshes (11k–250k faces; Table 2): retrieval replay, and a full zero-shot loop with an empty database. (i) The clean-then-decimate lesson does transfer: replay holds non-manifold ≤3 edges on 7/9 meshes (148 spurious edges total outside one failure case), and the zero-shot loop stays at ≤16 edges on 7/9 meshes (bunny, 112, toy duck, 332, excepted). These are Stanford bunny and dragon, a reconstructed cup, a thin shell, a sphere, a toy duck, and three LATO.2 examples, spanning organic surfaces, thin walls, and up to ∼1100 components. (ii) Numeric budget calibration does not transfer: replayed absolute budgets pin outputs near the 2,000-face floor regardless of scale, whereas zero-shot respects the 1% ratio on 6/9 (Figure 9a). (iii) Negative transfer is real: on the thin-wall toy duck, building experience yields 2,716 non-manifold edges versus 332 without (Figure 9b). Procedural knowledge is domain-robust; numeric calibration is domain-bound.

    4.11 Tool-Tier Evolution

    The knowledge-tier experiments address what the agent knows; this section evaluates the tool tier (§3.2.3) through a pre-registered three-stage experiment. Six candidate operators—parameter variants beyond the built-in enumeration—are each evaluated on three probe meshes under pre-registered criteria (zero non-manifold edges, faces within ±20%, Chamfer within 3× of built-in); all pass and are mounted (§3.2.3).

    On eight training meshes, every mounted operator competes under a pre-registered adoption rule (≥15% Chamfer gain, zero non-manifold edges): 0/8 adoptions in the primary run and 0/8 under two additional seeds (seeds 45 and 46); best per-mesh gain 0–3% (median 1%). The uniform zero adoption—cross-confirming the equal-budget kernel A/B (supplementary, S2)—shows this parameter space is exhausted; a productive tool tier must mount structurally different operators.

    In deployment, retrieval replay needs no LLM call (11.7 s per mesh on CPU, building test split); the full acquisition loop costs 4.3/12.2 min and the training campaign about a day (supplementary, S3). Under 12 single-dimension ±50% and 100 in-band weight perturbations the best accepted state beats the baseline in every one (18–19/19 per mesh; 100/100 positive); flipped micro-decisions are the marginal accepts near Δ_\min≈0.022, per the resolution law.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented RemeshingAgent, the first agent for repair-based decimation of generated building meshes: a budget decomposition delimiting the cliff and mandating clean-first; a drift bound calibrated from the training trace; and a two-tier self-evolving agent under one strict gate—without a single regressed update. Limitations: S^∗ is a declared closure, not observed ground truth; ablation arms are single-run (canonical: three seeds, 8.983±0.011, zero regressed updates); corpora are generated buildings, and numeric calibration does not transfer across domains (Section 4.10); zero non-manifold edges and one dominant component are necessary, not sufficient, manifold evidence—outputs are not certified structural geometry. We intend to extend the evaluation to broader mesh families and to ground skill acquisition in synthetic validation so that new operators can be validated without human-curated corpora. Code, skills, database, prompts, thresholds, seeds, and splits will be released—a step toward agents that verify their own improvement.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：表面看着完整，拓扑其实碎了：10³–10⁴ 个连通块、非流形薄墙。

要点：

  • 现象描述很具体：把生成的高模建筑网格压到原面数的 **0.5–1%** 会撞上硬上限——表面看着完整，但网格在拓扑上已经碎裂（10³–10⁴ 个连通块、非流形薄墙）；低于某个预算，实用的 decimator 全都「化了」：删部件、焊薄墙，或突破误差容限
  • 作者把它归因为**实例特有的病症**：哪些连通块是重要的、崩溃点在哪里，每个网格都不一样，因此没有单一固定算法，抽取就变成一个「清理 → 简化 → 验证」的迭代循环
  • RemeshingAgent 把这个循环做成**有验证契约的过程**：0.5% 预算下在拓扑上保持干净（QEM 与顶点聚类会化掉），在 20 个未见城市建筑上与商业重网格器持平，盲测 168:48 更受欢迎（p=0.0195）；训练出的技能以检索重放方式部署，**CPU 上每网格 11.7 秒、不调用 LLM**

为什么值得看：生成式资产进引擎最脏的一步就是「面数太高、拓扑烂」。这条把 agent 用在了正确的位置——不是生成，而是**带验证契约的修复循环**；更关键的是落地形态：训练完的技能变成检索重放，不烧 LLM 调用、CPU 11.7 秒一个网格，这才是能进资产管线的样子。

中文摘要：把生成得到的高模建筑网格激进简化到原面数的 0.5%–1% 会撞上一道硬上限：表面看起来依然完整，但网格在拓扑上已经碎裂——出现 10³ 到 10⁴ 个连通分量与非流形薄墙；一旦低于某个三角形预算，几乎所有实用 decimator 都会「化掉」：删掉部件、把薄墙焊在一起，或者突破误差容限。作者把根因归为实例特有的病症：哪些连通块是关键、崩溃点落在哪里，每个网格都不同，因此不存在单一固定算法，抽取必然成为「清理、简化、验证」的迭代循环。RemeshingAgent 把这个循环变成有验证契约的过程：在 0.5% 预算下，它在拓扑上保持干净而 QEM 与顶点聚类已经化掉；在 20 个未见过的城市建筑上与商业重网格器持平，并在 24 个训练建筑的九人单机盲测中以 168:48 更受欢迎（p=0.0195）。学到的技能以检索重放形式部署：CPU 上每个网格 11.7 秒，不产生任何 LLM 调用。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-18

RemeshingAgent: An Iterative Agent for Repair-Based Decimation of Generated Building Meshes

Abstract

Aggressively simplifying a generated high-poly building mesh to 0.5–1% of its faces confronts a hard limit. The surface looks complete, yet the mesh is topologically shattered: 10³–10⁴ connected components and non-manifold thin walls. Below a certain budget, every practical decimator “melts”: it deletes parts, welds thin walls, or breaks the error tolerance. We attribute this to instance-specific pathology: which components are significant and where the cliff sits vary from mesh to mesh, so no single fixed algorithm suffices, and decimation becomes an iterative loop of cleaning, simplifying, and verifying. We present RemeshingAgent, an agent that turns this loop into a validated process. The melting follows from a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms: below the component floor, no output satisfies the repair contract, and cleaning first is the theory-mandated response. At a 0.5% budget the agent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, and on the 24 training buildings a nine-participant single-workstation blind study prefers our outputs 168:48 (p=0.0195, subject-level sign test). The trained skill deploys as retrieval replay: 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU, with no LLM calls.

Keywords: mesh decimation, topology repair, LLM agents, validation-gated evolution, geometry processing, self-evolving systems

1 Introduction

Mesh decimation is a fundamental operation in interactive rendering, digital twins, and asset pipelines, where high-poly meshes must be reduced to lightweight counterparts. In generated building meshes, a striking discrepancy exists between appearance and structure: the surface appears complete and geometrically sound, yet the underlying mesh is topologically shattered into 10³–10⁴ connected components with abundant non-manifold thin walls (Figure 1, left; Figure 2, left). Because the visible topology is already satisfactory and only the face count is excessive, the natural objective is repair-based decimation. This work addresses the aggressive regime of this problem, namely budgets of 0.5–1% of the input faces on generated building meshes.

Existing strategies share a common limitation: all assume that a single fixed policy suffices to reach the target budget. At aggressive budgets this assumption fails—every preservation-contract decimator we test eventually melts on fragmented inputs, manifested as part deletion, wall welding, or tolerance violation. Existing theory neither predicts where melting must occur—its budget results cover smooth convex bodies [10, 12] and plane curves [10] but not fragmented piecewise-smooth surfaces—nor addresses whether a self-improving decimator converges or how much validation evidence suffices to certify improvement. The absence of theoretical guidance is consequential: each mesh shatters differently, rendering run-once policies inadequate; manual orchestration of the cleaning-simplification-verification loop is prohibitively tedious; and unguided agent-based approaches are unstable, as erroneous early decisions propagate irrecoverably. Furthermore, once the decimation process is governed by a strict validation gate, it becomes a drift process whose convergence can be quantified.

Our central insight is that the melting point is not an algorithmic artifact but a geometric property of the input itself, and therefore a theory-mandated strategy can be derived from measured geometry rather than discovered through blind search. We therefore present RemeshingAgent, an agent for repair-based decimation of generated building meshes that combines a frozen geometry engine with a validation-gated evolution discipline [35]. The agent operationalizes the decimation craft as a validated Clean–Execute–Verify–Reflect loop (Figure 1, center–right): it cleans the fragmented input, executes decimation pipelines on the frozen engine, verifies candidates against held-out geometric scores and visual inspection, and reflects on the trajectory to refine its skill document and operator vocabulary, accepting modifications only when they strictly improve held-out validation.

Empirically, trained on 24 commercial high-poly building meshes with 19 held-out validation meshes, the agent improves its gate score monotonically from 8.8358 to 8.9811 across five accepted updates; deployed inference replays the retrieved pipelines on CPU in 11.7 s per mesh without LLM or VLM calls.

1.1 Contributions

  • •

    We present RemeshingAgent, the first agent for repair-based decimation of generated building meshes, turning fragment clouds of thousands of components into single clean components (Figure 2, right).

  • •

    We give the agent a self-evolving discipline that tunes the skill document and the operator vocabulary along the theory’s direction chain under a strict held-out validation gate, improving by +0.145 gate score without a single regressed update.

  • •

    We prove the theory behind both, a budget decomposition prescribing the clean-first direction, and a component threshold below which no output satisfies the repair contract.

    • First, the triangle budget admits a decomposition into a curvature term A_curv/ε, a crease term A_crease/√ε, and a component floor 4n_sig, with the maximum determining the active constraint (Theorem 3.1). Second, below the component threshold, no output satisfying the repair contract exists, transforming melting from an empirical observation into a prediction with a precise location, and establishing cleaning as the theory-mandated response (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3). Third, under an explicit improvement assumption, the gated evolution admits an additive-drift hitting-time bound together with a resolution law characterizing the validation-set size required to resolve improvements (He–Yao [14], Eq. (6)), with all parameters estimated from the agent’s training trace.

    2 Related Work

    LLM Agents for 3D. LLM-based agents have been applied to 3D generation [27] and procedural modeling. ReAct [37] and Voyager [30] establish observation-action loops; PhotoAgent [36], aDSL [31], and CADDesigner [8] couple LLM planning with graphics tools—none evolves its own operator vocabulary under validation discipline, establishes convergence guarantees, or addresses repair-based decimation at aggressive budgets. Our approach treats the entire remeshing policy as a trainable object, with convergence analyzed in Section 3.2.

    Level of Detail and Decimation. Classical approximation theory characterizes the triangulation complexity of smooth surfaces: the Θ(∫√|K| dA/ε) face-count bound for convex surfaces [10, 12], Fejes Tóth’s optimal polygonal curves [10], and Erickson’s sampling complexity [7]—but none of these addresses the repair-contract minimum face count of fragmented piecewise-smooth surfaces; field reports [21] document such failures without a theoretical account. Preservation-based decimators maintain input connectivity (quadric error metrics [11], progressive meshes [15], vertex clustering, recent variants for weak features and artist quad topology [3, 18]; surveys [6, 5, 24]), whereas reconstruction rebuilds the surface from samples (voxel hulls, alpha wrap, cell cuts [34], generative remeshers [22]). City-scale LOD frameworks [4] prescribe level contents but not decimation limits; our budget law supplies this missing quantitative layer. Head-to-head comparisons with these robust baselines appear in the supplementary (S11–S12). Our two-contract analysis (supplementary, S10) predicts when each family prevails; learned representations [25, 26, 13, 19] need training sets incompatible with our single-mesh setting.

    Self-Evolving Agents. Self-improving frameworks (Reflexion [29], Gödel Agent [38]) update task and meta policies; prompt optimizers (DSPy [17], TextGrad [39], GEPA [1]) refine instructions. SkillOpt [35] contributes the discipline we adopt—rollout batches, bounded edits, validation gating, a rejected-edit buffer—for a frozen geometry engine. RE-TRAC [40] addresses cross-trajectory state compression, and complementary work distills skills from multimodal resources [9] and evaluates them via checklists [20]. E-value gating [33, 28] and validation-gated skill evolution [32] provide error-control guarantees but leave open the power analysis behind our resolution law (Eq. (6)) and our planner’s multi-candidate selection; our convergence analysis builds on the additive-drift theorem [14] and hitting-time bounds [2].

    3 The Geometry of Decimation

    Section 3.1 derives the agent’s direction from measured geometry, and Section 3.2 adds a self-evolving loop that verifies every candidate against held-out scores.

    3.1 The Minimal Triangle Budget

    A generated building’s mesh arrives shattered into 10³–10⁴ components (Figure 2, left); the objective is repair-based decimation—consolidating 8,223 components into one at 0.87% of the input faces (right).

    3.1.1 The Topology-Preserving Contract

    We model the input S as piecewise-smooth with n components of total genus g; a mesh T is an ε-approximation if δ_H(S,T)≤ε diag(S). Topology is measured against the intended surfaceS^∗, the welding closure of S at the seam scale δ₀: the intended building parts, pairwise separated well beyond ε diag(S) at our budgets. S^∗ is a declared reference computed from S alone—generated assets carry no pre-fragmentation ground truth—so preservation is always relative to S^∗: welding and dust removal repair S toward S^∗ by definition; Section 4.9 audits this structure component-wise. Under the preservation contract (A), T must satisfy the tolerance and T≅S^∗ (homeomorphic)—welding is repair, not a topology change (raw-input preservation would force F≥4n if every component were a closed shell—a floor no budget meets). In the agent the welding threshold defaults to this seam scale, 0.1% of the diagonal, and adopted pipelines kept it throughout. Under the reconstruction contract (B), the output is rebuilt from samples (voxel hulls, alpha wrap, generative remeshers [22]); its budget law differs. A component is ε-significant if its diameter exceeds 2ε diag(S); deleting it violates the approximation. Significant components are closed shells (thin-walled solids); boundary components admit lower floors (supplementary, S10).

    3.1.2 The Budget Law

    Theorem 3.1(Minimal triangle budget, decomposition).

    Under the preservation contract, as the absolute tolerance ε_abs=ε diag(S)→0,

    F_\min \asymp \max (c₁A_curv/ε_abs, c₂A_crease/√ε_abs, 4 n_sig, c₄g),

    		(1)

    where A_curv=∫_Sₛₘₒₒₜₕ√|K| dA and A_crease=∑ⱼ∫_Cⱼ√κ ds, and c₁,c₂,c₄ depend only on the smoothness constants; \asymp is two-sided asymptotic equivalence.

    Each term is classical [10, 12, 23, 16]. Developable patches (K=0)—cylindrical towers—cost Θ(ε_abs^-1/2) and fold into the crease term (prism bound π√R/(2ε_abs)); the distinct exponents (ε_abs⁻¹, ε_abs^-1/2, ε_abs⁰) make the decomposition identifiable. For predominantly planar, low-genus buildings, Eq. (1) reduces to

    F_\min \asymp \max (c₂ (A_crease)/(√ε_abs), 4 n_sig),

    		(2)

    so classical analysis alone predicts near-free decimation—and the missed component floor 4n_sig is what makes every practical decimator we test melt on generated ones; the operational reading—clean first, weld, then decimate—follows (Figure 2, right).

    Theorem 3.1 is asymptotic; at 0.5–1% budgets we claim only the regional structure as evidence, validated in Section 4.3.

    3.1.3 The Operational Limit

    Fitted per algorithm family with a calibration factor ĉ,

    F̂(S,ε)=ĉ₁(A_curv)/(ε diag)+ĉ₂(A_crease)/(√ε diag)+4n_sig,

    		(3)

    Equations (1), (2), and (4) use the absolute tolerance ε_abs defined above; ε elsewhere is the contract’s dimensionless relative tolerance, so every term is a face count. n_sig is measured on the post-cleaning, welded estimate of S^∗ (the surface the contract references), with the 0.1% area threshold (rank-consistent with the diameter caliber, ρ=0.68–0.89). Fitting QEM and clustering sweeps gives ĉ∈[1.1×,2.4×] (Section 4.3): an additive working form, its max-to-sum gap absorbed by ĉ—calibrated on the sweep corpus, not predicted beyond it; the tested content is the exponent structure and the cliff shift, and a split-half probe predicts held-out error floors rank-consistently (Spearman ρ=0.83 median; supplementary, S6).

    Theorem 3.2(Component cliff).

    Let S^∗ have n_sigε-significant components, pairwise separated by more than 2ε diag(S)—true of intended building parts at our budgets—and take a budget

    F

    		(4)

    Then no mesh T with at most F triangles satisfies both δ_H(S^∗,T)≤ε diag(S) and T≅S^∗: the separation keeps the components’ ε diag(S)-neighborhoods disjoint, so no triangle serves two components, and the piece of T standing for each closed shell Sⱼ pays its own floor,

    F ≥ ∑ₖ₌₁^n_sig\max (4, c₁A_curv(Sₖ)/ε_abs) = F_comp > F,

    		(5)

    The bound is combinatorial, not statistical; it holds for every algorithm (Figure 3; proof and breaking-mode classification in the supplementary, S10).

    Corollary 3.3(The value of cleaning).

    A component is ε-deletable if every point of it lies within ε diag(S) of the retained surface; deleting such components preserves the ε-approximation. Dust is deletable by construction—shards of the intended shell—so cleaning lowers n_sig from n to n_sig≪n and F_comp accordingly. Cleaning before decimation is the theory-mandated first move (supplementary, S7).

    From fragments to one component. Three theory-licensed moves: delete dust (Corollary 3.3), weld vertices closer than δ≤ε diag (perturbs by at most δ), then pay the budget law at the reduced n_sig—realized by the agent’s clean_repair (conservative cleanup, or aggressive welding plus small-component removal), stopping before the threshold rather than melting (Section 4.4); the operators’ own perturbation is 0.0009–0.0017 normalized Chamfer, within tolerance.

    3.2 Convergence of Validation-Gated Skill Evolution

    Figure 4 illustrates the loop: the direction of Section 3.1 fixes what to do but not its parameters, which the agent tunes by evolving a skill document s through reflect-and-gate cycles. With selection set Dₛₑₗ and deterministic reward r(s,m), the empirical potential is V(s)=target-(1)/(|Dₛₑₗ|)∑ₘr(s,m), with hitting time T_ε=\min{t:V(sₜ)≤ε}. If the reflect kernel Q(s→s^′) satisfies condition (H1)—improving V by at least Δ with probability ≥p_\min (supplementary, S10)—and the gate uses strict acceptance with elite retention, the additive-drift bound of He–Yao [14] yields 𝔼[ T_ε|s₀ ]≤V(s₀)/(p_\minΔ); calibrated on our system, it agrees in order of magnitude with the observed trajectory—a consistency check, not an independent prediction. The per-group law pΔ is the testable content.

    3.2.1 The Validation Gate

    The reward is a scalarized score G(M;M₀)=∑ᵢ₌₁⁶wᵢ gᵢ with w=(0.30,0.15,0.20,0.05,0.20,0.10) over face-count, manifold, shape-preservation, planarity, sharp-edge, and compactness dimensions (calibrated in Section 4.2; supplementary S9). The gate’s statistical power limits the smallest per-step improvement it can resolve—the sub-Gaussian resolution scale

    Δ_\min(n) = σ̂√(2\ln(1/α))/(n),

    		(6)

    with σ̂ the cross-mesh std of paired differences.

    3.2.2 Forward and Backward Passes

    The harness returns scored trajectories (τ,r)=h(M_geo,M₀,s); at round k the planner samples B candidates and submodular selection picks a diverse subset. A pipeline template in s is the parameterized chain of Section 3.1 made executable. An LLM reflector proposes discrete text edits over the success/failure split, guided by a cross-trial parameter→reward contrast table; accepted edits are capped by Lₖ (the “learning rate”), yielding candidate s̃ₖ, gated on the held-out set:

    sₖ₊₁=s̃ₖ\iffrₛₑₗ(s̃ₖ)>rₛₑₗ(sₖ);

    		(7)

    otherwise sₖ₊₁=sₖ (elite retention); a pre-check skips “inert” candidates. Candidates run in an isolated read-only copy, so rejections never enter the deployed skill; the best score is non-decreasing and the initial skill is a safe lower bound (supplementary, S10). Because Dₛₑₗ is reused, the deployed skill is re-scored on a test set it never touches (Section 4.9): test numbers measure transfer, not gate fitness.

    3.2.3 The Rejected-Edit Buffer and the Tool Tier

    Rejected edits are retained as negative feedback; at epoch boundaries a meta-reflector writes longitudinal guidance into a protected slow-update region. Skill training optimizes what the agent knows but cannot escape its operator vocabulary; the tool tier removes that ceiling—an LLM proposes new operators, each passing a feasibility probe, with adoption adjudicated by the ordinary gate (Section 4.11)—and no gate is ever relaxed.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Datasets and Baselines

    The training set comprises 24 high-poly Hunyuan3D building meshes (0.9M–1.5M faces, 7,000–21,000 components), each decimated to three budgets (1%, 0.75%, 0.5%); the validation set holds 19 landmark meshes (∼740K faces) for gate evaluation; and the theory corpus covers the same 43 meshes, 12 of which also run QEM/clustering sweeps at eight budgets (10%–0.1%). We evaluate on every mesh in each split: failed epochs are scored, all 19 validation meshes enter every gate round, no mesh is added, removed, or re-weighted after results, and group order follows a pre-registered seed.

    Five method families are compared. Direct QEM is quadric-error decimation (pymeshlab, preserve-topology enabled); vertex clustering is meshing_decimation_clustering; the zoo additionally reports QEM with preserve-topology disabled (the only configuration reaching aggressive budgets). LATO.2 [22] is a learned generative remesher served on its released inference server with the vertex budget specified directly; our pipeline and all preservation baselines are CPU-only. The reconstruction pipeline chains voxel shell → nvdiff deformation → alpha wrap → refined QEM as the contract-B representative. RemeshingAgent runs zero-shot (S₀) and trained (S_K, K=24 groups).

    All experiments run on CPU (pymeshlab, trimesh, Open3D); the LLM planner and reflector employ MiniMax-M3, and the VLM bonus is disabled in training for deterministic evaluation. Reward weights derive from a calibration episode (an initial planarity weight admitted degenerate slivers); recalibration (shape/sharp reweighting, a non-linear cap >7.0, a degenerate-face penalty) aligned gate decisions with perceptual quality, robust under ±50% and 100 in-band perturbations (supplementary, S9).

    4.2 Self-Evolution of the Agent

    Figure 5 shows the gate score over 24 groups: S₀=8.8358→8.9811 (+0.145) through 5 accepted updates; all 19 validation meshes improve (supplementary, S1b), the smallest gain +0.021. The drift law predicts 24 pΔ≈0.115 vs. observed +0.145.

    4.3 The Two-Regime Structure

    QEM and clustering sweeps (12 meshes × 8 budgets) exhibit a two-regime structure (Figure 6). On clean meshes, error follows a power law with exponent 0.13–0.40 (corr(\logA,\logbudget)=0.95); on fragmented meshes, error exhibits a floor regime with exponent ≈0 for the melting families, decreasing only until the component term 4n_sig of Theorem 3.1 becomes dominant. The cliff position shifts with the predicted F_comp, consistent with component-dominated breaking. Both algorithm families exhibit identical behavior, indicating that the regional structure is a geometric property rather than an algorithmic artifact.

    4.4 The Five-Family Zoo

    All five families target the same 0.5% budget on identical fragmented meshes, measured by normalized Chamfer (50k area-weighted samples, symmetric bidirectional mean, normalized by the output diagonal). Reached face counts differ and are part of the comparison: preservation-enabled QEM cannot reach the target, whereas melting configurations reach it by deleting and welding. The agent achieves the best fidelity at 0.0015 (24/24); the reconstruction pipeline 0.005–0.009 (watertight); LATO.2 0.003–0.011, floored at low budgets by its generative prior; bare QEM and clustering 0.05–0.18, melting. An equal-cleaning control separates recipe from adaptation: conservative clean-then-QEM reaches the budget on 1/24, the fixed aggressive recipe on 19/24 (0.0014 median Chamfer on hits, clean topology)—cleaning carries most of the effect; the rest is per-mesh variation fixed parameters miss and selection covers (the agent: 24/24; supplementary, S7). The topology metrics and Section 4.5 carry the preservation verdict. Figure 7 shows the same separation per mesh.

    A regime-conditional stress test makes the scope explicit (Table 1): on Hunyuan-style shattered inputs the method is necessary, while on the independently-sourced test buildings every arm completes at the same relative budgets—and aggressive cleaning induces its own melt, stalling QEM on 2/20 meshes with 760k/660k faces remaining; per-mesh selection avoids both failure modes. The Think-stage fragmentation statistics identify the regime before any run.

    The ordering matches the two-contract prediction (supplementary, S10): preservation methods pay the component tax or melt, and the agent’s cleaning reduces n_sig to the preservation side. The epoch-3 cliff-avoidance response (face-count dimension -4 at 0.5% budget, Chamfer holding at 0.0015) and PolyFit’s contract-B verdict (18/20 test meshes complete, immaculate topology, median Chamfer 0.029 vs. ours 0.001; supplementary, S7) complete the picture.

    4.5 Isolating the Component Term

    Controlled fragmentation is applied to a clean constant-curvature mesh (∫√|K|dA≈26.2; N=1,13,35,90 pieces). At the most aggressive budget (0.1%), normalized Chamfer error rises 0.0030→0.0069 (2.3×) while curvature stays fixed. The component term is independent and identifiable (Figure 8; supplementary S6). Against known truth the lesson repeats: shattering 19 clean landmarks into hundreds of pieces, the fixed clean-then-QEM recipe recovers the true component count to a median error of 1.5 parts on ≤20-part buildings but loses 16 on more complex ones, while preservation-QEM leaves component clouds in the hundreds (supplementary, S6).

    4.6 Gate Statistics

    Each accept is a paired difference over the 19 validation meshes; Bernstein bounds (S5) put only the first two accepts above the resolution floor. Eq. (6) prices one paired comparison; under candidate multiplicity and validation reuse it is a resolution scale, not an anytime-valid certificate—the strict gate and the untouched test set carry the endpoint claim. Trajectory-level evidence escapes the per-step floor (all 19 meshes improve; supplementary S1b).

    p̂=5/21≈0.24 (95% CI [0.08,0.47], Clopper–Pearson), Δ̂≈0.02, σ̂≈0.04; regression candidates: 0 of 21 groups (95% upper bound 0.143 by the Rule of Three). The predicted 24-group gain 24p̂Δ̂≈0.115 matches the observed 0.145.

    4.7 Component Ablation

    Table 3 reports the six single-factor arms (reflector, gate, retriever, selector) against the canonical configuration. The canonical run (same shuffle seed 44) is an independent rerun of the main campaign—6/24 accepted here vs. 5/24 there; its higher endpoint reflects single-run seed variance. Every arm starts from S₀=8.8358 under the identical 24-group protocol and 19-mesh held-out gate.

    Removing the gate is the only intervention that degrades the final score (-0.086): 17/24 proposals are accepted, including negative-gain edits, and the population drifts below its start—without selection pressure, edit frequency is not learning. Thresholding (ε=0.01, +0.141) sits just under canonical. Random-attribute edits still improve (the gate filters noise) but trail LLM attribution by 0.031; uniform retrieval (+0.103) and random selection (+0.124) fall below canonical—weighting and selection each contribute, neither load-bearing alone. Removing retrieval entirely stops evolution (all 24 groups inert). Across three shuffle seeds the canonical configuration ends at 8.983±0.011—every seed above baseline, zero regressed updates in 72 groups. Attribution’s 0.031 edge exceeds this spread, and equal-budget search lands below the deployed state: random, Bayesian, and evolutionary search over sixteen clean–QEM configurations peak at 8.67/8.59/8.69, a per-mesh oracle 8.75, deployed 8.83 (supplementary, S7).

    Per-arm details are in the supplementary (S4); sensitivity orders: gating removal (the unique degradation, -0.086 vs. S₀), retrieval removal (no learning), then, against the canonical endpoint, weighting ≈ selection ≈ reflection.

    4.8 Comparison with Vendor Baseline

    The commercial comparator is the Hunyuan3D vendor remesher (the low-poly output of the same pipeline that generated our training inputs), evaluated as released. Under the face-aligned verdict protocol (20 meshes scored at the vendor’s own face counts; supplementary, S2b), our outputs win 5, tie 13, and lose 2. The protocols answer different questions: verdict ties mean both outputs meet the spec, whereas the discriminative comparison is the budget-aligned composite (17 wins to 3 losses, p=0.001).

    Budget band: 1% with -50% tolerance; per-mesh metrics for any caliber are in the supplementary (S2b).

    A blind human study corroborates the verdict: the 24 training buildings are rendered as white-model blue-wireframe images, left/right randomized, and 9 independent participants (one session each, on a single workstation) pick the mesh that “looks cleaner and more regular, with fewer tiny or stretched triangles.” Aggregating 216 paired judgments: ours 168, vendor 48, tie 0; 8 of 9 subjects prefer ours (one prefers the vendor, 11–13); the one-sided sign test on the 8-to-1 split gives p=0.0195 (Wilcoxon p=0.0039). A test-set counterpart is not informative: the 20 unseen buildings are simple block-like geometry with visually indistinguishable outputs, so preference is reported on the training geometry where triangle quality is discriminable.

    4.9 Test-Set Evaluation

    On 20 unseen German city buildings (110k–800k faces, independently sourced; supplementary S2b), the trained skill keeps zero non-manifold edges on all 20 and consolidates each into a single dominant component (gate towers or residual dust aside, ≤195 faces, against main bodies of 800–7,400), leading the composite (mean 8.82 vs. 7.83; paired n=20: p=0.001, Wilcoxon p=0.0005, 17 wins 3 losses; bootstrap 95% CI of the mean gap [0.51,1.48]). The vendor trails on planarity (3.56 vs. 3.22), sharp edges (5.79 vs. 5.67) despite 1.5× our median faces, and worst-case distance (one-sided Hausdorff median 0.0105 vs. 0.0081); AutoRemesher fails on 45% of inputs. These medians are the delivered approximation scale: the contract’s ε fixes the significance scale (Section 3.1.1), not a per-output bound—at aggressive budgets the binding side is topology, which the outputs hold (zero non-manifold edges, single dominant component, all 20)—with full manifold metrics agreeing: self-intersections 1.5 vs. 14.5 median, degenerate faces 0/20 vs. 12/20, boundary edges 3/20 vs. 13/20 (supplementary, S2b). The zero-non-manifold transfer is direct evidence that “clean before decimating” generalizes (Figure 11).

    Retrieval-only inference (KNN replay, no LLM calls) is zero-non-manifold on 19/20 of the same meshes and trails the full loop (20/20) but beats the vendor—transferable knowledge lives in the experience database itself. The evolution claim is tested directly on this untouched set: the zero-shot baseline S₀ (empty database, full loop; 16/20 buildings completed before a runner fault) reaches a median composite of 8.61 against the trained skill’s 8.85—paired n=16, the trained skill wins 15 (Wilcoxon p=0.0001)—while S₀ itself holds zero non-manifold edges on 15/16, locating the evolution gain on held-out data in quality beyond topology.

    4.10 Cross-Domain Transfer

    We evaluate the same trained database (13 per-mesh records, all of Paris buildings) on nine non-architectural meshes (11k–250k faces; Table 2): retrieval replay, and a full zero-shot loop with an empty database. (i) The clean-then-decimate lesson does transfer: replay holds non-manifold ≤3 edges on 7/9 meshes (148 spurious edges total outside one failure case), and the zero-shot loop stays at ≤16 edges on 7/9 meshes (bunny, 112, toy duck, 332, excepted). These are Stanford bunny and dragon, a reconstructed cup, a thin shell, a sphere, a toy duck, and three LATO.2 examples, spanning organic surfaces, thin walls, and up to ∼1100 components. (ii) Numeric budget calibration does not transfer: replayed absolute budgets pin outputs near the 2,000-face floor regardless of scale, whereas zero-shot respects the 1% ratio on 6/9 (Figure 9a). (iii) Negative transfer is real: on the thin-wall toy duck, building experience yields 2,716 non-manifold edges versus 332 without (Figure 9b). Procedural knowledge is domain-robust; numeric calibration is domain-bound.

    4.11 Tool-Tier Evolution

    The knowledge-tier experiments address what the agent knows; this section evaluates the tool tier (§3.2.3) through a pre-registered three-stage experiment. Six candidate operators—parameter variants beyond the built-in enumeration—are each evaluated on three probe meshes under pre-registered criteria (zero non-manifold edges, faces within ±20%, Chamfer within 3× of built-in); all pass and are mounted (§3.2.3).

    On eight training meshes, every mounted operator competes under a pre-registered adoption rule (≥15% Chamfer gain, zero non-manifold edges): 0/8 adoptions in the primary run and 0/8 under two additional seeds (seeds 45 and 46); best per-mesh gain 0–3% (median 1%). The uniform zero adoption—cross-confirming the equal-budget kernel A/B (supplementary, S2)—shows this parameter space is exhausted; a productive tool tier must mount structurally different operators.

    In deployment, retrieval replay needs no LLM call (11.7 s per mesh on CPU, building test split); the full acquisition loop costs 4.3/12.2 min and the training campaign about a day (supplementary, S3). Under 12 single-dimension ±50% and 100 in-band weight perturbations the best accepted state beats the baseline in every one (18–19/19 per mesh; 100/100 positive); flipped micro-decisions are the marginal accepts near Δ_\min≈0.022, per the resolution law.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented RemeshingAgent, the first agent for repair-based decimation of generated building meshes: a budget decomposition delimiting the cliff and mandating clean-first; a drift bound calibrated from the training trace; and a two-tier self-evolving agent under one strict gate—without a single regressed update. Limitations: S^∗ is a declared closure, not observed ground truth; ablation arms are single-run (canonical: three seeds, 8.983±0.011, zero regressed updates); corpora are generated buildings, and numeric calibration does not transfer across domains (Section 4.10); zero non-manifold edges and one dominant component are necessary, not sufficient, manifold evidence—outputs are not certified structural geometry. We intend to extend the evaluation to broader mesh families and to ground skill acquisition in synthetic validation so that new operators can be validated without human-curated corpora. Code, skills, database, prompts, thresholds, seeds, and splits will be released—a step toward agents that verify their own improvement.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: System-1 世界模型该长什么样：Frame First, Decode Once 用「先给坐标系、再一次解码」换实时 ｜ Frame First, Decode Once: Object-Centric Coordinates and Single-Pass Decoding for System-1 World Models
item.description:
一句话：单次前向解出全部量化坐标的 primitive 解码器，可以当快速的 System-1 世界模型用。

要点：

  • 对象是「单次前向」的 primitive 解码器（如 LocateAnything、VFlash）：一次前向就预测出一个几何 primitive 的全部量化坐标 token，因此适合做**快速的 System-1 视觉规划**
  • 论文研究的是：当这种解码器充当 System-1 世界模型——即一个由动作条件驱动、按预测结果给候选动作排序的快速预测器——**什么才是真正重要的**
  • 实验在 ManiSkill3 PushT-v1（512 个留出测试族、8,192 次 rollout）等环境上做，聚焦「先定坐标系、只解码一次」这两个设计选择

为什么值得看：「快」和「准」在运行时规划里是硬冲突。这条把结论落在两个具体设计选择上（对象中心坐标 + 单次解码），比泛泛地说「用更小的模型」有用得多——对做 AI 决策进引擎的团队，是可直接试的工程取舍。

中文摘要：LocateAnything、VFlash 这类「单次前向」的 primitive 解码器，能在一次前向中预测出一个几何 primitive 的全部量化坐标 token，因而适合充当快速的 System-1 视觉规划模块。这篇研究的是：当这样的解码器被用作 System-1 世界模型——一个由动作条件驱动、通过预测结果来给候选动作排序的快速预测器——究竟哪些设计最重要。作者围绕「先确定对象中心坐标系」与「只解码一次」这两个选择展开实验，并在 ManiSkill3 PushT-v1（512 个留出测试族、8,192 次 rollout）等环境上验证。结论的价值在于把「实时世界模型」拆成了可执行的工程选择，而不是笼统地追求更小的模型。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-18

Frame First, Decode Once: Object-Centric Coordinates and Single-Pass Decoding for System-1 World Models

Abstract

Single-pass primitive decoders such as LocateAnything and VFlash predict all quantized coordinate tokens of a geometric primitive in one forward pass, enabling fast, System-1 visual planning. We study what matters when such a decoder serves as a System-1 world model: a fast action-conditioned predictor that ranks candidate pushes by their predicted outcome. On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (512 held-out test families, 8,192 rollouts) and on human demonstrations from lerobot/pusht (2,384 test windows), we compare decoders, training losses, rigid-body projections and coordinate frames, using matched checkpoints, hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm correction. Two factors of similar size dominate. First, expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object’s initial pose lowers decision regret by 1.9×–2.2× for each of five decoders (p_Holm(9)<0.005), and the object-frame model trained on 128 families matches the world-frame model trained on 512. Second, single-pass decoding outperforms iterative decoding: in the object frame, single-pass heads reach 0.020–0.021 regret at 1.6–1.8 ms per decision, against 0.046 for 10-step DDIM diffusion and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression at 10.3 and 12.9 ms. The choice among single-pass heads has no measurable effect on regret, and our registered hypothesis that the frame effect exceeds the decoder spread is not supported (0.0345 vs. 0.0389 regret). Soft-token expectation with an end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection gives the lowest trajectory error (11.35 px on ManiSkill3, 3.78 px on lerobot/pusht), exact rigid-body consistency, and lower regret than diffusion at every budget from 4 to 50 DDIM steps, at 3×–29× lower latency.

Index Terms:

World models, robotic manipulation, parallel decoding, coordinate frames, SE(2) equivariance, orthogonal Procrustes, diffusion models.

I Introduction

Action-conditioned world models let an agent evaluate candidate actions by predicting their outcomes before acting [3, 18, 19]. A model that is queried inside the control loop, a fast “System-1” model in the sense of Kahneman [20], must do two things: run within a few milliseconds, and rank the candidate actions correctly. Vision-language and vision-language-action models represent geometry as sequences of quantized coordinate tokens ⟨0⟩…⟨1000⟩[16, 17, 15]. Decoding such a trajectory token by token takes one sequential step per token, i.e. P×C steps for P time steps of C coordinates (100 for P=C=10). Even a coarser autoregression that emits one time step at a time, as in our baseline, needs about 12 ms per decision for a 3.8M-parameter model with a key-value cache, against about 1 ms for a single forward pass.

LocateAnything [2] and VFlash [1] remove this bottleneck. Once the type of a primitive is known, its coordinate layout is fixed, so all of its coordinate slots can be predicted jointly in a single forward pass: slot positions attend to each other and to the preceding context. VFlash applies this flash primitive decoding (FPD) to visual plans such as robot trajectories and driving waypoints, and trains the slots with token-level cross-entropy.

We study single-pass slot decoders used as System-1 world models for contact-rich manipulation. The model predicts the trajectory of a pushed T-block under each of four candidate actions, and the agent picks the action with the highest predicted utility. Prior work leaves several design choices open, which we phrase as five questions:

  • 1.

    How does single-pass decoding compare with iterative decoders (DDIM diffusion, autoregression) built on the same backbone and data?

  • 2.

    Does supervising a soft-token expectation with a metric loss improve on token cross-entropy?

  • 3.

    Should rigid-body consistency come from direct SE(2) pose tokens or from redundant keypoints followed by a Procrustes projection?

  • 4.

    Should the projection be applied only at test time or trained end to end?

  • 5.

    Which matters more for decision quality, the coordinate frame or the decoder?

    • We answer these questions on ManiSkill3 PushT-v1[4] and on the human demonstrations of lerobot/pusht[3, 5]. The study has three stages. A benchmark of twelve models was pre-registered before its test split was generated. Exploratory controls followed, including the object-frame models. Finally, a 2×5 frame × decoder grid was registered after the exploratory object-frame result and run as a confirmatory replication on the same test families. Projected and unprojected variants of each head are evaluated on the same checkpoints, and each table of paired tests applies one Holm correction across all competitors it reports.

    Our findings are:

  • •

    The coordinate frame. Expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object’s initial pose halves decision regret for every decoder we tested and gives roughly 4× sample efficiency. Controls on the RGB input show that the gain comes from the coordinate frame and not from removing the image.

  • •

    Single-pass versus iterative decoding. On the same backbone, single-pass heads have 2.3×–2.9× lower regret than a 10-step DDIM diffusion model and a KV-cached autoregressive model, and are 6×–8× faster. Which single-pass head is used makes no measurable difference to regret. The frame effect and the decoder effect are of comparable size, so our registered hypothesis that the frame dominates is not supported.

  • •

    Procrustes-FPD. Soft-token expectation followed by a closed-form 2D Kabsch projection gives exact rigid-body consistency and the lowest trajectory error. Redundant keypoints with Procrustes fitting outperform direct SE(2) tokens in the world frame. We characterize when to apply the projection at test time and when to train through it, and we relate this trade-off to the rank of the projection’s Jacobian.

    • We also report an implementation error in our original diffusion baseline, its correction, and how it changed the results (Section V-D, Appendix A).

    Throughout, “VFlash-style CE head” denotes our reimplementation of VFlash’s slot loss and decoding inside the same 2M-parameter backbone as every other model. We do not evaluate NVIDIA’s released model, and our results concern design choices for small action-conditioned predictors, not the VFlash system.

    II Related Work

    II-AParallel Primitive Decoding

    LocateAnything [2] decodes each bounding box or point of a grounding answer as one unit in a single step, and VFlash [1] extends this idea to visual plans on top of a speculative drafter. Given the context of a frozen vision-language model, VFlash appends the B positions of a primitive block. Positions inside the block attend to each other and to the context before the block, and all are predicted in one forward pass. Primitive positions are trained with token-level cross-entropy (Eq. 4 of [1], with unit weights on primitive positions):

    L_CE=-1/PC∑ₜ₌₁^P∑_c=1^C\logP_θ (z^*_t,c|x₀,a),

    		(1)

    where, in our setting, z^*_t,c=round(1000·y^*_t,c/512)∈{0,…,1000}. Eq. (1) removes the latency of autoregressive decoding. It is, however, indifferent to the distance between bins: predicting ⟨501⟩ or ⟨999⟩ for a target ⟨500⟩ incurs the same loss as long as both receive the same probability.

    II-BSoft-Bin Regression and Keypoint-Based Pose Estimation

    Taking the expectation over discrete bins so that a continuous metric loss can be applied was introduced in integral human pose regression [6], differentiable spatial-to-numerical transforms [7], and Distribution Focal Loss for bounding-box edges [8]. In 6-DoF pose estimation and point-cloud registration, predicting redundant keypoints and fitting the pose in closed form with Kabsch [11] or orthogonal Procrustes [12] is known to outperform direct regression of angles or quaternions [9, 10, 14, 13]. We combine the two ideas inside a single-pass slot decoder and analyze the difference between applying the projection at test time and training through it.

    II-CObject-Centric and Equivariant Coordinate Frames

    Expressing states and actions in an agent- or object-centric frame is standard in motion forecasting, e.g. VectorNet [21] and MTR [22], and equivariant architectures exploit the same symmetry in manipulation, e.g. Equivariant Diffusion Policy [23] and EquiBot [24]. Tokenized decoders, in contrast, usually express coordinates in the frame of the sensor: VFlash normalizes image coordinates to [0,1000] and places 3D robot coordinates in the current camera frame (and driving waypoints in the ego frame), and general-purpose VLA models also tokenize image or robot-base coordinates [16, 17, 15]. We measure how much the frame matters relative to the choice of decoder, for five decoder families, and examine where the gain comes from.

    III Method

    III-AProblem Formulation

    At decision time t₀ the world model receives an RGB image I_t₀∈[0,1]^3×128×128, a 4-step history H_t₀-3:t₀∈ℝ^4×10 of the K=4 object keypoints Kₜ∈ℝ^4×2 and the pusher position eₜ∈ℝ², the goal keypoints G∈ℝ^4×2, and a candidate action a∈ℝ⁴. It predicts the P=10-step future Y_1:P={(Kₜ,eₜ)}ₜ₌₁^P∈[0,512]^P×10. Each candidate is scored with the task utility U(Y_1:P,G,K₀)∈[0,1], which rewards final keypoints close to the goal and penalizes the final orientation error (Section IV-B), and the agent selects the candidate with the highest predicted utility.

    III-BSoft-Token Expectation

    Let L_t,c∈ℝ¹⁰⁰¹ be the logits of slot (t,c), for time step t∈{1,…,P} and coordinate c∈{1,…,10}, and p_t,c,b=softmax_b(L_t,c,b). Instead of decoding the most likely token, as the CE head does, we take the expectation [6, 8] in workspace units:

    ŷ_t,c=512/1000∑_b=0¹⁰⁰⁰b·p_t,c,b.

    		(2)

    Its gradient with respect to each logit is proportional to the distance between that bin and the current estimate,

    (∂ŷ_t,c)/(∂L_t,c,b)=512/1000 p_t,c,b (b-1000/512ŷ_t,c),

    		(3)

    so a metric loss on ŷ_t,c penalizes far-away bins more than near ones.

    III-C2D Procrustes (Kabsch) Projection

    Even with a metric loss, the four keypoints are predicted independently in ℝ⁸. Small inconsistencies between their predicted motions deform the block: the Soft-L1 head has a mean pairwise-distance error of 9.14 px on ManiSkill3, and every predicted trajectory violates rigidity (Table I).

    To enforce rigidity, let K₀={k_0,i}ᵢ₌₁^K be the observed initial keypoints with centroid k̄₀ and centered coordinates k̃_0,i=k_0,i-k̄₀. For the predicted keypoints K̂ₜ={k̂_t,i}ᵢ₌₁^K at step t we find the rigid motion that best explains them:

    (R̂ₜ,ĉₜ)=\undersetR∈SO(2), c∈ℝ²\arg\min∑ᵢ₌₁^K∥c+Rk̃_0,i-k̂_t,i∥₂².

    		(4)

    In 2D the minimizer has a closed form that needs neither an SVD nor an atan2[11, 12]:

    ĉₜ=1/K∑ᵢ₌₁^Kk̂_t,i, k̃_t,i=k̂_t,i-ĉₜ,(5)
    αₜ=∑ᵢ₌₁^K(k̃_0,i,xk̃_t,i,x+k̃_0,i,yk̃_t,i,y),(6)
    βₜ=∑ᵢ₌₁^K(k̃_0,i,xk̃_t,i,y-k̃_0,i,yk̃_t,i,x),(7)
    \cosθ̂ₜ=(αₜ)/(√αₜ²+βₜ²+ε), \sinθ̂ₜ=(βₜ)/(√αₜ²+βₜ²+ε).(8)

    The projected keypoints are Π_Kabsch(K̂ₜ,K₀)ᵢ=ĉₜ+R̂(θ̂ₜ)k̃_0,i. The map is differentiable wherever αₜ²+βₜ²>0.

    Why keypoints rather than pose tokens. Suppose each keypoint slot had independent, isotropic error with variance σ² per coordinate. Linearizing (5)–(8) around the true pose shows that the projection keeps only the component of the 2K-dimensional error that lies in the 3-dimensional tangent space of SE(2). It removes the 2K-3=5 non-rigid components, which carries 5/8 of the error energy. Slot errors from a shared backbone are correlated, so this is a motivation, not a guarantee. A second consideration is that predicting the visible corners in image coordinates preserves the spatial correspondence between output and input, whereas a rotation token Δθₜ turns an angular error into a position error scaled by the object’s moment arm ∥k̃_0,i∥₂. Section V tests this choice directly.

    III-DPre-L1 versus E2E-L1 Supervision

    All trajectory decoders are trained with

    L(α)=L_CE^ls=0.02(L,z^*)+0.5 L_CE(m,m^*)
    +15 α L_SL1(Ŷ,Y^*)
    +15 (1-α) L_SL1(Π_Kabsch(Ŷ,K₀),Y^*),(9)

    where the first term is token cross-entropy with label smoothing 0.02, m are the logits of an auxiliary contact-mode head, and L_SL1 is the Smooth-L₁ loss on coordinates divided by 512. The CE head uses the first two terms only, without label smoothing: Eq. (1) plus the same auxiliary contact-mode term. With α=1 (Pre-L1) the Smooth-L₁ loss acts on the raw soft-token outputs and the projection is applied only at test time; Pre-L1 is therefore the Soft-L1 head followed by Π_Kabsch. With α=0 (E2E-L1) the loss acts on the projected trajectory, and its gradient flows through Π_Kabsch. Both variants have 2,050,733 parameters and the same inference cost.

    Proposition 1(Rank of the projection Jacobian).

    For K=4 planar keypoints, ŷₜ∈ℝ⁸, the image of Π_Kabsch(·,K₀) is the 3-dimensional manifold M(K₀)⊂ℝ⁸ of rigid motions of K₀. At any ŷₜ with αₜ²+βₜ²>0, the Jacobian J_Π=∂Π_Kabsch(ŷₜ,K₀)/∂ŷₜ∈ℝ^8×8 has rank 3. Its 5-dimensional null space consists of the perturbations that leave (ĉₜ,θ̂ₜ) unchanged to first order.

    Proof.

    Π_Kabsch factors as ψ∘φ, where φ(ŷₜ)=(ĉ_t,x,ĉ_t,y,θ̂ₜ)∈ℝ²×S¹ and ψ(c,θ)ᵢ=c+R(θ)k̃_0,i. The map φ is a submersion where αₜ²+βₜ²>0: the centroid depends on all coordinates with full rank 2, and a rigid rotation of the centered prediction changes θ̂ₜ at unit rate. The map ψ is an immersion for any non-degenerate shape K₀. Hence rank(J_Π)=rank(dψ dφ)=3 and \dim\kerJ_Π=8-3=5. ∎

    Proposition 1 is consistent with the trade-off we observe between the two variants. With Pre-L1, the Smooth-L₁ gradient constrains all 8 keypoint coordinates, so each slot is trained to track its own corner. With E2E-L1, the loss gives no gradient along the 5 non-rigid directions, so the slots are only constrained through the pose they jointly imply. On the continuous human demonstrations of lerobot/pusht this lowers trajectory error (11.76→10.17 px). On ManiSkill3, where the decision depends on small differences between candidate actions, it raises regret (0.040→0.048; Section V). The proposition does not by itself predict the sign of either effect.

    IV Experimental Setup

    IV-ABenchmarks

    ManiSkill3 PushT-v1. We build a counterfactual benchmark on ManiSkill3 [4] (SAPIEN/PhysX on CPU, Panda arm with a stick tool). It has 512 training, 256 validation and 512 test families. A family fixes the initial T-block and pusher state; from it, 4 candidate actions are each rolled out under 4 hidden physics realizations that vary friction ([0.05,2.5]), center-of-gravity offset, mass and inertia. This gives 16 rollouts per family and 8,192 test rollouts. The test split was generated after the benchmark was registered and was not used for any model selection. As a reference, an oracle that knows the true distribution over four contact modes and scores each action by its mean training utility per mode reaches 0.069 $[0.059, 0.080]$ regret (47.1% Top-1). Ranking actions therefore requires predicting trajectory geometry, not only the contact mode.

    lerobot/pusht. The second benchmark uses the 206 human-teleoperated demonstrations of the simulated Push-T task released with Diffusion Policy [3] and distributed through LeRobot [5] (25,650 frames at 10 Hz). Splits are episode-disjoint: episodes 0–139 for training (7,663 windows), 140–165 for validation (1,487 windows) and 166–205 for testing (2,384 windows). The same test split was used in every stage of the study. The four T-block keypoints (junction, stem tip, left and right bar ends) are midpoints of the eight vertices given in lerobot/pusht_keypoints; their pairwise distances vary by less than 10⁻⁵ px over all frames. Utility is computed against the fixed goal pose [256,256,π/4] of the environment. Because every window has only one recorded outcome, this benchmark measures trajectory error, not decision regret.

    IV-BMetrics

    Coordinates are in workspace units: the planar workspace is mapped to [0,512], and we report distances in these units as px. The utility of a predicted outcome is

    U=clip (1-(d_final)/(\max(dᵢₙᵢₜ,30)), 0, 1)\exp (-(Δθ/0.35)²),

    		(10)

    where d is the mean keypoint distance to the goal and Δθ is the wrapped orientation error of the junction-to-stem-tip vector.

  • •

    Regret: for each test family, the true mean utility (over the four realizations) of the best action minus that of the action the model selects, averaged over families. Top-1: the percentage of families in which the selected action is the best one.

  • •
