    MAP-ADE: the mean Euclidean error over the 10 steps and 5 points (four keypoints and the pusher) of the model’s point prediction, averaged over realizations. MinADE16: the same for the best of 16 samples (stochastic decoders only).

  • •

    RB-Err: the mean absolute deviation of the six pairwise keypoint distances from those of the true shape. RB-Viol: the percentage of predicted trajectories whose per-step deviation exceeds 2.5 px at any step.

  • •

    Brier: the Brier score of the predicted contact-mode distribution. U-MAE: the absolute error of the predicted utility (lerobot/pusht).

    • IV-CModels

    All models share the same context encoder: a small convolutional image encoder and a 3-layer transformer of width d=192 over eight prefix tokens (image features, keypoint history, relative geometry, goal and action). They differ only in the output head and decoding procedure. The CE head (VFlash-style) is trained with Eq. (1). The Soft-L1 head adds the soft-token Smooth-L₁ term (α=1), and Procrustes-FPD adds the Kabsch projection (Pre-L1 or E2E-L1). The MDN head predicts a 4-component mixture of trajectories, and Bi-FPD routes its components by predicted contact mode. The SE(2)-token variants of the CE, Soft-L1 and MDN heads predict the block pose (Δxₜ,Δyₜ,Δθₜ) and the pusher with 50 slots instead of 100 keypoint slots. The iterative baselines are an autoregressive decoder that emits one time step (all 10 coordinates) per step, with a key-value cache (10 sequential steps), and a DDIM diffusion model over whole trajectories (10 steps unless stated). Both draw 16 samples per candidate. We also include a direct utility regressor and a contact-mode classifier that score actions without predicting a trajectory. Parameter counts range from 1.9M to 4.2M, mainly because of the output layers. The slot heads share one 1001-way output layer across slots (about 0.19M parameters), whereas the autoregressive and mixture heads predict all 10 coordinates of a step from one token (d×10×1001≈1.9M parameters per output layer). Latency is the median of 200 calls for one decision, i.e. a batch of four candidate actions with S=16 samples where applicable, on one GPU. Latencies in Tables I and V come from separate measurement runs (the latter includes the frame transform) and should be compared only within a table. Table VI maps model names to identifiers in the released code.

    IV-DStudy Design and Statistics

  • 1.

    Pre-registered benchmark. Twelve models, including the CE, Soft-L1, MDN, Bi-FPD, autoregressive, diffusion, direct-regression and classifier models above, were registered with their hypotheses before the ManiSkill3 test split was generated. Learning rate, weight decay, dropout and loss weights were selected on the validation split only and then frozen. The remaining four registered models, a CE head with an in-block contact-mode token and three Bi-FPD ablations, address a question outside this paper; we omit them from the tables, and their results will be included in the released files.

  • 2.

    Exploratory controls. The Kabsch-projected variants, the SE(2)-token variants, E2E-L1 and all object-frame models were added afterwards. They reuse the frozen hyperparameters of their parent models without re-tuning, and we label them as exploratory.

  • 3.

    Matched checkpoints. The CE, Soft-L1 and MDN heads were retrained together with their projected and SE(2)-token variants, and each projected variant is evaluated on exactly the same checkpoints as its unprojected parent. Retraining the CE head with identical seeds (0–4) and configuration moved its mean test regret from 0.0457 to 0.0423, a difference of 0.0034 caused by non-deterministic CUDA kernels. The Soft-L1 head moved from 0.0424 to 0.0423, and the MDN head from 0.0440 to 0.0443. Family-cluster bootstrap intervals condition on the trained checkpoints, so regret differences below about 0.0035 in Tables I–IV are within run-to-run variation. Bi-FPD, the autoregressive model, the direct regressor and the classifier were not retrained and come from the original benchmark run. Their regret gaps to Pre-L1 (0.0082 and larger) exceed this retraining shift.

  • 4.

    Registered grid. After the exploratory object-frame results, we registered a 2×5 frame × decoder grid with hypotheses H1–H5, a corrected diffusion model and a data-scaling sweep, and ran it on the same test families. The grid uses a single training path for all decoders, removes the RGB input in both frames, and uses a seed × family hierarchical bootstrap that also resamples training seeds.

  • 5.

    Multiple comparisons. Each table of paired tests applies one Holm step-down correction across all competitors it reports against its reference, including weak and close ones, plus the superseded diffusion arm; family sizes are stated in each table. All bootstraps use B=2000 resamples. A reported p=0.0005 means that no resample crossed zero.

一句话：单次前向解出全部量化坐标的 primitive 解码器，可以当快速的 System-1 世界模型用。

要点：

  • 对象是「单次前向」的 primitive 解码器（如 LocateAnything、VFlash）：一次前向就预测出一个几何 primitive 的全部量化坐标 token，因此适合做**快速的 System-1 视觉规划**
  • 论文研究的是：当这种解码器充当 System-1 世界模型——即一个由动作条件驱动、按预测结果给候选动作排序的快速预测器——**什么才是真正重要的**
  • 实验在 ManiSkill3 PushT-v1（512 个留出测试族、8,192 次 rollout）等环境上做，聚焦「先定坐标系、只解码一次」这两个设计选择

为什么值得看：「快」和「准」在运行时规划里是硬冲突。这条把结论落在两个具体设计选择上（对象中心坐标 + 单次解码），比泛泛地说「用更小的模型」有用得多——对做 AI 决策进引擎的团队，是可直接试的工程取舍。

中文摘要：LocateAnything、VFlash 这类「单次前向」的 primitive 解码器，能在一次前向中预测出一个几何 primitive 的全部量化坐标 token，因而适合充当快速的 System-1 视觉规划模块。这篇研究的是：当这样的解码器被用作 System-1 世界模型——一个由动作条件驱动、通过预测结果来给候选动作排序的快速预测器——究竟哪些设计最重要。作者围绕「先确定对象中心坐标系」与「只解码一次」这两个选择展开实验，并在 ManiSkill3 PushT-v1（512 个留出测试族、8,192 次 rollout）等环境上验证。结论的价值在于把「实时世界模型」拆成了可执行的工程选择，而不是笼统地追求更小的模型。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-18

Frame First, Decode Once: Object-Centric Coordinates and Single-Pass Decoding for System-1 World Models

Abstract

Single-pass primitive decoders such as LocateAnything and VFlash predict all quantized coordinate tokens of a geometric primitive in one forward pass, enabling fast, System-1 visual planning. We study what matters when such a decoder serves as a System-1 world model: a fast action-conditioned predictor that ranks candidate pushes by their predicted outcome. On ManiSkill3 PushT-v1 (512 held-out test families, 8,192 rollouts) and on human demonstrations from lerobot/pusht (2,384 test windows), we compare decoders, training losses, rigid-body projections and coordinate frames, using matched checkpoints, hierarchical bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm correction. Two factors of similar size dominate. First, expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object’s initial pose lowers decision regret by 1.9×–2.2× for each of five decoders (p_Holm(9)<0.005), and the object-frame model trained on 128 families matches the world-frame model trained on 512. Second, single-pass decoding outperforms iterative decoding: in the object frame, single-pass heads reach 0.020–0.021 regret at 1.6–1.8 ms per decision, against 0.046 for 10-step DDIM diffusion and 0.059 for KV-cached autoregression at 10.3 and 12.9 ms. The choice among single-pass heads has no measurable effect on regret, and our registered hypothesis that the frame effect exceeds the decoder spread is not supported (0.0345 vs. 0.0389 regret). Soft-token expectation with an end-to-end 2D Kabsch projection gives the lowest trajectory error (11.35 px on ManiSkill3, 3.78 px on lerobot/pusht), exact rigid-body consistency, and lower regret than diffusion at every budget from 4 to 50 DDIM steps, at 3×–29× lower latency.

Index Terms:

World models, robotic manipulation, parallel decoding, coordinate frames, SE(2) equivariance, orthogonal Procrustes, diffusion models.

I Introduction

Action-conditioned world models let an agent evaluate candidate actions by predicting their outcomes before acting [3, 18, 19]. A model that is queried inside the control loop, a fast “System-1” model in the sense of Kahneman [20], must do two things: run within a few milliseconds, and rank the candidate actions correctly. Vision-language and vision-language-action models represent geometry as sequences of quantized coordinate tokens ⟨0⟩…⟨1000⟩[16, 17, 15]. Decoding such a trajectory token by token takes one sequential step per token, i.e. P×C steps for P time steps of C coordinates (100 for P=C=10). Even a coarser autoregression that emits one time step at a time, as in our baseline, needs about 12 ms per decision for a 3.8M-parameter model with a key-value cache, against about 1 ms for a single forward pass.

LocateAnything [2] and VFlash [1] remove this bottleneck. Once the type of a primitive is known, its coordinate layout is fixed, so all of its coordinate slots can be predicted jointly in a single forward pass: slot positions attend to each other and to the preceding context. VFlash applies this flash primitive decoding (FPD) to visual plans such as robot trajectories and driving waypoints, and trains the slots with token-level cross-entropy.

We study single-pass slot decoders used as System-1 world models for contact-rich manipulation. The model predicts the trajectory of a pushed T-block under each of four candidate actions, and the agent picks the action with the highest predicted utility. Prior work leaves several design choices open, which we phrase as five questions:

  • 1.

    How does single-pass decoding compare with iterative decoders (DDIM diffusion, autoregression) built on the same backbone and data?

  • 2.

    Does supervising a soft-token expectation with a metric loss improve on token cross-entropy?

  • 3.

    Should rigid-body consistency come from direct SE(2) pose tokens or from redundant keypoints followed by a Procrustes projection?

  • 4.

    Should the projection be applied only at test time or trained end to end?

  • 5.

    Which matters more for decision quality, the coordinate frame or the decoder?

    • We answer these questions on ManiSkill3 PushT-v1[4] and on the human demonstrations of lerobot/pusht[3, 5]. The study has three stages. A benchmark of twelve models was pre-registered before its test split was generated. Exploratory controls followed, including the object-frame models. Finally, a 2×5 frame × decoder grid was registered after the exploratory object-frame result and run as a confirmatory replication on the same test families. Projected and unprojected variants of each head are evaluated on the same checkpoints, and each table of paired tests applies one Holm correction across all competitors it reports.

    Our findings are:

  • •

    The coordinate frame. Expressing inputs and outputs in the SE(2) frame of the object’s initial pose halves decision regret for every decoder we tested and gives roughly 4× sample efficiency. Controls on the RGB input show that the gain comes from the coordinate frame and not from removing the image.

  • •

    Single-pass versus iterative decoding. On the same backbone, single-pass heads have 2.3×–2.9× lower regret than a 10-step DDIM diffusion model and a KV-cached autoregressive model, and are 6×–8× faster. Which single-pass head is used makes no measurable difference to regret. The frame effect and the decoder effect are of comparable size, so our registered hypothesis that the frame dominates is not supported.

  • •

    Procrustes-FPD. Soft-token expectation followed by a closed-form 2D Kabsch projection gives exact rigid-body consistency and the lowest trajectory error. Redundant keypoints with Procrustes fitting outperform direct SE(2) tokens in the world frame. We characterize when to apply the projection at test time and when to train through it, and we relate this trade-off to the rank of the projection’s Jacobian.

    • We also report an implementation error in our original diffusion baseline, its correction, and how it changed the results (Section V-D, Appendix A).

    Throughout, “VFlash-style CE head” denotes our reimplementation of VFlash’s slot loss and decoding inside the same 2M-parameter backbone as every other model. We do not evaluate NVIDIA’s released model, and our results concern design choices for small action-conditioned predictors, not the VFlash system.

    II Related Work

    II-AParallel Primitive Decoding

    LocateAnything [2] decodes each bounding box or point of a grounding answer as one unit in a single step, and VFlash [1] extends this idea to visual plans on top of a speculative drafter. Given the context of a frozen vision-language model, VFlash appends the B positions of a primitive block. Positions inside the block attend to each other and to the context before the block, and all are predicted in one forward pass. Primitive positions are trained with token-level cross-entropy (Eq. 4 of [1], with unit weights on primitive positions):

    L_CE=-1/PC∑ₜ₌₁^P∑_c=1^C\logP_θ (z^*_t,c|x₀,a),

    		(1)

    where, in our setting, z^*_t,c=round(1000·y^*_t,c/512)∈{0,…,1000}. Eq. (1) removes the latency of autoregressive decoding. It is, however, indifferent to the distance between bins: predicting ⟨501⟩ or ⟨999⟩ for a target ⟨500⟩ incurs the same loss as long as both receive the same probability.

    II-BSoft-Bin Regression and Keypoint-Based Pose Estimation

    Taking the expectation over discrete bins so that a continuous metric loss can be applied was introduced in integral human pose regression [6], differentiable spatial-to-numerical transforms [7], and Distribution Focal Loss for bounding-box edges [8]. In 6-DoF pose estimation and point-cloud registration, predicting redundant keypoints and fitting the pose in closed form with Kabsch [11] or orthogonal Procrustes [12] is known to outperform direct regression of angles or quaternions [9, 10, 14, 13]. We combine the two ideas inside a single-pass slot decoder and analyze the difference between applying the projection at test time and training through it.

    II-CObject-Centric and Equivariant Coordinate Frames

    Expressing states and actions in an agent- or object-centric frame is standard in motion forecasting, e.g. VectorNet [21] and MTR [22], and equivariant architectures exploit the same symmetry in manipulation, e.g. Equivariant Diffusion Policy [23] and EquiBot [24]. Tokenized decoders, in contrast, usually express coordinates in the frame of the sensor: VFlash normalizes image coordinates to [0,1000] and places 3D robot coordinates in the current camera frame (and driving waypoints in the ego frame), and general-purpose VLA models also tokenize image or robot-base coordinates [16, 17, 15]. We measure how much the frame matters relative to the choice of decoder, for five decoder families, and examine where the gain comes from.

    III Method

    III-AProblem Formulation

    At decision time t₀ the world model receives an RGB image I_t₀∈[0,1]^3×128×128, a 4-step history H_t₀-3:t₀∈ℝ^4×10 of the K=4 object keypoints Kₜ∈ℝ^4×2 and the pusher position eₜ∈ℝ², the goal keypoints G∈ℝ^4×2, and a candidate action a∈ℝ⁴. It predicts the P=10-step future Y_1:P={(Kₜ,eₜ)}ₜ₌₁^P∈[0,512]^P×10. Each candidate is scored with the task utility U(Y_1:P,G,K₀)∈[0,1], which rewards final keypoints close to the goal and penalizes the final orientation error (Section IV-B), and the agent selects the candidate with the highest predicted utility.

    III-BSoft-Token Expectation

    Let L_t,c∈ℝ¹⁰⁰¹ be the logits of slot (t,c), for time step t∈{1,…,P} and coordinate c∈{1,…,10}, and p_t,c,b=softmax_b(L_t,c,b). Instead of decoding the most likely token, as the CE head does, we take the expectation [6, 8] in workspace units:

    ŷ_t,c=512/1000∑_b=0¹⁰⁰⁰b·p_t,c,b.

    		(2)

    Its gradient with respect to each logit is proportional to the distance between that bin and the current estimate,

    (∂ŷ_t,c)/(∂L_t,c,b)=512/1000 p_t,c,b (b-1000/512ŷ_t,c),

    		(3)

    so a metric loss on ŷ_t,c penalizes far-away bins more than near ones.

    III-C2D Procrustes (Kabsch) Projection

    Even with a metric loss, the four keypoints are predicted independently in ℝ⁸. Small inconsistencies between their predicted motions deform the block: the Soft-L1 head has a mean pairwise-distance error of 9.14 px on ManiSkill3, and every predicted trajectory violates rigidity (Table I).

    To enforce rigidity, let K₀={k_0,i}ᵢ₌₁^K be the observed initial keypoints with centroid k̄₀ and centered coordinates k̃_0,i=k_0,i-k̄₀. For the predicted keypoints K̂ₜ={k̂_t,i}ᵢ₌₁^K at step t we find the rigid motion that best explains them:

    (R̂ₜ,ĉₜ)=\undersetR∈SO(2), c∈ℝ²\arg\min∑ᵢ₌₁^K∥c+Rk̃_0,i-k̂_t,i∥₂².

    		(4)

    In 2D the minimizer has a closed form that needs neither an SVD nor an atan2[11, 12]:

    ĉₜ=1/K∑ᵢ₌₁^Kk̂_t,i, k̃_t,i=k̂_t,i-ĉₜ,(5)
    αₜ=∑ᵢ₌₁^K(k̃_0,i,xk̃_t,i,x+k̃_0,i,yk̃_t,i,y),(6)
    βₜ=∑ᵢ₌₁^K(k̃_0,i,xk̃_t,i,y-k̃_0,i,yk̃_t,i,x),(7)
    \cosθ̂ₜ=(αₜ)/(√αₜ²+βₜ²+ε), \sinθ̂ₜ=(βₜ)/(√αₜ²+βₜ²+ε).(8)

    The projected keypoints are Π_Kabsch(K̂ₜ,K₀)ᵢ=ĉₜ+R̂(θ̂ₜ)k̃_0,i. The map is differentiable wherever αₜ²+βₜ²>0.

    Why keypoints rather than pose tokens. Suppose each keypoint slot had independent, isotropic error with variance σ² per coordinate. Linearizing (5)–(8) around the true pose shows that the projection keeps only the component of the 2K-dimensional error that lies in the 3-dimensional tangent space of SE(2). It removes the 2K-3=5 non-rigid components, which carries 5/8 of the error energy. Slot errors from a shared backbone are correlated, so this is a motivation, not a guarantee. A second consideration is that predicting the visible corners in image coordinates preserves the spatial correspondence between output and input, whereas a rotation token Δθₜ turns an angular error into a position error scaled by the object’s moment arm ∥k̃_0,i∥₂. Section V tests this choice directly.

    III-DPre-L1 versus E2E-L1 Supervision

    All trajectory decoders are trained with

    L(α)=L_CE^ls=0.02(L,z^*)+0.5 L_CE(m,m^*)
    +15 α L_SL1(Ŷ,Y^*)
    +15 (1-α) L_SL1(Π_Kabsch(Ŷ,K₀),Y^*),(9)

    where the first term is token cross-entropy with label smoothing 0.02, m are the logits of an auxiliary contact-mode head, and L_SL1 is the Smooth-L₁ loss on coordinates divided by 512. The CE head uses the first two terms only, without label smoothing: Eq. (1) plus the same auxiliary contact-mode term. With α=1 (Pre-L1) the Smooth-L₁ loss acts on the raw soft-token outputs and the projection is applied only at test time; Pre-L1 is therefore the Soft-L1 head followed by Π_Kabsch. With α=0 (E2E-L1) the loss acts on the projected trajectory, and its gradient flows through Π_Kabsch. Both variants have 2,050,733 parameters and the same inference cost.

    Proposition 1(Rank of the projection Jacobian).

    For K=4 planar keypoints, ŷₜ∈ℝ⁸, the image of Π_Kabsch(·,K₀) is the 3-dimensional manifold M(K₀)⊂ℝ⁸ of rigid motions of K₀. At any ŷₜ with αₜ²+βₜ²>0, the Jacobian J_Π=∂Π_Kabsch(ŷₜ,K₀)/∂ŷₜ∈ℝ^8×8 has rank 3. Its 5-dimensional null space consists of the perturbations that leave (ĉₜ,θ̂ₜ) unchanged to first order.

    Proof.

    Π_Kabsch factors as ψ∘φ, where φ(ŷₜ)=(ĉ_t,x,ĉ_t,y,θ̂ₜ)∈ℝ²×S¹ and ψ(c,θ)ᵢ=c+R(θ)k̃_0,i. The map φ is a submersion where αₜ²+βₜ²>0: the centroid depends on all coordinates with full rank 2, and a rigid rotation of the centered prediction changes θ̂ₜ at unit rate. The map ψ is an immersion for any non-degenerate shape K₀. Hence rank(J_Π)=rank(dψ dφ)=3 and \dim\kerJ_Π=8-3=5. ∎

    Proposition 1 is consistent with the trade-off we observe between the two variants. With Pre-L1, the Smooth-L₁ gradient constrains all 8 keypoint coordinates, so each slot is trained to track its own corner. With E2E-L1, the loss gives no gradient along the 5 non-rigid directions, so the slots are only constrained through the pose they jointly imply. On the continuous human demonstrations of lerobot/pusht this lowers trajectory error (11.76→10.17 px). On ManiSkill3, where the decision depends on small differences between candidate actions, it raises regret (0.040→0.048; Section V). The proposition does not by itself predict the sign of either effect.

    IV Experimental Setup

    IV-ABenchmarks

    ManiSkill3 PushT-v1. We build a counterfactual benchmark on ManiSkill3 [4] (SAPIEN/PhysX on CPU, Panda arm with a stick tool). It has 512 training, 256 validation and 512 test families. A family fixes the initial T-block and pusher state; from it, 4 candidate actions are each rolled out under 4 hidden physics realizations that vary friction ([0.05,2.5]), center-of-gravity offset, mass and inertia. This gives 16 rollouts per family and 8,192 test rollouts. The test split was generated after the benchmark was registered and was not used for any model selection. As a reference, an oracle that knows the true distribution over four contact modes and scores each action by its mean training utility per mode reaches 0.069 $[0.059, 0.080]$ regret (47.1% Top-1). Ranking actions therefore requires predicting trajectory geometry, not only the contact mode.

    lerobot/pusht. The second benchmark uses the 206 human-teleoperated demonstrations of the simulated Push-T task released with Diffusion Policy [3] and distributed through LeRobot [5] (25,650 frames at 10 Hz). Splits are episode-disjoint: episodes 0–139 for training (7,663 windows), 140–165 for validation (1,487 windows) and 166–205 for testing (2,384 windows). The same test split was used in every stage of the study. The four T-block keypoints (junction, stem tip, left and right bar ends) are midpoints of the eight vertices given in lerobot/pusht_keypoints; their pairwise distances vary by less than 10⁻⁵ px over all frames. Utility is computed against the fixed goal pose [256,256,π/4] of the environment. Because every window has only one recorded outcome, this benchmark measures trajectory error, not decision regret.

    IV-BMetrics

    Coordinates are in workspace units: the planar workspace is mapped to [0,512], and we report distances in these units as px. The utility of a predicted outcome is

    U=clip (1-(d_final)/(\max(dᵢₙᵢₜ,30)), 0, 1)\exp (-(Δθ/0.35)²),

    		(10)

    where d is the mean keypoint distance to the goal and Δθ is the wrapped orientation error of the junction-to-stem-tip vector.

  • •

    Regret: for each test family, the true mean utility (over the four realizations) of the best action minus that of the action the model selects, averaged over families. Top-1: the percentage of families in which the selected action is the best one.

  • •

    MAP-ADE: the mean Euclidean error over the 10 steps and 5 points (four keypoints and the pusher) of the model’s point prediction, averaged over realizations. MinADE16: the same for the best of 16 samples (stochastic decoders only).

  • •

    RB-Err: the mean absolute deviation of the six pairwise keypoint distances from those of the true shape. RB-Viol: the percentage of predicted trajectories whose per-step deviation exceeds 2.5 px at any step.

  • •

    Brier: the Brier score of the predicted contact-mode distribution. U-MAE: the absolute error of the predicted utility (lerobot/pusht).

    • IV-CModels

    All models share the same context encoder: a small convolutional image encoder and a 3-layer transformer of width d=192 over eight prefix tokens (image features, keypoint history, relative geometry, goal and action). They differ only in the output head and decoding procedure. The CE head (VFlash-style) is trained with Eq. (1). The Soft-L1 head adds the soft-token Smooth-L₁ term (α=1), and Procrustes-FPD adds the Kabsch projection (Pre-L1 or E2E-L1). The MDN head predicts a 4-component mixture of trajectories, and Bi-FPD routes its components by predicted contact mode. The SE(2)-token variants of the CE, Soft-L1 and MDN heads predict the block pose (Δxₜ,Δyₜ,Δθₜ) and the pusher with 50 slots instead of 100 keypoint slots. The iterative baselines are an autoregressive decoder that emits one time step (all 10 coordinates) per step, with a key-value cache (10 sequential steps), and a DDIM diffusion model over whole trajectories (10 steps unless stated). Both draw 16 samples per candidate. We also include a direct utility regressor and a contact-mode classifier that score actions without predicting a trajectory. Parameter counts range from 1.9M to 4.2M, mainly because of the output layers. The slot heads share one 1001-way output layer across slots (about 0.19M parameters), whereas the autoregressive and mixture heads predict all 10 coordinates of a step from one token (d×10×1001≈1.9M parameters per output layer). Latency is the median of 200 calls for one decision, i.e. a batch of four candidate actions with S=16 samples where applicable, on one GPU. Latencies in Tables I and V come from separate measurement runs (the latter includes the frame transform) and should be compared only within a table. Table VI maps model names to identifiers in the released code.

    IV-DStudy Design and Statistics

  • 1.

    Pre-registered benchmark. Twelve models, including the CE, Soft-L1, MDN, Bi-FPD, autoregressive, diffusion, direct-regression and classifier models above, were registered with their hypotheses before the ManiSkill3 test split was generated. Learning rate, weight decay, dropout and loss weights were selected on the validation split only and then frozen. The remaining four registered models, a CE head with an in-block contact-mode token and three Bi-FPD ablations, address a question outside this paper; we omit them from the tables, and their results will be included in the released files.

  • 2.

    Exploratory controls. The Kabsch-projected variants, the SE(2)-token variants, E2E-L1 and all object-frame models were added afterwards. They reuse the frozen hyperparameters of their parent models without re-tuning, and we label them as exploratory.

  • 3.

    Matched checkpoints. The CE, Soft-L1 and MDN heads were retrained together with their projected and SE(2)-token variants, and each projected variant is evaluated on exactly the same checkpoints as its unprojected parent. Retraining the CE head with identical seeds (0–4) and configuration moved its mean test regret from 0.0457 to 0.0423, a difference of 0.0034 caused by non-deterministic CUDA kernels. The Soft-L1 head moved from 0.0424 to 0.0423, and the MDN head from 0.0440 to 0.0443. Family-cluster bootstrap intervals condition on the trained checkpoints, so regret differences below about 0.0035 in Tables I–IV are within run-to-run variation. Bi-FPD, the autoregressive model, the direct regressor and the classifier were not retrained and come from the original benchmark run. Their regret gaps to Pre-L1 (0.0082 and larger) exceed this retraining shift.

  • 4.

    Registered grid. After the exploratory object-frame results, we registered a 2×5 frame × decoder grid with hypotheses H1–H5, a corrected diffusion model and a data-scaling sweep, and ran it on the same test families. The grid uses a single training path for all decoders, removes the RGB input in both frames, and uses a seed × family hierarchical bootstrap that also resamples training seeds.

  • 5.

    Multiple comparisons. Each table of paired tests applies one Holm step-down correction across all competitors it reports against its reference, including weak and close ones, plus the superseded diffusion arm; family sizes are stated in each table. All bootstraps use B=2000 resamples. A reported p=0.0005 means that no resample crossed zero.

item.title: 「轨迹好坏」不等于「每一步动作好不好」：LightAct 把游玩经验压成可检索的技能库，再内化进策略 ｜ What Makes a Good Move? Learning to Act from Experience in Visual Worlds
item.description:
一句话：轨迹级结果掩盖了单步动作质量，而无引导探索又会反复回到熟悉局面。

要点：

  • 两个障碍：**轨迹级的结果会掩盖单步动作的质量**（赢了不代表每步都对），而**无引导的探索**又会反复回到熟悉的局面
  • LightAct 的做法是把交互片段总结成「经验条目」，再整合成**游戏专属的技能库**（skill library），把技能引导的探索与策略内化连起来
  • 框架目标是让视觉策略学会「把交互经验转成对单个决策的指导」，而不是只从稀疏的任务成败里学

为什么值得看：玩游戏的 agent 很多，但「从自己的游玩里学到可复用的招式」才是引擎侧真正需要的——它对应的是技能库与行为树，而不是一个端到端模型。这条给了从经验到技能、再到策略的两段式结构。

中文摘要：学习视觉策略的关键，是把交互经验转化为对单个决策的指导，而这中间有两个障碍：一方面，轨迹层面的最终结果会掩盖单个动作的质量（赢了并不代表每一步都对）；另一方面，没有引导的探索又会反复回到熟悉的局面、学不到新东西。LightAct 因此提出一个经验学习框架，把「技能引导的探索」与「策略内化」连接起来：它先把交互片段总结成经验条目，再把这些条目整合成一个游戏专属的技能库，使策略能够借助可复用的技能来改进单步决策，而不是只从稀疏的任务成败信号里学习。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-18

What Makes a Good Move? Learning to Act from Experience in Visual Worlds

Abstract

Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present LightAct, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, LightAct improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

1 Introduction

Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly serve as agents that connect visual perception and language reasoning to action in interactive environments [31, 32, 25, 14]. Video games expose the demands of this process: an agent must recognize the current situation, choose an executable move, and adapt as its actions change the environment [17, 16, 9]. Interaction also provides experience from which to improve. Prior work retains such experience as contextual guidance [29, 21] or uses it to update policy parameters through reinforcement learning [1, 8].

The central challenge is to turn this experience into guidance about individual decisions. A trajectory records the actions taken and their realized outcomes, leaving alternatives at the same decision point unobserved [24]. Its final outcome combines many choices: a useful move can be followed by a mistake, while a poor move can be rescued later. Environment scores summarize these outcomes, but do not directly reveal which action would have been preferable at a particular state [18]. The states encountered during exploration introduce a second limitation. Repeatedly visiting familiar situations concentrates experience on a narrow range of decisions [5, 15].

These observations suggest organizing experience around both the states reached and the choices available there. Summaries of prior interaction can guide exploration toward a broader set of decision states. At a selected state, executing alternative actions under a shared continuation policy makes their subsequent outcomes comparable. Averaging score gains over short rollouts then yields an estimate of each action’s value, which can be converted into supervision for policy learning.

We present LightAct, an experience-learning framework that combines skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. We partition preliminary trajectories collected by a frozen pretrained VLM into short interaction segments. The model summarizes each segment into an experience entry describing the observed conditions, behavior, and outcome, then consolidates these entries into a game-specific textual skill. The skill guides subsequent exploration by providing reusable advice on effective behavior and recurring failures. We retain distinct visited states and their visual decision contexts as a bank of decision roots.

At each root, we compare the available actions through repeated short continuations under the same frozen policy. The resulting environment-reported score gains are averaged and normalized within the root to produce relative action rewards. Pairing these rewards with the collected decision contexts forms a fixed training set. Reinforcement learning then updates the policy by sampling responses to these contexts and assigning rewards to their parsed actions.

We instantiate LightAct at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales using Qwen3.5 [19] and evaluate on all 170 GameWorld tasks across 34 games and five categories [16]. With experience collected in 2048, overall progress improves by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the three scales, respectively. LightAct-2B reaches 36.9% progress and 13.9% success, exceeding the pretrained 9B baseline on both metrics, while LightAct-9B achieves 41.8% progress, competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Further experiments show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance, gains across three RL optimizers, and benefits from source-game experience across game categories. Qualitative examples illustrate how rollout comparisons reveal action preferences that immediate gains alone cannot distinguish.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided source exploration with reinforcement learning from action-level feedback.

  • •

    We construct reusable action-reward tables by comparing continuations from shared decision roots under a frozen policy and normalizing their environment-reported score gains.

  • •

    We demonstrate improvements across three model scales on GameWorld and examine how skill guidance, source environments, and policy optimizers contribute to learning from interaction.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Vision-Language Game Agents

    Video games test whether visual understanding supports sequential decisions [36]. Cradle [25] combines perception, planning, and memory to operate through screenshots and keyboard or mouse controls. BALROG [17] evaluates language and vision-language agents across games and reveals weaknesses in visually grounded interaction. VideoGameBench [34] examines play from raw visual input under real-time and paused interaction, separating decision quality from the effects of inference latency. GameWorld [16] provides browser games with standardized interfaces and state-verifiable task evaluation. Complementing these benchmarks, lmgame-Bench [8] studies perception and memory scaffolds and reports that reinforcement learning on individual games can transfer beyond the training environment. Our work examines how source-game interaction supports such policy learning.

    2.2 Experience Learning of VLMs

    VLM agents learn from accumulated interaction through contextual guidance and parameter updates. External memory retains experience for retrieval at decision time [13], while parameter updates encode it in the policy [6]. JARVIS-1 [29] retrieves multimodal Minecraft experience to support planning, while ELITE [30] extracts reusable strategies from trajectories and retrieves them according to task intent. ICAL [21] refines suboptimal demonstrations through execution and human feedback, annotating causal relations, state changes, and subgoals; the resulting examples support both retrieval and supervised fine-tuning. For reinforcement learning, DigiRL [1] adapts a pretrained VLM for device control through offline initialization and online interaction, using a VLM evaluator for feedback. VAGEN [27] improves explicit state estimation and transition prediction in multi-turn visual interaction through reinforcement learning. We connect experience-guided source exploration with policy internalization.

    2.3 Rollout-Based Policy Learning

    Rollouts estimate the value of an action from the outcomes that follow it. Monte Carlo policy improvement compares candidate moves by continuing each with a common base policy [26]. In combinatorial optimization and stochastic scheduling, heuristic continuations estimate the future cost of each choice [3, 2]. Sparse sampling [10] estimates action values over sampled lookahead trees, while UCT [11] uses a bandit rule to allocate simulations among branches. Rollout comparisons also provide supervision for policy learning [35]. Classification-based policy iteration [12] uses the preferred action at a sampled state as a training label. AggreVaTe [20] trains on expert cost-to-go estimates, while LOLS [4] evaluates decisions under both reference and learned policies. For language models, LATS [37] guides tree search with model evaluations and environment feedback, and Math-Shepherd [28] uses sampled completions to assess intermediate reasoning steps. We use score gains from a shared game state to supervise action selection.

    3 Method

    Experience gathered during interaction can guide subsequent decisions through both contextual guidance and policy learning. Building on this view, LightAct (Fig. ) distills source-game trajectories into textual skills for exploration and compares action outcomes at the collected roots to construct action-level rewards for policy internalization.

    3.1 Decision-Making in Game Environment

    In GameWorld [16], an agent pursues a game-specific objective through sequential interaction. At each decision, it receives the game rules, task instruction, role information, and available semantic actions, together with the current screenshot and recent observation–action history. The agent generates a response, parses it into an executable action, observes its effect on the game, and continues toward the objective. This interaction links visual understanding to decisions whose consequences unfold over subsequent steps.

    For a game environment e with a fixed, finite action space Aₑ, let sₜ∈Sₑ be its state, aₜ∈Aₑ an action, and oₜ=Ωₑ(sₜ) the visual observation. Interaction follows

    sₜ₊₁∼pₑ(·|sₜ,aₜ), xₜ=(g,oₜ,hₜ),

    		(1)

    where g denotes the task specification together with the game instructions, oₜ is the current screenshot, and hₜ contains the recent observations and actions. The instructions describe the objective, rules, acting role, and semantic action interface. A task-specific evaluator Eval_e,g determines whether the current environment state satisfies the task’s completion criteria, with Eval_e,g(sₜ)=1 indicating success. Let π_θ denote the policy parameterized by θ. Its pretrained parameters θ₀ define the frozen initial policy π₀=π_θ₀. The policy generates a response yₜ∼π_θ(·|xₜ) from this context. The parser ℙ attempts to extract an executable action from yₜ: successful parsing yields aₜ=ℙ(yₜ), while invalid responses yield no executable action. For games with multiple acting roles, the other roles’ behavior is part of the transition process.

    3.2 Exploration and Root-State Collection

    The states reached during source interaction determine the decisions available for policy learning. We collect trajectories with a collection policy βₑ, sampling responses yₜ∼βₑ(·|xₜ) and executing successfully parsed actions. The basic collection policy is βₑ(·|xₜ)=π₀(·|xₜ).

    Among the nonterminal states visited during collection, we retain the first occurrence under an environment-specific equivalence criterion. For temporally ordered candidates indexed by ℂ, the selected indices are

    I={i∈ℂ:Deduplicateₑ(sᵢ)=1}.

    		(2)

    Each selected state is stored with its decision context xᵢ. The selected states form the root bank:

    Dᵣₒₒₜ={(sᵢ,xᵢ):i∈I}, N=|I|.

    		(3)

    Their original contexts xᵢ=(g,oᵢ,hᵢ) and the action rewards constructed below form the training examples for policy internalization.

    3.3 Skill-Guided Exploration

    To guide exploration toward a richer set of decision states, we first collect preliminary trajectories Tₑⁱⁿⁱᵗ with π₀ and partition them into short interaction segments{σⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^M. Each segment contains consecutive visual observations, executed actions, and their resulting changes. Under an entry-summarization prompt, the frozen model distills each segment into an experience entry:

    ηⱼ=F_θ₀ᵉⁿᵗʳʸ(g,σⱼ).

    		(4)

    Each entry captures the observed conditions, behavior, and outcome within its segment.

    The same model then consolidates the entries across segments into one textual skill for environment e:

    κₑ=F_θ₀ˢᵏⁱˡˡ(g,{ηⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^M).

    		(5)

    Through a skill-consolidation prompt, recurring observations are combined into concise guidance on useful behavior and failure patterns, tied to the conditions under which they arise. This guidance helps the agent reuse effective interactions and adjust its behavior when exploration stalls.

    We include this skill in the collection policy’s decision context:

    yₜ∼βₑ(·|xₜ)=π₀(·|xₜ,κₑ).

    		(6)

    The policy interprets the guidance using the current observation and recent history. The skill and model parameters remain fixed throughout guided collection.

    We construct the root bank Dᵣₒₒₜ from the guided trajectories using the root-selection procedure above.

    3.4 Rollout-Based Action Value Estimation

    For each decision root, we restore the same environment state sᵢ and decision context xᵢ before evaluating each candidate action. Starting from sᵢ, we execute action a and let π₀ select the subsequent actions. The resulting branch contains at most H decisions, including the initial action, and ends at the first episode termination if it occurs earlier:

    B_i,a∼B_H(·|sᵢ,xᵢ,a,π₀).

    		(7)

    At each subsequent decision, π₀ conditions on the task, current observation, and recent interaction history within the branch. Using the same frozen policy across actions and roots provides a shared basis for comparing their outcomes.

    Let Sₑ(s) denote the game score returned by the environment at state s and s_B the final state of branch B. A continuation from sᵢ contributes the score gain

    Gₑ(sᵢ,B)=Sₑ(s_B)-Sₑ(sᵢ).

    		(8)

    For a terminal branch, s_B is the state before reset. The finite-horizon action value and its estimate from K continuations are

    Q_H^π₀(i,a)=𝔼_B_i,a[Gₑ(sᵢ,B_i,a)],(9)
    Q̂ᵢ(a)=1/K∑ₖ₌₁^KGₑ(sᵢ,B_i,a⁽ᵏ⁾).(10)

    The estimate measures score gain after choosing a and continuing under π₀ for the specified horizon.

    3.5 Reward Shaping

    The estimated score gains Q̂ᵢ(a) quantify the outcomes of candidate actions in the game’s score units. To express action preferences on a common reward scale, we normalize these values within each root:

    rᵢ(a)=\begincases\dfracQ̂ᵢ(a)-qᵢ⁻qᵢ⁺-qᵢ⁻,&qᵢ⁺>qᵢ⁻, [4.0pt] 0,&qᵢ⁺=qᵢ⁻,\endcases

    		(11)

    where qᵢ⁻=\min_a∈AₑQ̂ᵢ(a) and qᵢ⁺=\max_a∈AₑQ̂ᵢ(a). This normalization preserves the estimated ordering of actions and expresses their relative quality within a shared decision context. When all action values coincide, the root supplies no preference signal and all action rewards are zero.

    3.6 RL-Based Policy Internalization

    After collection, we pair each decision context in Dᵣₒₒₜ with its constructed reward function rᵢ:Aₑ→[0,1]:

    D_reward={(xᵢ,rᵢ)|(sᵢ,xᵢ)∈Dᵣₒₒₜ}.

    		(12)

    This converts the action comparisons in source experience into policy-learning examples: xᵢ supplies the task and visual history, while rᵢ provides feedback on the selected action. Starting from θ=θ₀, we train π_θ to select valuable actions directly from xᵢ.

    The policy π_θ generates a response y from the decision context xᵢ, which is parsed into an action a=ℙ(y) when valid. A response is valid when it satisfies the public action syntax and argument constraints and selects an action in Aₑ. The response reward is

    Rᵢ(y)=\begincasesrᵢ(a),&ifyis valid, 0,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(13)

    Sampling examples uniformly from D_reward, we optimize the expected response reward with reference-policy regularization:

    J_RL(θ)=𝔼_(xᵢ,rᵢ)∼D_reward[(14)
    𝔼_y∼π_θ(·|xᵢ)[Rᵢ(y)]
    -λD_KL (π_θ(·|xᵢ) ∥ π₀(·|xᵢ))],

    where λ≥0 controls deviation from the initial policy π₀. The current policy samples responses conditioned on xᵢ and receives Rᵢ(y); the collected contexts and reward maps remain fixed during these updates. Established policy-gradient algorithms optimize this objective, with their configurations specified in the experiments.

    After learning, the policy generates yₜ∼π_θ^⋆(·|xₜ) and executes the parsed action aₜ=ℙ(yₜ) using the task description, visual observations, and action interface of the environment being played.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Benchmark and Evaluation Setting

    We evaluate LightAct on GameWorld [16], which comprises 34 games and 170 tasks across five categories: Arcade, Platformer, Puzzle, Runner, and Simulation. Each run has a budget of 100 decisions, with the environment paused during inference. At each decision, the policy receives the game instructions, the current screenshot, and two rounds of image–text interaction history, and selects an action from the game’s interface. Action duration, episode termination, and resets follow the protocol. Published GameWorld results use greedy decoding with one run per task. Our Qwen3.5 and LightAct evaluations use temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, a 2,048-token output cap, and three runs per task. We use GameWorld’s state-based evaluator to measure success rate (SR), the fraction of successful runs, and progress (PG), normalized completion toward task-specific targets.

    4.2 Implementation Details

    We instantiate LightAct with Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3.5-4B, and Qwen3.5-9B [19]. At each scale, experience collection, branch continuation, and skill extraction use frozen copies of the same model that initializes the trainable policy. Acting uses the native non-thinking mode. For each source game–task pair, we collect trajectories within a budget of 10,000 decisions and retain up to 1,024 deduplicated roots, with seed 42 for the initial reset. We equip source games with snapshot support through exportSnapshot() and importSnapshot(), restoring each decision root before evaluating candidate actions. Collection and branch continuation use temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and a 2,048-token output cap. Branch valuation uses H=10 including the initial action and K=4 continuations, processing eight roots concurrently. Rewards use environment-reported score gains with per-root min–max normalization. We train with GRPO [22], REINFORCE++ [7], or DAPO [33] in verl/HybridFlow [23]. Tables  and  in the appendix give the collection and reward settings and the training hyperparameters, respectively.

    4.3 Baselines and Main Comparisons

    LightAct achieves competitive progress against proprietary models.

    LightAct brings compact policies close to strong proprietary models in benchmark progress (Table ). At 4B, it reaches 40.5% overall PG, comparable to GPT-5.2 at 40.6%; at 9B, it reaches 41.8%, approaching Gemini-3-Flash-Preview at 41.9%. On Puzzle tasks, LightAct-9B achieves 59.2% PG, exceeding the reported progress of both models. The remaining gap is clearer in task completion, where overall SR reaches 18.4% for LightAct-9B compared with 21.2% for Gemini. By comparing actions from a shared state, LightAct turns interaction outcomes into supervision for policy learning. These results suggest that internalizing such experience enables compact VLMs to achieve competitive game-playing performance through direct policy inference.

    LightAct consistently improves policy performance across model scales.

    LightAct increases both SR and PG in all five game categories at 2B, 4B, and 9B, indicating benefits for task completion as well as partial progress. The overall PG gains are 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points, respectively. The 4B policy gains most on Runner tasks, where PG rises from 8.2% to 49.7%, even though its training experience comes from a puzzle game. Notably, LightAct-2B surpasses the pretrained 9B baseline in both PG (36.9% versus 28.8%) and SR (13.9% versus 10.0%), showing that adaptation through experience can improve the effectiveness of a smaller policy. The 9B model also gains 8.4 percentage points in SR over its initialization, demonstrating that stronger pretrained performance still leaves room for improvement through supervision from interaction.

    4.4 Ablations and Diagnostics

    Policy internalization yields consistent gains across RL algorithms.

    We compare GRPO, REINFORCE++, and DAPO, using the same reward tables for each model scale (Table ). All nine trained configurations improve overall PG over their base policies, with gains ranging from 10.8 to 29.2 percentage points. This pattern suggests that the action-level rewards provide useful supervision across different policy-update rules. The optimizer still affects how these gains are distributed across games: at 4B, DAPO achieves higher Puzzle and Simulation PG than GRPO, while GRPO attains higher overall PG. Thus, the common benefit of learning from action outcomes persists alongside algorithm-dependent differences in performance across categories.

    Skill guidance broadens the score distribution of collected roots.

    Figure  compares 1,024 roots collected with and without skill guidance in 2048; Figure  shows the skill used during collection. By drawing on interaction experience, the skill guides the policy away from repeated ineffective moves and helps it explore a broader range of game states. Guided collection extends the score range from 0–552 to 0–944 and raises the mean score from 186.6 to 280.2. The proportion of roots scoring at least 500 increases from 1.3% to 19.4%, while lower-score states remain represented. With GRPO, skill guidance raises PG from 32.98% to 36.90% and SR from 12.35% to 13.92% (lower panels of Figure ). With REINFORCE++, PG changes little (34.60% to 34.55%), while SR rises from 11.96% to 12.75%. These results suggest that skill guidance broadens the experience available for policy learning, with benefits that depend on the optimizer.

    Source-game experience supports generalization across game categories.

    With Tetris as the source game, both GRPO and REINFORCE++ improve PG over the 2B base policy across all five categories (Figure ). Arcade PG, for example, rises from 5.6% to 29.8% and 29.6%, respectively. These gains extend beyond the source game’s Puzzle category, suggesting that policy internalization helps LightAct apply experience to different game mechanics. Experience from a single game can provide supervision for broader visual decisions. The varying gains across categories indicate that transfer is uneven, leaving room to improve the breadth of behaviors learned from source experience.

    Rollout outcomes distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

    In Figure , moving left or right from the same root yields an immediate score gain of 24, but the resulting boards support different continuations. The rightward branch produces a 64 tile, whereas the leftward branch retains a maximum tile of 32. Across four rollouts, moving right achieves a mean gain of 144 versus 67 for moving left, yielding normalized rewards of 1.000 and 0.330. The rollout comparison turns delayed action outcomes into a training preference that immediate score gains alone cannot provide.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented LightAct, a framework that turns interaction experience into guidance for exploration and supervision for policy learning. Game-specific skills broaden root-state coverage, while short rollouts from shared roots reveal the relative utility of candidate actions. Experiments on GameWorld show consistent improvements across model scales and policy optimizers, with compact policies achieving competitive progress against proprietary models. These findings demonstrate the value of organizing experience around states and action outcomes for learning game-playing policies.

    6 Limitations

    Generalization across source environments remains limited, and the current framework does not directly support action spaces with continuous parameters. Our study focuses on short-horizon decisions; long-horizon decision-making remains to be validated. Future work will investigate integration with multi-turn reinforcement learning and evaluation on games that require sustained planning. Reward shaping currently relies on scores read from environment states. We will further explore purely visual self-improvement that derives learning signals from observations without access to internal environment states.

    LLM Usage Statement

    OpenAI Codex was used to assist with code generation and completion, and OpenAI GPT models assisted with related-literature discovery. Codex also assisted with drafting and editing manuscript text. The authors led the research process, problem formulation, computational experiments, and factual verification, and take full responsibility for the scientific claims, results, references, and final manuscript.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Collection details.

    At each model scale, π₀ denotes the corresponding frozen Qwen3.5 initialization. In 2048, deduplication uses the ordered grid of tile values, including empty cells, and retains the first occurrence across episodes. Collection continues after task success and resets at termination or after 100 decisions. During collection and branch continuation, an invalid response consumes one decision step without executing an action or advancing game time.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：轨迹级结果掩盖了单步动作质量，而无引导探索又会反复回到熟悉局面。

要点：

  • 两个障碍：**轨迹级的结果会掩盖单步动作的质量**（赢了不代表每步都对），而**无引导的探索**又会反复回到熟悉的局面
  • LightAct 的做法是把交互片段总结成「经验条目」，再整合成**游戏专属的技能库**（skill library），把技能引导的探索与策略内化连起来
  • 框架目标是让视觉策略学会「把交互经验转成对单个决策的指导」，而不是只从稀疏的任务成败里学

为什么值得看：玩游戏的 agent 很多，但「从自己的游玩里学到可复用的招式」才是引擎侧真正需要的——它对应的是技能库与行为树，而不是一个端到端模型。这条给了从经验到技能、再到策略的两段式结构。

中文摘要：学习视觉策略的关键，是把交互经验转化为对单个决策的指导，而这中间有两个障碍：一方面，轨迹层面的最终结果会掩盖单个动作的质量（赢了并不代表每一步都对）；另一方面，没有引导的探索又会反复回到熟悉的局面、学不到新东西。LightAct 因此提出一个经验学习框架，把「技能引导的探索」与「策略内化」连接起来：它先把交互片段总结成经验条目，再把这些条目整合成一个游戏专属的技能库，使策略能够借助可复用的技能来改进单步决策，而不是只从稀疏的任务成败信号里学习。

BALROG [17] evaluates language and vision-language agents across games and reveals weaknesses in visually grounded interaction. VideoGameBench [34] examines play from raw visual input under real-time and paused interaction, separating decision quality from the effects of inference latency. GameWorld [16] provides browser games with standardized interfaces and state-verifiable task evaluation. Complementing these benchmarks, lmgame-Bench [8] studies perception and memory scaffolds and reports that reinforcement learning on individual games can transfer beyond the training environment. Our work examines how source-game interaction supports such policy learning.

    2.2 Experience Learning of VLMs

    VLM agents learn from accumulated interaction through contextual guidance and parameter updates. External memory retains experience for retrieval at decision time [13], while parameter updates encode it in the policy [6]. JARVIS-1 [29] retrieves multimodal Minecraft experience to support planning, while ELITE [30] extracts reusable strategies from trajectories and retrieves them according to task intent. ICAL [21] refines suboptimal demonstrations through execution and human feedback, annotating causal relations, state changes, and subgoals; the resulting examples support both retrieval and supervised fine-tuning. For reinforcement learning, DigiRL [1] adapts a pretrained VLM for device control through offline initialization and online interaction, using a VLM evaluator for feedback. VAGEN [27] improves explicit state estimation and transition prediction in multi-turn visual interaction through reinforcement learning. We connect experience-guided source exploration with policy internalization.

    2.3 Rollout-Based Policy Learning

    Rollouts estimate the value of an action from the outcomes that follow it. Monte Carlo policy improvement compares candidate moves by continuing each with a common base policy [26]. In combinatorial optimization and stochastic scheduling, heuristic continuations estimate the future cost of each choice [3, 2]. Sparse sampling [10] estimates action values over sampled lookahead trees, while UCT [11] uses a bandit rule to allocate simulations among branches. Rollout comparisons also provide supervision for policy learning [35]. Classification-based policy iteration [12] uses the preferred action at a sampled state as a training label. AggreVaTe [20] trains on expert cost-to-go estimates, while LOLS [4] evaluates decisions under both reference and learned policies. For language models, LATS [37] guides tree search with model evaluations and environment feedback, and Math-Shepherd [28] uses sampled completions to assess intermediate reasoning steps. We use score gains from a shared game state to supervise action selection.

    3 Method

    Experience gathered during interaction can guide subsequent decisions through both contextual guidance and policy learning. Building on this view, LightAct (Fig. ) distills source-game trajectories into textual skills for exploration and compares action outcomes at the collected roots to construct action-level rewards for policy internalization.

    3.1 Decision-Making in Game Environment

    In GameWorld [16], an agent pursues a game-specific objective through sequential interaction. At each decision, it receives the game rules, task instruction, role information, and available semantic actions, together with the current screenshot and recent observation–action history. The agent generates a response, parses it into an executable action, observes its effect on the game, and continues toward the objective. This interaction links visual understanding to decisions whose consequences unfold over subsequent steps.

    For a game environment e with a fixed, finite action space Aₑ, let sₜ∈Sₑ be its state, aₜ∈Aₑ an action, and oₜ=Ωₑ(sₜ) the visual observation. Interaction follows

    sₜ₊₁∼pₑ(·|sₜ,aₜ), xₜ=(g,oₜ,hₜ),

    		(1)

    where g denotes the task specification together with the game instructions, oₜ is the current screenshot, and hₜ contains the recent observations and actions. The instructions describe the objective, rules, acting role, and semantic action interface. A task-specific evaluator Eval_e,g determines whether the current environment state satisfies the task’s completion criteria, with Eval_e,g(sₜ)=1 indicating success. Let π_θ denote the policy parameterized by θ. Its pretrained parameters θ₀ define the frozen initial policy π₀=π_θ₀. The policy generates a response yₜ∼π_θ(·|xₜ) from this context. The parser ℙ attempts to extract an executable action from yₜ: successful parsing yields aₜ=ℙ(yₜ), while invalid responses yield no executable action. For games with multiple acting roles, the other roles’ behavior is part of the transition process.

    3.2 Exploration and Root-State Collection

    The states reached during source interaction determine the decisions available for policy learning. We collect trajectories with a collection policy βₑ, sampling responses yₜ∼βₑ(·|xₜ) and executing successfully parsed actions. The basic collection policy is βₑ(·|xₜ)=π₀(·|xₜ).

    Among the nonterminal states visited during collection, we retain the first occurrence under an environment-specific equivalence criterion. For temporally ordered candidates indexed by ℂ, the selected indices are

    I={i∈ℂ:Deduplicateₑ(sᵢ)=1}.

    		(2)

    Each selected state is stored with its decision context xᵢ. The selected states form the root bank:

    Dᵣₒₒₜ={(sᵢ,xᵢ):i∈I}, N=|I|.

    		(3)

    Their original contexts xᵢ=(g,oᵢ,hᵢ) and the action rewards constructed below form the training examples for policy internalization.

    3.3 Skill-Guided Exploration

    To guide exploration toward a richer set of decision states, we first collect preliminary trajectories Tₑⁱⁿⁱᵗ with π₀ and partition them into short interaction segments{σⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^M. Each segment contains consecutive visual observations, executed actions, and their resulting changes. Under an entry-summarization prompt, the frozen model distills each segment into an experience entry:

    ηⱼ=F_θ₀ᵉⁿᵗʳʸ(g,σⱼ).

    		(4)

    Each entry captures the observed conditions, behavior, and outcome within its segment.

    The same model then consolidates the entries across segments into one textual skill for environment e:

    κₑ=F_θ₀ˢᵏⁱˡˡ(g,{ηⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^M).

    		(5)

    Through a skill-consolidation prompt, recurring observations are combined into concise guidance on useful behavior and failure patterns, tied to the conditions under which they arise. This guidance helps the agent reuse effective interactions and adjust its behavior when exploration stalls.

    We include this skill in the collection policy’s decision context:

    yₜ∼βₑ(·|xₜ)=π₀(·|xₜ,κₑ).

    		(6)

    The policy interprets the guidance using the current observation and recent history. The skill and model parameters remain fixed throughout guided collection.

    We construct the root bank Dᵣₒₒₜ from the guided trajectories using the root-selection procedure above.

    3.4 Rollout-Based Action Value Estimation

    For each decision root, we restore the same environment state sᵢ and decision context xᵢ before evaluating each candidate action. Starting from sᵢ, we execute action a and let π₀ select the subsequent actions. The resulting branch contains at most H decisions, including the initial action, and ends at the first episode termination if it occurs earlier:

    B_i,a∼B_H(·|sᵢ,xᵢ,a,π₀).

    		(7)

    At each subsequent decision, π₀ conditions on the task, current observation, and recent interaction history within the branch. Using the same frozen policy across actions and roots provides a shared basis for comparing their outcomes.

    Let Sₑ(s) denote the game score returned by the environment at state s and s_B the final state of branch B. A continuation from sᵢ contributes the score gain

    Gₑ(sᵢ,B)=Sₑ(s_B)-Sₑ(sᵢ).

    		(8)

    For a terminal branch, s_B is the state before reset. The finite-horizon action value and its estimate from K continuations are

    Q_H^π₀(i,a)=𝔼_B_i,a[Gₑ(sᵢ,B_i,a)],(9)
    Q̂ᵢ(a)=1/K∑ₖ₌₁^KGₑ(sᵢ,B_i,a⁽ᵏ⁾).(10)

    The estimate measures score gain after choosing a and continuing under π₀ for the specified horizon.

    3.5 Reward Shaping

    The estimated score gains Q̂ᵢ(a) quantify the outcomes of candidate actions in the game’s score units. To express action preferences on a common reward scale, we normalize these values within each root:

    rᵢ(a)=\begincases\dfracQ̂ᵢ(a)-qᵢ⁻qᵢ⁺-qᵢ⁻,&qᵢ⁺>qᵢ⁻, [4.0pt] 0,&qᵢ⁺=qᵢ⁻,\endcases

    		(11)

    where qᵢ⁻=\min_a∈AₑQ̂ᵢ(a) and qᵢ⁺=\max_a∈AₑQ̂ᵢ(a). This normalization preserves the estimated ordering of actions and expresses their relative quality within a shared decision context. When all action values coincide, the root supplies no preference signal and all action rewards are zero.

    3.6 RL-Based Policy Internalization

    After collection, we pair each decision context in Dᵣₒₒₜ with its constructed reward function rᵢ:Aₑ→[0,1]:

    D_reward={(xᵢ,rᵢ)|(sᵢ,xᵢ)∈Dᵣₒₒₜ}.

    		(12)

    This converts the action comparisons in source experience into policy-learning examples: xᵢ supplies the task and visual history, while rᵢ provides feedback on the selected action. Starting from θ=θ₀, we train π_θ to select valuable actions directly from xᵢ.

    The policy π_θ generates a response y from the decision context xᵢ, which is parsed into an action a=ℙ(y) when valid. A response is valid when it satisfies the public action syntax and argument constraints and selects an action in Aₑ. The response reward is

    Rᵢ(y)=\begincasesrᵢ(a),&ifyis valid, 0,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(13)

    Sampling examples uniformly from D_reward, we optimize the expected response reward with reference-policy regularization:

    J_RL(θ)=𝔼_(xᵢ,rᵢ)∼D_reward[(14)
    𝔼_y∼π_θ(·|xᵢ)[Rᵢ(y)]
    -λD_KL (π_θ(·|xᵢ) ∥ π₀(·|xᵢ))],

    where λ≥0 controls deviation from the initial policy π₀. The current policy samples responses conditioned on xᵢ and receives Rᵢ(y); the collected contexts and reward maps remain fixed during these updates. Established policy-gradient algorithms optimize this objective, with their configurations specified in the experiments.

    After learning, the policy generates yₜ∼π_θ^⋆(·|xₜ) and executes the parsed action aₜ=ℙ(yₜ) using the task description, visual observations, and action interface of the environment being played.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Benchmark and Evaluation Setting

    We evaluate LightAct on GameWorld [16], which comprises 34 games and 170 tasks across five categories: Arcade, Platformer, Puzzle, Runner, and Simulation. Each run has a budget of 100 decisions, with the environment paused during inference. At each decision, the policy receives the game instructions, the current screenshot, and two rounds of image–text interaction history, and selects an action from the game’s interface. Action duration, episode termination, and resets follow the protocol. Published GameWorld results use greedy decoding with one run per task. Our Qwen3.5 and LightAct evaluations use temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, a 2,048-token output cap, and three runs per task. We use GameWorld’s state-based evaluator to measure success rate (SR), the fraction of successful runs, and progress (PG), normalized completion toward task-specific targets.

    4.2 Implementation Details

    We instantiate LightAct with Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3.5-4B, and Qwen3.5-9B [19]. At each scale, experience collection, branch continuation, and skill extraction use frozen copies of the same model that initializes the trainable policy. Acting uses the native non-thinking mode. For each source game–task pair, we collect trajectories within a budget of 10,000 decisions and retain up to 1,024 deduplicated roots, with seed 42 for the initial reset. We equip source games with snapshot support through exportSnapshot() and importSnapshot(), restoring each decision root before evaluating candidate actions. Collection and branch continuation use temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and a 2,048-token output cap. Branch valuation uses H=10 including the initial action and K=4 continuations, processing eight roots concurrently. Rewards use environment-reported score gains with per-root min–max normalization. We train with GRPO [22], REINFORCE++ [7], or DAPO [33] in verl/HybridFlow [23]. Tables  and  in the appendix give the collection and reward settings and the training hyperparameters, respectively.

    4.3 Baselines and Main Comparisons

    LightAct achieves competitive progress against proprietary models.

    LightAct brings compact policies close to strong proprietary models in benchmark progress (Table ). At 4B, it reaches 40.5% overall PG, comparable to GPT-5.2 at 40.6%; at 9B, it reaches 41.8%, approaching Gemini-3-Flash-Preview at 41.9%. On Puzzle tasks, LightAct-9B achieves 59.2% PG, exceeding the reported progress of both models. The remaining gap is clearer in task completion, where overall SR reaches 18.4% for LightAct-9B compared with 21.2% for Gemini. By comparing actions from a shared state, LightAct turns interaction outcomes into supervision for policy learning. These results suggest that internalizing such experience enables compact VLMs to achieve competitive game-playing performance through direct policy inference.

    LightAct consistently improves policy performance across model scales.

    LightAct increases both SR and PG in all five game categories at 2B, 4B, and 9B, indicating benefits for task completion as well as partial progress. The overall PG gains are 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points, respectively. The 4B policy gains most on Runner tasks, where PG rises from 8.2% to 49.7%, even though its training experience comes from a puzzle game. Notably, LightAct-2B surpasses the pretrained 9B baseline in both PG (36.9% versus 28.8%) and SR (13.9% versus 10.0%), showing that adaptation through experience can improve the effectiveness of a smaller policy. The 9B model also gains 8.4 percentage points in SR over its initialization, demonstrating that stronger pretrained performance still leaves room for improvement through supervision from interaction.

    4.4 Ablations and Diagnostics

    Policy internalization yields consistent gains across RL algorithms.

    We compare GRPO, REINFORCE++, and DAPO, using the same reward tables for each model scale (Table ). All nine trained configurations improve overall PG over their base policies, with gains ranging from 10.8 to 29.2 percentage points. This pattern suggests that the action-level rewards provide useful supervision across different policy-update rules. The optimizer still affects how these gains are distributed across games: at 4B, DAPO achieves higher Puzzle and Simulation PG than GRPO, while GRPO attains higher overall PG. Thus, the common benefit of learning from action outcomes persists alongside algorithm-dependent differences in performance across categories.

    Skill guidance broadens the score distribution of collected roots.

    Figure  compares 1,024 roots collected with and without skill guidance in 2048; Figure  shows the skill used during collection. By drawing on interaction experience, the skill guides the policy away from repeated ineffective moves and helps it explore a broader range of game states. Guided collection extends the score range from 0–552 to 0–944 and raises the mean score from 186.6 to 280.2. The proportion of roots scoring at least 500 increases from 1.3% to 19.4%, while lower-score states remain represented. With GRPO, skill guidance raises PG from 32.98% to 36.90% and SR from 12.35% to 13.92% (lower panels of Figure ). With REINFORCE++, PG changes little (34.60% to 34.55%), while SR rises from 11.96% to 12.75%. These results suggest that skill guidance broadens the experience available for policy learning, with benefits that depend on the optimizer.

    Source-game experience supports generalization across game categories.

    With Tetris as the source game, both GRPO and REINFORCE++ improve PG over the 2B base policy across all five categories (Figure ). Arcade PG, for example, rises from 5.6% to 29.8% and 29.6%, respectively. These gains extend beyond the source game’s Puzzle category, suggesting that policy internalization helps LightAct apply experience to different game mechanics. Experience from a single game can provide supervision for broader visual decisions. The varying gains across categories indicate that transfer is uneven, leaving room to improve the breadth of behaviors learned from source experience.

    Rollout outcomes distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

    In Figure , moving left or right from the same root yields an immediate score gain of 24, but the resulting boards support different continuations. The rightward branch produces a 64 tile, whereas the leftward branch retains a maximum tile of 32. Across four rollouts, moving right achieves a mean gain of 144 versus 67 for moving left, yielding normalized rewards of 1.000 and 0.330. The rollout comparison turns delayed action outcomes into a training preference that immediate score gains alone cannot provide.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented LightAct, a framework that turns interaction experience into guidance for exploration and supervision for policy learning. Game-specific skills broaden root-state coverage, while short rollouts from shared roots reveal the relative utility of candidate actions. Experiments on GameWorld show consistent improvements across model scales and policy optimizers, with compact policies achieving competitive progress against proprietary models. These findings demonstrate the value of organizing experience around states and action outcomes for learning game-playing policies.

    6 Limitations

    Generalization across source environments remains limited, and the current framework does not directly support action spaces with continuous parameters. Our study focuses on short-horizon decisions; long-horizon decision-making remains to be validated. Future work will investigate integration with multi-turn reinforcement learning and evaluation on games that require sustained planning. Reward shaping currently relies on scores read from environment states. We will further explore purely visual self-improvement that derives learning signals from observations without access to internal environment states.

    LLM Usage Statement

    OpenAI Codex was used to assist with code generation and completion, and OpenAI GPT models assisted with related-literature discovery. Codex also assisted with drafting and editing manuscript text. The authors led the research process, problem formulation, computational experiments, and factual verification, and take full responsibility for the scientific claims, results, references, and final manuscript.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Collection details.

    At each model scale, π₀ denotes the corresponding frozen Qwen3.5 initialization. In 2048, deduplication uses the ordered grid of tile values, including empty cells, and retains the first occurrence across episodes. Collection continues after task success and resets at termination or after 100 decisions. During collection and branch continuation, an invalid response consumes one decision step without executing an action or advancing game time.

item.title: 实测材质不必每次重扫：BTF 用「一个材质 = 256 维编码 + 共享解码器」，还能在编码空间里采样出新材质 ｜ One Code per Material: Neural Representation and Generation of Measured BTFs
item.description:
一句话：实测 BTF 能表达视差、自阴影与互反射，但每次测量都是几十亿个数，新材质就得再扫一次。

要点：

  • 为什么难：实测双向纹理函数（BTF）能表达解析 SVBRDF 无法描述的视差、自阴影与互反射，但**每次测量都是数十亿个数值**，而每加一种材质就要重新采集一次
  • 现有神经 BTF 把每个材质编码成庞大的逐 texel 潜变量图，**不是一个可以被采样的共享空间里的点**
  • 新做法给两个工作点：逐材质坐标网络在同尺寸下比先前方法高 **+3.2 dB PSNR**；紧凑模型则用**一个 256 维编码 + 全材质共享解码器**，以「每材质 256 个数」超过逐 texel 潜变量图（+1.2 dB），并因每个材质是一个点，可用**类别条件流在编码空间里采样新材质**——生成的材质能像完整 BTF 一样渲染与重打光

为什么值得看：材质库是 3D 内容里最贵、最难扩的资产之一。把「一个材质压成 256 维、共享解码器、还能采样生成新材质」这件事做成，等于把材质采集从「一件一件买」变成「在空间里取点」——对渲染管线是直接的产能变化。

中文摘要：实测的双向纹理函数（BTF）能捕捉真实材质的完整外观，包括视差、自阴影与互反射，而这些是解析式 SVBRDF 无法表达的；但问题在于规模——单次测量的数据量达数十亿个数值，而且每增加一种材质都要重新采集一次。现有神经 BTF 表示把每个材质编码成庞大的逐 texel 潜变量图，而不是共享空间中可被采样的一个点。这篇提出两个工作点的神经表示：逐材质的坐标网络在相同存储规模下比此前方法提升 3.2 dB PSNR，并在所有指标上超过既有基线；紧凑模型则用单个 256 维编码加一个所有材质共享的解码器，以「每种材质 256 个数值」达到比逐 texel 潜变量图更高的 PSNR（+1.2 dB）与更好的色彩准确度。由于每个材质都变成编码空间中的一个点，作者进一步用类别条件流在该空间上采样，生成的材质可以像完整 BTF 一样被渲染与重打光。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-18

One Code per Material: Neural Representation and Generation of Measured BTFs

Abstract

Measured bidirectional texture functions (BTFs) capture the full appearance of real materials—including parallax, self-shadowing and inter-reflections that analytic SVBRDFs cannot express—but each measurement is billions of values, and every new material requires a new capture. Existing neural BTF representations encode each material as large per-texel latent maps rather than as a point in a shared space from which new materials could be sampled. We present neural representations of measured BTFs at two operating points. A per-material coordinate network outperforms the recent neural BTF of Xia et al. at matched size (+3.2 dB PSNR) and all prior baselines on every metric. A compact model represents each material by a single 256-dimensional code that conditions a shared decoder; it exceeds the PSNR (+1.2 dB) and colour accuracy of the per-texel latent maps of Rainer et al. with 256 numbers per material instead of millions, and one decoder shared by all materials. Because each material is a single point in this code space, measured BTFs can be sampled: a class-conditional flow over the codes, trained on the 84 materials enlarged with colourways and hue rotations, generates materials that render and relight as full BTFs.

1 Introduction

Real materials owe much of their appearance to structure below the scale of a surface: the loops of a carpet, the crack network of leather, the weave of a fabric. Under changing light and view these structures cast shadows, occlude each other and shift with parallax. Bidirectional texture functions (BTFs) [5] capture this appearance directly by measuring a planar sample under many light and view directions, and measured BTF datasets such as UBO2014 [46] remain the reference for realistic material appearance. Analytic SVBRDFs, such as the metallic–roughness model of most material generators [3, 18], cannot represent such complex effects, which give real materials their realism (Sec.4.1).

The price of this fidelity is size. A single UBO2014 material is 400×400 texels under 151×151 light–view pairs, about 10¹⁰ values, and creating a new material requires a new capture. Neural BTF representations reduce the storage by decoding per-texel latent features with a small network: latent maps [33, 34], feature textures with neural offsets [22, 47], or feature planes [10]. These representations reconstruct well, but store a feature vector per texel and are not designed to sample new materials. Generative material models, on the other hand, learn from large synthetic corpora or from single flash photographs and produce parametric SVBRDFs [13, 61, 28] or neural materials fitted to synthetic data [32]; none of them learns from measured BTFs, of which only about a hundred are publicly available.

We bring the two together: a representation of measured BTFs that is accurate and compact, and whose codes can be sampled. We achieve this in three steps (Fig.2). A per-material coordinate network gives the most accurate representation. A compact model replaces the per-material network by a single global code per material and a shared decoder, so a material is described by 256 floats. Because each material is a point in this low-dimensional space, the codes also lend themselves to generation, which we explore with a flow model [26, 25] trained on the codes: it samples materials, and the same decoder renders them as full BTFs with measured angular behaviour.

Measured BTF datasets are inherently small, with UBO2014 containing only twelve materials per class, making it difficult to learn a distribution of material appearances. To address this limitation, we augment the training set through colourway transfer, combining the measured structure of one material with the colour characteristics of another material from the same class. This expands the dataset from 84 to 886 materials, so that the generator learns colour variation over the measured structures.

In summary, we contribute:

  • •

    a per-material neural BTF that outperforms all neural BTF baselines at comparable size (2.6–3.4M values per material);

  • •

    a compact model with one 256-float code per material and a shared decoder that exceeds the PSNR and colour accuracy of the per-texel latent maps of Rainer et al.[34] with 14× fewer values per material, even counting the shared decoder;

  • •

    a code space in which measured BTFs can be sampled: a class-conditional flow over the codes learns the distribution of 84 captures enlarged with colourways and hue rotations (released as an augmented dataset of 886 materials), and its samples render and relight as full BTFs.

    • 2 Related Work

    Measured BTFs and neural materials.

    BTFs were introduced by Dana et al.[5]; UBO2014 [46] provides 84 measured materials in seven classes at 151×151 light–view pairs and is distributed as a rank-limited factorisation. Classic compression factorises the six-dimensional function linearly or sparsely [19].
