    Dummy Forcing[11]: It exploits the varying historical context requirements of attention heads through heterogeneous memory allocation, dynamic head programming, and context packing.

  • •

    Forcing-KV[15]: To reduce historical KV redundancy, it distinguishes static and dynamic attention heads, applying structured pruning and similarity based pruning to their respective caches.

  • •

    Light Forcing[24]: It targets attention overhead in autoregressive video generation through chunk aware sparsity allocation and hierarchical selection of historical frames and spatial blocks. Unlike the other baselines, it requires additional post training.

    • Appendix B Hyperparameter Analysis

    Figure 5 examines the effects of key hyperparameters on generation quality and inference efficiency. As shown in Figure 5 (a,b), increasing the historical reading budget generally improves quality at the cost of inference speed, while larger budgets do not necessarily yield further gains. The default budget B=2LH achieves the highest Total Score on both backbones with a favorable speedup. Figure 5 (c-e) further evaluates the shallow feature projection dimension rₛ, staleness threshold A, and regularization scale λ/m. Performance remains relatively stable across different projection dimensions and staleness thresholds, while λ/m=1 achieves the best quality. These results demonstrate the robustness of ScoutCache to moderate hyperparameter variations.

    Appendix C Runtime Breakdown

    Diffusion Time Breakdown. To identify the sources of acceleration, we decompose the complete diffusion generation time into denoising, KV cache construction, and other overhead. As shown in Table 4, ScoutCache consistently reduces both denoising and cache construction costs across different video durations and backbones. Compared with Dummy Forcing, denoising time decreases by 25.4% and 23.6%, while KV cache construction time decreases by 19.3% and 17.5% for 120s generation on Self-Forcing and LongLive, respectively. Consequently, the total latency drops to 115.78s on both backbones, with minimal calibration and other overhead. Similar improvements are observed at shorter durations, demonstrating that ScoutCache achieves consistent efficiency gains by reducing computation in both major stages of diffusion generation.

    KV Cache Construction. We further isolate the cost of KV cache construction to evaluate the effectiveness of CCSC. As shown in Table 5, CCSC reduces the number of processed tokens from 4,680 to 3,510, decreasing construction latency by approximately 22% on both backbones. In contrast, compressing the KV cache after dense construction still requires processing all tokens and introduces additional overhead. Compared with this approach, CCSC reduces construction latency by approximately 25%, demonstrating the advantage of selecting spatial positions before Transformer processing.

一句话：加速方法各管一段，但历史 KV 读取与缓存构建在跨 chunk 时依然很贵。

要点：

  • 问题：少步自回归视频扩散能高效生成长视频，但推理仍因**反复去噪与 KV 缓存操作**付出大量算力；已有加速方法只各自削掉一部分开销，而**历史 KV 读取与缓存构建**在跨视频 chunk 时仍然很贵
  • ScoutCache 是**免训练**框架，同时优化三处：用 Conditional Denoising Readout 从浅层特征变化估计去噪更新；用 Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading 按注意力输出扰动分配历史读取预算；用 Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction 在保持空间覆盖的前提下挑信息量大的 token
  • 在 Self-Forcing 与 LongLive 上结合 VBench / MovieGen 测，分别取得最高 **2.28× 与 1.86×** 加速

为什么值得看：实时生成视频的成本大头往往不在「采样步数」而在「缓存怎么读」。这条把三处开销一起优化且不需要重训，属于那种能直接叠在现有管线上的加速。

中文摘要：少步自回归视频扩散让长视频生成变得高效，但推理时仍要为反复去噪与 KV 缓存操作付出可观算力。既有加速方法通常只削掉其中一部分开销，而「历史 KV 读取」与「缓存构建」在跨视频 chunk 时依然昂贵。ScoutCache 是一个免训练框架，同时优化三件事：其一是 Conditional Denoising Readout，利用浅层特征的变化来估计干净的潜变量更新；其二是 Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading，依据注意力输出的扰动来分配历史读取预算；其三是 Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction，在维持空间覆盖的前提下挑选信息量更高的 token 以降低缓存构建成本。作者指出历史 KV 的依赖程度随 Transformer 层与注意力头而变、但在不同视频 chunk 之间相对稳定，这为按需读取提供了依据。在 Self-Forcing 与 LongLive 上结合 VBench 与 MovieGen 评测，分别取得最高 2.28 倍与 1.86 倍加速。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-18

ScoutCache: Efficient Few-Step Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Conditional Readout and Selective Caching

Abstract

Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28× and 1.86× speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.

1  Introduction

Autoregressive video diffusion models have emerged as a promising approach to long-form video generation, synthesizing videos chunk by chunk while conditioning on previously generated content [13, 40, 3, 4]. Recent advances in few-step diffusion have further improved generation efficiency by substantially reducing the number of denoising iterations [42, 21]. For example, Self Forcing [13] enables efficient autoregressive generation through few-step denoising and KV caching, while LongLive [40] supports real-time long-video generation with short-window attention and a frame-level attention sink. However, despite these advances, autoregressive inference still involves substantial computational overhead, particularly when maintaining historical context across video chunks [34, 10]. In the few-step KV-cached setting, each video chunk requires repeated Transformer evaluations for denoising, historical KV reads to maintain temporal context, and an additional forward pass to construct KV caches for subsequent generation [9]. These recurring operations remain a significant bottleneck to efficient long-video generation.

Existing training-free acceleration methods reduce video diffusion costs by reusing model outputs across denoising steps [20, 25], caching attention features [44], or adapting cache reuse to video content [16]. Recent studies have also explored computation reuse across video chunks [28] and more selective access to historical KV caches [15, 30]. However, these approaches face different constraints in few-step autoregressive generation. With only a few denoising steps per chunk, there are fewer opportunities to reuse previous results, while changes in the current noisy input may still affect the prediction. Moreover, reducing historical attention requires identifying which past information is useful, and compressing KV caches after their construction leaves the computation spent on discarded representations unchanged. These challenges motivate a closer examination of how denoising predictions evolve and how historical information is utilized during few-step autoregressive video generation.

Examining consecutive denoising steps reveals that useful information about prediction updates is already present in shallow features. As shown in Figure 1 (a), changes in shallow features between consecutive denoising steps exhibit spatial correspondence with changes in the clean latent estimates produced by the full denoising network. This observation indicates that shallow features already capture part of how the prediction evolves, providing an opportunity to reduce repeated deep-network computation. Historical attention exhibits a different pattern. As shown in Figure 1 (b), different Transformer layers and attention heads rely on the historical KV cache to different degrees, but these differences remain largely stable across consecutive video chunks. This stability suggests that historical attention behavior observed in earlier chunks can guide subsequent generation, reducing the need to repeatedly assess how much of the historical KV cache each layer and head requires. Beyond reading the historical KV cache, constructing the cache for subsequent video chunks also incurs computational cost. After each chunk is generated, the model performs an additional forward pass to construct its KV representations. Compressing these representations afterward leaves the computation for discarded positions unchanged, highlighting the need to reduce the cost of KV cache construction itself.

Motivated by these findings, we propose ScoutCache, a unified training-free inference acceleration framework integrating denoising and KV cache optimization for few-step autoregressive video diffusion models. Specifically, ScoutCache introduces a Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) that estimates clean latent updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. Calibrated on early video chunks, this readout bypasses most Transformer layers at an intermediate denoising step while retaining the final refinement by the full network. To improve historical attention efficiency, we develop Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR), which measures the effect of removing cached frames on attention outputs and allocates reading budgets across Transformer layers and heads. The resulting allocation is reused across subsequent video chunks to avoid repeated evaluation. Finally, we introduce Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) that selects spatial positions based on content changes and spatial coverage before Transformer processing. This strategy reduces KV cache construction costs through sparse computation, while retaining dense representations of recent frames and a fixed historical anchor to preserve useful historical context. All components operate without modifying pretrained model parameters.

Experiments on VBench [14] and MovieGen [29] with Self-Forcing [13] and LongLive [40] demonstrate improvements in both inference efficiency and video quality. For shorter videos, ScoutCache achieves 2.19× and 1.83× speedups with quality improvements of 1.52% and 1.21%, respectively. For longer videos, it achieves 2.28× and 1.86× speedups with corresponding quality improvements of 5.44% and 1.11%. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We highlight the importance of shallow feature changes and stable historical attention dependencies for efficient few-step autoregressive video generation.

  • •

    We propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction.

  • •

    Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving both inference efficiency and video quality.

    • 2  Related work

    Autoregressive Video Generation. Autoregressive video generation enables long video synthesis by generating successive frames or chunks conditioned on previously generated content. Early approaches improved temporal continuity through chunkwise conditioning and progressive denoising [12, 38], while asynchronous diffusion and continuous visual representations introduced alternative generation formulations [33, 8]. Recent studies have further explored flexible generation schedules [26] and real-time streaming through few-step diffusion [13, 40], and adversarial post-training [19]. Other efforts improve causal distillation [45] and long-context modeling [7] to enhance generation quality and temporal consistency. Despite these advances, autoregressive generation still requires repeated denoising and historical context processing across video chunks. ScoutCache addresses these costs by estimating denoising updates from shallow features, allocating historical KV reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and selecting spatial tokens before Transformer processing.

    Diffusion Acceleration. Diffusion acceleration aims to reduce the computational overhead of iterative denoising. Existing methods exploit temporal redundancy by reusing encoder features [27], intermediate block outputs [35], or feature representations across denoising steps [32, 18]. Recent approaches extend feature caching to diffusion Transformers, adapting reuse strategies according to network depth and denoising stages [6, 31]. Other studies reduce redundant cross-attention computation [43] or merge similar tokens to accelerate inference [1]. However, these methods are primarily developed for conventional diffusion models, and their reuse strategies may be less effective in few-step autoregressive generation. ScoutCache addresses this challenge by estimating current denoising updates from shallow features, reducing deep-network computation while preserving final prediction refinement.

    KV Cache Optimization. KV cache optimization plays an important role in reducing the memory and attention costs of autoregressive video generation. Recent methods explore sparse historical attention [24] and adaptive KV selection based on frame relevance and attention head characteristics [2, 5]. Other approaches estimate future cache utility [23], identify informative historical tokens [37], or consolidate older representations into compact memory [22]. KV quantization [36] and cache maintenance strategies [17] further improve memory efficiency during long video generation. However, these methods mainly focus on which historical representations to retain or access. ScoutCache further considers the cost of generating these representations, combining calibrated historical KV reading with sparse cache construction to reduce computation.

    3  Method

    3.1  Problem Formulation

    We consider the inference-time acceleration of pretrained few-step autoregressive video diffusion models that generate latent chunks conditioned on previously generated content. Given a text condition c, let x_b⁽ˢ⁾ and z_b⁽ˢ⁾ denote the noisy input and predicted clean latent of chunk b at denoising step s, respectively. Each chunk contains three latent frames and undergoes four denoising steps, with re-noising applied after the first three steps:

    z_b⁽ˢ⁾=D_θ(x_b⁽ˢ⁾,tₛ,c,M_b-1),(1)
    x_b⁽ˢ⁺¹⁾=(1-σₛ₊₁)z_b⁽ˢ⁾+σₛ₊₁ε_b⁽ˢ⁺¹⁾.

    Here, D_θ is the denoising network with fixed pretrained parameters θ, σₛ=tₛ/1000 is the noise coefficient, and ε_b⁽ˢ⁾∼ℕ(0,I) is Gaussian noise, with x_b⁽¹⁾=ε_b⁽¹⁾. The historical KV cache M_b-1 provides temporal context from preceding chunks. After denoising, z_b⁽⁴⁾ is decoded into video frames, and an additional forward pass at the zero-noise timestep constructs KV representations for subsequent chunks.

    As illustrated in Figure 2, ScoutCache integrates three complementary components. CDR estimates intermediate clean latent updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. ORHR allocates historical KV reading budgets across layers and heads according to attention output perturbations, while CCSC reduces cache construction costs by selecting spatial tokens before Transformer processing. CDR and ORHR are calibrated on early chunks, and all components operate without modifying pretrained model parameters.

    3.2  Conditional Denoising Readout

    Motivated by the spatial correspondence observed in Figure 1 (a), CDR estimates clean latent updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. As illustrated in Figure 2 (a), it uses the full prediction at the second denoising step as a reference, evaluates only the first Transformer layer at the third step to estimate the update, and retains the full fourth step for final refinement. Let H_b⁽²⁾,H_b⁽³⁾∈ℝ^N×d denote the first Transformer layer outputs at the second and third denoising steps, where N is the number of tokens per chunk and d is the hidden dimension. To characterize the prediction update, we construct a conditioning feature that combines the known noise variation with the corresponding shallow feature difference:

    Φ_b=[ℙ(σ₃ε_b⁽³⁾-σ₂ε_b⁽²⁾),(H_b⁽³⁾-H_b⁽²⁾)Pₛ,1_N],

    		(2)

    where ℙ rearranges the latent into N patches of dimension p, and Pₛ∈ℝ^d×rₛ is a fixed Gaussian projection with entries independently sampled from ℕ(0,1/d), and rₛ denotes the shallow feature projection dimension. The resulting Φ_b∈ℝ^N×m, with m=p+rₛ+1, includes a constant column 1_N for the intercept. The noise term accounts for stochastic variations introduced by sampling, while the shallow feature difference captures the network response to the current latent and historical context. We calibrate the mapping from Φ_b to clean latent updates using the second and third generated chunks, where full denoising predictions are available. For each calibration chunk, the target update is defined as Y_b=ℙ(z_b⁽³⁾-z_b⁽²⁾). Stacking the conditioning features and target updates from both chunks yields X∈ℝ^2N×m and Y∈ℝ^2N×p. To account for differences in feature scales, we normalize the columns of X using a diagonal RMS scaling matrix D, whose diagonal entries are lower bounded by 10⁻³. The readout mapping is then obtained through regularized least squares:

    Z=XD⁻¹,(3)
    B=D⁻¹(Z^⊤Z+λΛ)⁻¹Z^⊤Y.

    where Z∈ℝ^2N×m is the normalized conditioning matrix, and B∈ℝ^m×p maps conditioning features to clean latent updates. Λ=diag(1,…,1,0) excludes the intercept from regularization, and λ=m controls the regularization strength. Feature normalization balances the contributions of noise variations and shallow feature differences, while regularization stabilizes the mapping estimated from a short video prefix. The resulting B is computed once per video and shared across subsequent chunks.

    For subsequent chunks b≥4, CDR executes only the first Transformer layer at the third denoising step and estimates the clean latent as:

    ẑ_b⁽³⁾=ℙ⁻¹(ℙ(z_b⁽²⁾)+Φ_bB),

    		(4)

    where ẑ_b⁽³⁾ denotes the estimated clean latent at the third denoising step, and ℙ⁻¹ restores the original latent layout. The predicted update Φ_bB adapts to the current chunk, allowing CDR to bypass the remaining Transformer layers at this step. The estimated latent is then used to construct the next noisy input following Eq. 1, while the fourth denoising step is evaluated using the full network for final refinement.

    3.3  Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading

    The varying yet stable historical dependencies observed in Figure 1 (b) motivate ORHR to allocate historical reading budgets based on the impact of cache removal on attention outputs, as illustrated in Figure 2 (b). The historical cache consists of four frame regions ℝ={0,1,2,3}, including the first latent frame of the video as a fixed anchor and the three frames from the preceding chunk. The current chunk, denoted by ∗, always participates in attention. For each Transformer layer ℓ and attention head h, ORHR selects a nonempty subset S_ℓh⊆ℝ of historical regions to access.

    To efficiently evaluate different historical subsets, we decompose attention into reusable regional statistics. For a query q, let oᵣ(q) denote the attention output normalized within region r, and ηᵣ(q)=\log∑_j∈r\exp(q^⊤kⱼ/√dₕ) denote its log normalization factor, where kⱼ is the key vector at position j and dₕ is the attention head dimension. Here, oᵣ(q) is the attention weighted average of the corresponding value vectors. The attention output for any historical subset S⊆ℝ can be reconstructed as:

    a(q;S)=(∑_r∈S∪{∗}\exp(ηᵣ(q))oᵣ(q))/(∑_r∈S∪{∗}\exp(ηᵣ(q))),

    		(5)

    where a(q;S) denotes the attention output using the selected historical regions and the current chunk. This formulation preserves softmax normalization while allowing regional statistics to be reused across candidate subsets. ORHR evaluates the perturbation after attention output projection using regional statistics collected from the third generated chunk over a fixed query set ℚ. Let T_ℓ denote the calibration steps for layer ℓ, including all four steps for the first layer and steps 1, 2, and 4 for deeper layers, consistent with CDR. The output risk of a historical subset S is defined as:

    e_ℓh⁽ˢ⁾(q;S)=([a_ℓh⁽ˢ⁾(q;S)-a_ℓh⁽ˢ⁾(q;ℝ)]W_ℓh^OΠ)/(ρ_ℓs),(6)
    R_ℓh(S)=(∑_s∈T_ℓ∑_q∈ℚ∥e_ℓh⁽ˢ⁾(q;S)∥₂²)/(|T_ℓ||ℚ|rₒ),

    where a_ℓh⁽ˢ⁾ denotes the attention output at layer ℓ, head h, and step s, and W_ℓh^O∈ℝ^dₕ×d is the corresponding output projection. Π∈ℝ^d×rₒ is a fixed Gaussian projection with entries independently sampled from ℕ(0,1/rₒ), where rₒ denotes the projection dimension. The normalization factor ρ_ℓs is the RMS magnitude of the projected full-history attention output aggregated across heads and measured over calibration queries and channels, lower bounded by 10⁻⁴. Accordingly, e_ℓh⁽ˢ⁾(q;S) represents the normalized output perturbation, and R_ℓh(S) measures its average squared magnitude, ensuring comparable risk scales across layers and steps.

    Based on the estimated risks, we allocate a global historical reading budget across the network. Since the squared norm of the aggregated head perturbations is bounded by H times the sum of their squared norms, minimizing individual risks provides a tractable surrogate for controlling the combined output perturbation. We formulate the allocation as:

    \min_{S_ℓh}∑_ℓ=1^L∑ₕ₌₁^HR_ℓh(S_ℓh),(7)
    s.t.∑_ℓ,h|S_ℓh|≤B, 1≤|S_ℓh|≤4,

    where L and H denote the numbers of Transformer layers and attention heads, |S_ℓh| is the number of selected historical frames, and B is the global reading budget in frame accesses. We solve Eq. 7 greedily, initializing each head with its lowest risk historical frame and iteratively adding the frame with the largest marginal risk reduction. We set B=2LH, providing an average budget of two historical frames per head while allowing individual heads to access one to four frames. The resulting policy is calibrated once and reused across subsequent chunks as recent regions are updated. During inference, selected historical KV representations are packed with current chunk representations for variable length attention computation.

    3.4  Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction

    While ORHR reduces historical KV reading costs, CCSC targets the additional forward pass for KV cache construction by selecting informative spatial positions before Transformer processing. The first three video chunks use dense cache construction for calibration. From the fourth chunk onward, CCSC constructs sparse representations for the first frame while retaining dense representations for the remaining two frames, as illustrated in Figure 2 (c).

    For each generated latent frame f, we apply 2×2 average pooling to its clean latent prediction to obtain spatial proxy features g_f(i)∈ℝ^C_z aligned with the Transformer token grid, where i denotes a spatial position and C_z is the latent channel dimension. Each position maintains its last selected proxy ḡ(i), a visited indicator v(i), and an age a_f(i) counting frames since its last selection. We define the content change and selection priority as:

    δ_f(i)=(∥g_f(i)-ḡ(i)∥₂)/(√C_z),(8)
    u_f(i)=δ_f(i)
    +(1+\maxⱼδ_f(j))1[v(i)=0∨a_f(i)≥A],

    where δ_f(i) measures the content change since the position was last selected, and A is the staleness threshold. The stored proxies are initialized using the spatial mean of the first latent frame. For unvisited or stale positions, the additional priority term exceeds the maximum content change in the current frame, promoting their refresh. To maintain spatial coverage, we divide the token grid into nonoverlapping 2×2 groups G and select the highest priority position in each group as I_f={\arg\max_i∈Gu_f(i)|G∈G}, where G denotes a spatial group and I_f contains P/4 selected positions. For each selected position i∈I_f, we update ḡ(i)=g_f(i), set v(i)=1, and reset a_f(i)=0, while the ages of unselected positions increase by one per frame. These states are updated sequentially across generated frames, while sparse cache construction is applied to the first frame of each chunk from the fourth chunk onward. For each chunk b≥4, the positions processed during cache construction are:

    J_b=({1}×I_b,1)∪({2,3}×{1,…,P}),

    		(9)

    where I_b,1 denotes the selected positions in the first frame of chunk b, P is the number of spatial tokens per latent frame, and the indices {1,2,3} identify its three latent frames. Consequently, |J_b|=P/4+2P=3N/4, reducing the number of processed tokens by 25% while preserving dense representations for the two most recent frames.

    After patch embedding, only the selected tokens enter the Transformer, with their original spatiotemporal coordinates preserved for rotary positional encoding. However, representing four neighboring positions with a single token reduces their aggregate contribution to attention normalization. To compensate for this effect, we introduce multiplicity weighted attention:

    Attn(q)=softmax((qK^⊤)/(√dₕ)+\logm^⊤)V.

    		(10)

    where q is the query vector, K and V contain the participating key and value vectors, and dₕ is the attention head dimension. The multiplicity vector m assigns mⱼ=4 to sparse representatives and mⱼ=1 to dense tokens, accounting for the four spatial slots represented by each sparse token in attention normalization. We implement this weighting by replicating each representative’s position-encoded KV vectors into its corresponding four slots, preserving the regular cache layout without additional Transformer computation. The new KV representations are constructed using the existing historical cache and replace the previous recent chunk only after all Transformer layers have been processed. The fixed dense anchor remains unchanged, while the expanded KV representations form the updated three-frame history, maintaining compatibility with ORHR’s historical reading policy.

    4  Experiments

    4.1  Experimental Setup

    Implementation Details. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 40GB GPU using PyTorch with BF16 precision and a batch size of 1. Videos are generated at 832 × 480 resolution and 16 FPS, with four denoising steps per chunk of three latent frames. ScoutCache performs full computation for the first three chunks and enables acceleration thereafter. CDR uses a shallow feature projection dimension rₛ=128 and regularization strength λ=m=193, with the readout mapping calibrated on chunks 2–3 and applied at the third denoising step. ORHR uses a random projection dimension rₒ=32, 120 calibration queries from the third chunk, and a global historical reading budget B=720=2LH. CCSC sets the staleness threshold A=18 and selects one position per 2×2 spatial group, reducing cache construction to 3,510 processed tokens per chunk.

    Backbones and Baselines. We evaluate ScoutCache on Self-Forcing [13] and LongLive [40], using their publicly released 1.3B checkpoints. We compare with six training-free methods, including TeaCache [20], FlowCache [28], MotionCache [39], SVG2 [41], Dummy Forcing [11], and Forcing-KV [15], as well as Light Forcing [24], which requires 2,000 additional post-training iterations on pretrained weights. We evaluate it using its officially released checkpoint. The original backbones serve as references for both quality and efficiency. For all training-free baselines, we adopt their official implementations and released hyperparameter configurations, including method-specific caching settings. Within each backbone, these methods share the same pretrained weights, prompts, random seeds, resolution, and sampling schedule.

    Benchmarks and Metrics. We evaluate video quality on VBench [14] and MovieGen [29] using five random seeds per prompt. For VBench, we generate 5-second videos from all 946 prompts and report the official Total Scores across 16 dimensions. For MovieGen, we use the first 128 prompts from Self-Forcing’s extended prompt list to generate videos of 30, 60, and 120 seconds. Following Forcing-KV [15], we evaluate six VBench-Long dimensions: subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic quality, and imaging quality. These six dimensions are aggregated into a Total Score following the official VBench normalization rules and corresponding weights. Efficiency is measured by latency, generation FPS, and speedup. Latency measures the complete diffusion generation time, including online calibration, denoising, sampling updates, and cache maintenance. Speedup is the ratio of backbone to method latency, while generation FPS denotes inference throughput.

    4.2  Main Results

    Results on Self-Forcing. Table 1 compares ScoutCache with existing acceleration methods on Self-Forcing across different video durations. ScoutCache achieves the lowest latency, highest generation FPS, and highest Total Score in all four settings. Specifically, it delivers a 1.60× speedup on VBench and 2.19×, 2.25×, and 2.28× speedups on MovieGen at 30, 60, and 120 seconds, respectively. The increasing speedup with video duration reflects the reduced relative overhead of initial calibration. Notably, for 120-second generation, ScoutCache reduces latency from 264.32s to 115.78s while improving the Total Score from 75.03 to 79.11, corresponding to a 5.44% relative quality improvement. We further conduct two-sided paired t-tests over five matched random seeds against the strongest competing method at each duration. The mean Total Score improvements are 0.11, 0.19, 0.36, and 0.09 points for 5s, 30s, 60s, and 120s, respectively, with corresponding 95% confidence intervals of [0.085, 0.135], [0.165, 0.215], [0.335, 0.385], and [0.065, 0.115]. All improvements are statistically significant (p<0.001).

    Results on LongLive. To further validate the effectiveness of ScoutCache across different autoregressive backbones, we evaluate it on LongLive. As shown in Table 2, ScoutCache consistently achieves the lowest latency and highest generation FPS across all video durations, delivering a 1.52× speedup on VBench and 1.83×, 1.85×, and 1.86× speedups on MovieGen at 30, 60, and 120 seconds, respectively. In terms of generation quality, ScoutCache improves the Total Score over the original LongLive in all settings and achieves the highest scores across all three MovieGen durations. Notably, for 120-second generation, it reduces latency from 215.83s to 115.78s while improving the Total Score from 80.06 to 80.95. We further conduct two-sided paired t-tests over five matched random seeds against Forcing-KV, the strongest competing method across all three MovieGen durations. The mean Total Score improvements are 0.54, 0.73, and 0.51 points for 30s, 60s, and 120s, respectively, with corresponding 95% confidence intervals of [0.410, 0.670], [0.580, 0.880], and [0.348, 0.672]. All improvements are statistically significant (p<0.001). Together with the results on Self-Forcing, these findings demonstrate that ScoutCache consistently improves inference efficiency and generation quality across different autoregressive video diffusion backbones.

    4.3  Ablation Studies

    Table 3 evaluates the contributions of CDR, ORHR, and CCSC, with additional experiments across video durations and backbones. On Self-Forcing, using a fixed four-frame history reduces the 30s latency from 65.59s to 39.47s, while CDR alone further reduces it to 32.23s. Combining all three components achieves 29.99s with a Total Score of 80.30. Removing CDR increases latency to 36.29s, confirming its major contribution to denoising acceleration. ORHR is important for generation quality, as its removal decreases the Total Score by 0.47 points. Assigning two historical frames to each head or estimating risk before output projection also leads to lower quality, supporting the proposed risk guided allocation. CCSC provides additional efficiency gains, with its removal increasing the 120s latency from 115.78s to 123.10s. The consistent trends on LongLive further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the three components across different backbones and video durations.

    4.4  Chunkwise Latency Analysis

    We further examine how the efficiency gains of ScoutCache evolve across video chunks. As shown in Fig. 4, ScoutCache achieves a substantial latency reduction from the fourth chunk onward and maintains stable performance throughout 160 chunks. After the initial calibration, its average per-chunk latency reaches 0.72s on Self-Forcing and 0.70s on LongLive, representing reductions of 25.0% and 23.5% compared with Dummy Forcing, respectively. While the original backbones exhibit increasing latency during early generation, ScoutCache maintains consistently low latency across subsequent chunks. These results demonstrate that ScoutCache provides sustained acceleration without increasing per-chunk overhead as video generation progresses.

    4.5  Qualitative Results

    As shown in Figure 3, ScoutCache preserves visual details and scene structure while substantially reducing generation time. In the abandoned street example, the original Self-Forcing exhibits severe color distortions and loses much of the scene detail, while Forcing-KV shows noticeable blurring in some frames. In contrast, ScoutCache maintains clear balloon contours and recognizable building structures throughout the sampled frames. These observations complement the quantitative results, demonstrating that ScoutCache achieves substantial acceleration while retaining strong visual quality across diverse scenes and video durations.

    Due to space limitations, further analyses of hyperparameter sensitivity, runtime breakdowns, and component mechanisms, along with additional qualitative comparisons and detailed video quality scores, are provided in the supplementary material.

    5  Conclusion

    In this paper, we introduced ScoutCache, a training-free framework for accelerating few-step autoregressive video diffusion. ScoutCache improves inference efficiency by jointly reducing the computational costs of denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. Specifically, we develop CDR to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce ORHR to allocate historical KV reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and CCSC to reduce cache construction costs through spatial token selection guided by content changes and spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28× and 1.86× speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality across different video durations. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of jointly optimizing denoising and KV cache operations for efficient long video generation without modifying pretrained model parameters.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Baseline Methods

    We compare ScoutCache with six representative training-free acceleration methods, including TeaCache[20], FlowCache[28], MotionCache[39], SVG2[41], Dummy Forcing[11], and Forcing-KV[15], as well as the training-based Light Forcing[24]. A brief introduction to each baseline is provided below:

  • •

    TeaCache[20]: It focuses on reusing denoising outputs by estimating their changes from timestep embedding modulated inputs, with polynomial rescaling to improve estimation accuracy.

  • •

    FlowCache[28]: To accommodate varying redundancy across video chunks, it adopts adaptive chunkwise feature caching and compresses historical KV caches based on importance and redundancy.

  • •

    MotionCache[39]: It exploits motion differences between video frames to guide token level cache reuse, allowing more frequent updates in dynamic regions while reducing computation in static areas.

  • •

    SVG2[41]: By clustering and reordering tokens according to semantic similarity, it improves sparse attention efficiency through more accurate token selection and dynamic computation budgets.

  • •

    Dummy Forcing[11]: It exploits the varying historical context requirements of attention heads through heterogeneous memory allocation, dynamic head programming, and context packing.

  • •

    Forcing-KV[15]: To reduce historical KV redundancy, it distinguishes static and dynamic attention heads, applying structured pruning and similarity based pruning to their respective caches.

  • •

    Light Forcing[24]: It targets attention overhead in autoregressive video generation through chunk aware sparsity allocation and hierarchical selection of historical frames and spatial blocks. Unlike the other baselines, it requires additional post training.

    • Appendix B Hyperparameter Analysis

    Figure 5 examines the effects of key hyperparameters on generation quality and inference efficiency. As shown in Figure 5 (a,b), increasing the historical reading budget generally improves quality at the cost of inference speed, while larger budgets do not necessarily yield further gains. The default budget B=2LH achieves the highest Total Score on both backbones with a favorable speedup. Figure 5 (c-e) further evaluates the shallow feature projection dimension rₛ, staleness threshold A, and regularization scale λ/m. Performance remains relatively stable across different projection dimensions and staleness thresholds, while λ/m=1 achieves the best quality. These results demonstrate the robustness of ScoutCache to moderate hyperparameter variations.

    Appendix C Runtime Breakdown

    Diffusion Time Breakdown. To identify the sources of acceleration, we decompose the complete diffusion generation time into denoising, KV cache construction, and other overhead. As shown in Table 4, ScoutCache consistently reduces both denoising and cache construction costs across different video durations and backbones. Compared with Dummy Forcing, denoising time decreases by 25.4% and 23.6%, while KV cache construction time decreases by 19.3% and 17.5% for 120s generation on Self-Forcing and LongLive, respectively. Consequently, the total latency drops to 115.78s on both backbones, with minimal calibration and other overhead. Similar improvements are observed at shorter durations, demonstrating that ScoutCache achieves consistent efficiency gains by reducing computation in both major stages of diffusion generation.

    KV Cache Construction. We further isolate the cost of KV cache construction to evaluate the effectiveness of CCSC. As shown in Table 5, CCSC reduces the number of processed tokens from 4,680 to 3,510, decreasing construction latency by approximately 22% on both backbones. In contrast, compressing the KV cache after dense construction still requires processing all tokens and introduces additional overhead. Compared with this approach, CCSC reduces construction latency by approximately 25%, demonstrating the advantage of selecting spatial positions before Transformer processing.

item.title: 固定 PD 增益让「动作跟踪」与「接触力准确」互斥：ImpedanceMimic 把阻抗本身当成动作空间来学 ｜ ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
item.description:
一句话：同一段动作可以由不同控制器复现，但产生的接触力并不一样——这是个病态问题。

要点：

  • 问题本质：从动作反推力是**病态的**——不同控制器可以复现同一段运动，却产生不同的接触力；基于物理的动作模仿靠仿真消解这个歧义，但依赖**固定增益的 PD 控制**
  • 作者证明固定增益会强加一个取舍：**接触与摆动对关节刚度的需求是冲突的**，于是动作跟踪与力跟踪无法同时做好
  • ImpedanceMimic 因此把**学到的阻抗（impedance）作为动作空间**，让刚度本身随情境变化，从而实现力准确的模仿

为什么值得看：角色碰物体、推门、踩地面，力不对就会穿模或飘。把阻抗当动作空间，等于让控制系统自己决定「该多硬」，这是物理驱动角色动画从「像」走向「有重量感」的关键一步。

中文摘要：从一段动作反推其背后的力是病态问题：不同控制器可以复现同一段运动，却产生不同的接触力。基于物理的动作模仿通过仿真来消解这种歧义，但通常依赖固定增益的比例-微分（PD）控制。作者指出，固定增益会强加一种取舍：接触阶段与摆动阶段对关节刚度的需求彼此冲突，因此在动作跟踪与力跟踪之间无法两全。ImpedanceMimic 因此改变动作空间本身——把学到的阻抗作为动作表示，让刚度随情境自适应，从而在保持动作模仿质量的同时实现力的准确复现。对需要「有重量感」的角色与物体交互，这条从控制表示层面解决问题。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv::cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-17

本期推送：2026-11-18

ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action
Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation

Abstract

Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional–derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

1 Introduction

Movement is governed by forces, which in locomotion arise from foot–ground contact and determine a sprinter’s acceleration, a patient’s loading asymmetry and a humanoid robot’s balance. Cameras have made motion datasets abundant [(Ionescu et al., 2014; Mahmood et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2026)], but force data remains scarce. Force plates confine recordings to the laboratory, and wearable insoles resolve only the normal component and drift over time [(Koch et al., 2016)]. Recovering forces from motion alone would extend movement analysis into natural, unconstrained settings.

Recent corpora synchronize motion capture with force-plate measurements [(Werling et al., 2024)], extending beyond steady gait to tasks like cutting, lunging and jumping [(Scherpereel et al., 2023)]. Learning-based methods use such data to map kinematics to ground reaction forces (GRF), either through direct regression [(Mourot et al., 2022)] or generative modeling [(Tan et al., 2026)]. Their predictions can violate physics, for example by loading the ground during flight or placing the center of pressure (CoP) outside the foot, since a loss term at best encourages physical consistency. The learned mapping is also opaque, going from motion to force directly without modeling the actuation and body dynamics that produce it, and therefore cannot drive a simulated body or robot.

Physics-based motion imitation addresses both limitations. Tracking a recorded motion in a physics engine yields contact forces that are dynamically consistent by construction [(Peng et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2023)], and the controller producing these forces is explicitly defined. However, dynamic consistency does not imply agreement with measured forces. Most imitation policies output joint-position targets, which a proportional–derivative (PD) controller with hand-tuned gains converts into joint torques to drive the simulated body [(Peng & Van De Panne, 2017)]. Different gains can track the same motion, yet produce different contact forces. Recent work incorporates measured force as an observation [(Hori et al., 2026)] or a reward [(Liu et al., 2026)], but fixes the gains and reports accuracy either with force sensors available at inference or on a single participant. Alternative actuation models, including learned gains [(Yuan et al., 2021)], muscle models [(Li et al., 2026)] and direct torque control [(Cotton, 2025)], have not been systematically evaluated against measured forces.

Here, we present ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning imitation policy that outputs per-joint stiffness, damping and position setpoints, supervised by reference kinematics, force-plate GRF and CoP. On 129 participants, nine datasets and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms fixed-PD, direct-torque, muscle and existing imitation controllers on kinematic and force accuracy. To our knowledge, no prior controller reproduces measured per-foot contact forces across subjects and activities, including unseen ones, without force at inference. We contribute:

  • 1.

    Action-space bounds on force recovery. We derive a lower bound on stiffness, set by the torque the reference force demands, and an upper bound on damping, set by discrete-time stability, which oppose each other between contact and swing. Empirically, a fixed-gain policy forfeits either motion or force tracking, whereas learned impedance satisfies both, extending the action-space analysis of [Peng & Van De Panne (2017)] to force.

  • 2.

    A morphology-agnostic controller. Expressing impedance as a scaled inertia prior, our policy, trained on 107 subject-specific models without anthropometric input, transfers zero-shot to 22 subjects and a simulated humanoid robot (G1). To our knowledge, this is the first physics-based imitator to transfer across unseen biomechanical and robotic embodiments.

  • 3.

    Learned impedance encodes motor state. The learned gains form a low-dimensional, interpretable representation in which stiffness scales with load and damping anticipates unloading. It generalizes to withheld activities better than fixed action spaces and identifies the activity from a single cycle of gains. This representation carries over to unseen subjects.

  • 4.

    An open benchmark. We release code, checkpoints and splits for a benchmark spanning 129 participants and six activities, with ablations, fixed-PD, direct-torque and muscle action spaces, and the existing methods PHC [(Luo et al., 2023)], SimPoE [(Yuan et al., 2021)] and GaitDynamics [(Tan et al., 2026)].

    • 2 Related Work

    Physics-based motion imitation.

    Executing a recorded motion in a simulator makes the resulting forces dynamically consistent. Reinforcement learning has made this routine at scale, from single-clip tracking [(Peng et al., 2018)] through adversarial objectives [(Peng et al., 2021)] to controllers covering large motion corpora [(Luo et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2024; Tessler et al., 2024)] and kinetic labeling [(Liu et al., 2025)]. These methods pursue a kinematic objective because they originate in character animation, where simulation corrects generated motion [(Yuan et al., 2023)] rather than recovering the forces behind it. Comparing action spaces on motion-tracking tasks, [Peng & Van De Panne (2017)] found fixed-gain PD control superior to torque, velocity and muscle parameterizations, and most later work adopted it. In biomechanics, trajectory optimization over musculoskeletal models [(Dembia et al., 2020)] estimates individual muscle forces, but each trial requires its own slow optimization. Recent work extends RL imitation to anatomically grounded models with torque or muscle actuation [(Cotton, 2025; Simos et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2026)], with limited validation of the resulting forces against measured ones. [Hori et al. (2026)] provide measured force as an observation and therefore need inertial and insole sensors at inference. [Liu et al. (2026)] add GRF and CoP to the reward, but validate on a single walking participant and rely on an external pelvis wrench [(Yuan & Kitani, 2020)]. ImpedanceMimic is trained on measured per-foot force and CoP from 129 participants and six activities, and needs neither sensors nor an external wrench at inference.

    Learned impedance control.

    Letting a policy set its own impedance originates in robotics, where variable stiffness and damping were learned to make contact-rich manipulation and legged hopping robust to contact uncertainty [(Buchli et al., 2011; Martín-Martín et al., 2019; Bogdanovic et al., 2020)], the contact force being a quantity to minimize rather than to reproduce. The idea has since entered physics-based character control and motion capture. SimPoE [(Yuan et al., 2021)] scales nominal gains at every PD step and adds a residual root wrench to the action, ReGAIL [(Boursin et al., 2025)] puts servo gains and damping in the action so that a controller can alternate tension and relaxation, and Neural PhysCap [(Shimada et al., 2021)] and OSDCap [(Le et al., 2024)] regress the gains from video, the latter together with an external force inside a neural Kalman filter. In all four, the gains serve motion imitation or pose estimation, without being tied to the controlled body or evaluated against measured force. [Le et al. (2026)] come closest, predicting the gains of a center-of-mass PD controller against force plates, though they distribute the force over body vertices instead of controlling joints. No prior work has learned the impedance of an articulated human model against measured contact forces. ImpedanceMimic learns joint impedance against measured force, with gains expressed as multiples of inertia-scaled priors that tie them to the body. We first motivate our approach on a single joint, which we then scale to human motion imitation.

    3 Method

    Ill-posed contact forces.

    We model the body as a floating-base rigid-body system with generalized coordinates q∈ℝⁿ, n=31, six of which describe the pelvis and m=15 of which are actuated joints. Its dynamics obey the Newton–Euler equations of motion,

    \vskip-1.00006ptM(q) q̈ + h(q,q̇) = S^⊤τ + J_c(q)^⊤λ,\vskip-1.00006pt

    		(1)

    with mass matrix M, bias forces h (Coriolis, centrifugal, gravitational), joint torques τ mapped by the selection matrix S, and contact forces λ through their Jacobian J_c (dimensions in App. A.2.2). Each GRF is the resultant of its contact forces applied at its CoP. A recorded motion q^*(t) fixes the left-hand side of Eq. 1, and its torque-free pelvis rows fix the net contact wrench to the rate of change of whole-body momentum, but not how that wrench is realized: in double support, its split between the feet and each CoP remains undetermined. Simulation resolves this through a contact model and a joint-torque trajectory τ(t), so the accuracy of the recovered forces is that of τ(t).

    3.1 Action-space Impedance Bounds

    A policy π_θ(aₜ|oₜ) acts every Δt=10 ms while the simulator steps every h=2 ms. The action space determines how the joint torque τ̂ in Eq. 1 evolves over the N=5 substeps: a direct-torque policy holds τ̂=τ_scale aₜ fixed, so it cannot react between queries. [Peng & Van De Panne (2017)] wrap it in a proportional–derivative controller recomputed every substep, to smooth learning:

    τ̂ = kᵖ∘(q^*ₜ₊₁+α δq-q) + kᵈ∘(q̇^*ₜ₊₁-q̇),

    		(2)

    clipped to ±τˡⁱᵐ, where δq∈[-1,1]ᵐ are per-joint position offsets scaled by α, and ∘ the element-wise product. We extend this controller by emitting per-joint gain residuals Δkᵖ,Δkᵈ∈[-1,1]ᵐ,

    kᵖ=kᵖ₀∘\exp (sₚ Δkᵖ), kᵈ=kᵈ₀∘\exp (s_d Δkᵈ),

    		(3)

    about base gains kᵖ₀,kᵈ₀, with log-scales sₚ,s_d>0 setting the gain range. The exponential keeps gains strictly positive, as stability at the joint requires. We define two PD action spaces: Fixed-PD (a=δq, gains held at (kᵖ₀,kᵈ₀)), and Learned-PD (a=(Δkᵖ,Δkᵈ,δq)). As observed empirically by [Bogdanovic et al. (2020)], in contact the environment constrains the joint, so kᵈ has little effect and kᵖ sets the force the PD can produce. Out of contact the joint drives only the light distal segment, so kᵈ governs the closed-loop dynamics. We formalize this as two bounds.

    Proposition 1(Force authority, Bound 1).

    At the reference state (q,q̇)=(q^*,q̇^*) the velocity-error term of Eq. 2 vanishes and the displacement is O(Δt)-small, so the PD torque reduces to τ≈α kᵖ∘δq: the offset δq is the policy’s sole lever for torque production at the reference pose, giving an achievable interval of half-width αkᵖ. Producing the reference contact force therefore requires the inverse-dynamics torque τ^* of Eq. 1, which is attainable at the reference pose only if

    kᵖ ≥ (\maxₜ|τ^*(t)|)/(α).

    		(4)

    Below this bound, the lever αkᵖ is too small to supply the torque required by the reference force. The offset δq saturates, leaving the tracking term kᵖ∘(q^*-q) as the only source of torque. A fixed-gain policy below the bound must therefore choose between forfeiting kinematic or force tracking.

    Proposition 2(Feedback stability, Bound 2).

    In continuous time any positive kᵈ is stabilizing. In simulation the PD of Eq. 2 is applied as an explicit actuator force at every physics step h[(Peng & Van De Panne, 2017)]. On a free joint of inertia I, discretizing the error dynamics yields a 2×2 linear map whose eigenvalues must lie inside the unit circle. The Jury criterion gives (App. A.2.1)

    0

    		(5)

    The damping condition is the more restrictive case, and depends on I, the changing inertia that the joint drives at a given moment. During contact the joint acts on the kinematic chain of the whole body above it, whereas in swing it drives only the distal segment, whose inertia is orders of magnitude smaller. A damping gain that is stable in contact can therefore be unstable in flight, where the feedback amplifies the error between policy steps and the torque alternates at ±τˡⁱᵐ. This chatter is the classical limit on the impedance a sampled-data controller can render [(Colgate & Brown, 1994)]. Under the explicit PD of Eq. 2, each joint thus inherits a damping ceiling set by its distal inertia. Stable PD avoids it by evaluating the controller at the next state [(Tan et al., 2011)], and implicit damping by moving the damping term into the integrator [(Todorov et al., 2012)].

    Remark 1(Phase-dependent feasibility).

    A stiff joint, as Bound 1 demands in contact, needs higher damping against oscillation, whereas Bound 2 needs a lightly damped joint in swing. Fixed gains must therefore favor one phase over the other, whereas state-dependent gains can match each bound.

    Validation.

    We test both bounds on the rod of Fig. 2a, where they evaluate to kᵖ≥32 Nm/rad and kᵈ<20 Nm s/rad (App. A.2.1). Trained with identical base gains, reward and PPO [(Schulman et al., 2017)], Fixed-PD forfeits force tracking when its stiffness is below Bound 1 (Fig. 2b) and loses kinematic and force tracking for damping above Bound 2 (Fig. 2c). Learned-PD instead reaches the same force accuracy by raising kᵖ to Bound 1 in contact and holding kᵈ under Bound 2 throughout (Fig. 2d). Section 4.1 verifies these bounds on the human model (Fig. 9, Table 16).

    3.2 ImpedanceMimic

    Action space.

    The policy outputs aₜ=(Δkᵖₜ,Δkᵈₜ,δqₜ)∈[-1,1]³ᵐ with log-scales sₚ=1.25 and s_d=1.5. A first-order lag mimics activation dynamics by smoothing gain changes,

    Δk̃ₜ=Δk̃ₜ₋₁+β(Δkₜ-Δk̃ₜ₋₁), β=1-e^-Δt/T_act, T_act=50~ms,

    		(6)

    that would otherwise appear as force transients, and requires the policy to stiffen ahead of touchdown. Base gains scale with each subject i’s diagonal joint-space inertia Iⱼⱼ(i) at the rest pose,

    kᵖ₀=Iⱼⱼ∘ωₙ², kᵈ₀=2 ζ∘Iⱼⱼ∘ωₙ,

    		(7)

    where the natural frequency ωₙ and damping ratio ζ are set per joint by nominal gains (Table 8), such that a multiple of the nominal results in the same closed-loop behavior across bodies.

    Kinematics-to-GRF estimator.

    Setting the impedance before touchdown requires anticipating the contact force, which the policy cannot read from a force plate at inference. The actor therefore receives an estimate \smashF̂ₜ computed from the reference kinematics. A center-of-mass physics prior, corrected by a residual network ensemble, is fitted once per split on the plate-valid frames of the training clips and then frozen (App. A.2.2). It reaches a GRF correlation of 0.979 on seen and 0.943 on unseen subjects, on par with the dedicated GaitDynamics regressor [(Tan et al., 2026)].

    Observations.

    The actor observes oₜ∈ℝ²¹⁵ (Table 7): proprioception and contact state from the simulator, and three lookaheads at {10,50,250} ms, namely the kinematic offset q^*ₜ₊ₖ-qₜ, the estimated GRF \smashF̂ₜ₊ₖ, and foot positioning. Every entry is a simulator state or a function of the reference kinematics, so no force-plate signal reaches the actor and the policy runs plate-free at inference (Fig. 1). The critic receives the current-frame GRF to lower advantage variance [(Pinto et al., 2017)], and a linear head on the actor, discarded at inference, regresses the measured GRF at three lookahead offsets through an auxiliary Huber loss in the PPO objective (App. A.2.2).

    Reward.

    The reward combines kinematic imitation with force-plate supervision,

    rₜ=rᵏⁱⁿₜ+w_grf r^grfₜ+0.25 rˢʰᵉᵃʳₜ+0.15 rᵉᵉₜ,

    		(8)

    with w_grf annealed linearly from 0.25 to 0.5, such that the policy first learns to track and then to produce faithful forces. The kinematic term combines pose, velocity and pelvis tracking (App. A.2.2). Each joint’s pose error is normalized by its amplitude over the clip, and the root term tracks pelvis velocity, independent of the subject’s leg length. With ΔF_f=F_f-F^*_f and Δc_f=c_f-c^*_f the force and CoP errors of foot f, and F̄_f=\max(F^*_z,f, 0.5) the load that scales the force error,

    r^grf=\exp(-∑_fg_f[α_grf\tfrac∥ΔF_f∥²F̄_f²+5 ∥Δc_f∥²]), rˢʰᵉᵃʳ=\exp(-5∑_fg_f ∥ΔF_f,∥∥²),

    		(9)

    with α_grf=4. The contact gate g_f is active when either the simulated or the reference vertical force exceeds 0.1 BW, to penalize mistimed contacts. rᵉᵉ tracks heel and toe positions.

    Datasets.

    We assemble 20 h of motion from 129 participants across 9 public datasets with synchronized force plates (Fig. 1, App. A.1.1), distributed through AddBiomechanics [(Werling et al., 2024)] with joint kinematics, per-foot GRF and centers of pressure. Recordings cover six activity classes, walking, running, standing, lateral movements, flexion and jumping, with body masses ranging from 44 to 126 kg and heights from 1.46 to 1.95 m. We resample to 100 Hz, low-pass filter, cut event-aligned clips of 1–10 s and normalize forces to body weight (App. A.1).

    Simulation model.

    Every subject is simulated with the no-arm Rajagopal model, scaled by AddBiomechanics and converted to MuJoCo [(Todorov et al., 2012)] with MyoConverter [(Wang et al., 2022; Ikkala & Hämäläinen, 2022)], with torque-driven joints. All subjects share 14 bodies and the n=31 coordinates of Eq. 1, while masses, inertias, segment lengths, contact geometry and joint ranges are subject-specific. Each foot carries eight contact spheres building on [Falisse et al. (2019)] (App. A.2.2). The policy runs at 100 Hz, the rate of the reference data, and the physics at h=2 ms.

    Training and evaluation.

    We train the actor and critic, each an MLP ([512,256,128], SiLU), with PPO for 2 billion steps on 8,192 parallel worlds in one batched MuJoCo Warp environment, each world carrying its own subject-scaled model (App. A.2.2). Episodes start at a uniformly sampled frame with noise on pose and velocity and terminate when the clip ends or the pelvis drops below 0.4 m [(Peng et al., 2018)]. Our policy receives no subject identifier or anthropometric descriptor: morphology enters only through the priors of Eq. 7. We report three benchmarks for every method (App. A.1.4): seen (train on all 129 subjects, evaluate on the held-out 20 % of each subject’s clips), unseen (train on 107 subjects, evaluate zero-shot on 22 held out) and leave-one-activity-out (train on five activities, evaluate on the sixth). Evaluation rollouts report survival, RMSE and Pearson correlation for joint angles and per-foot forces, center-of-pressure error and torque consistency (App. A.3).

    Baselines.

    We compare ImpedanceMimic to other action spaces, extending the analysis of [Peng & Van De Panne (2017)] to contact forces. The baselines match ImpedanceMimic in everything but actuation, as far as training allowed. (i)Fixed-PD outputs the position offset δqₜ with fixed inertia-scaled base gains (App. A.3.5). (ii)Torque outputs τ̂ₜ=τ_scale∘aₜ with per-joint, per-subject scale τ_scale=α kᵖ₀, its authority inertia-normalized like the PD baselines (App. A.2.2). (iii)Muscle outputs excitations for the 80 Hill-type muscles of each participant’s scaled model (App. A.2.3). We also compare against existing methods. (iv)GaitDynamics[(Tan et al., 2026)] regresses bilateral GRF and CoP from joint kinematics (App. A.2.3). With no physics and no kinematics to imitate, it serves as a reference for force accuracy. (v)PHC[(Luo et al., 2023)] and (vi)SimPoE[(Yuan et al., 2021)] are physics-based imitation controllers, the latter with learned PD gains, re-implemented as faithfully as paper and code allow, on the same data, physics and evaluation (App. A.2.3).We retrain Fixed-PD and ImpedanceMimic under stable PD and implicit damping, repeat every action space without the force reward, and run ablations of ImpedanceMimic and robustness tests (§4.4, App. A.5).

    4 Results

    4.1 Action Space Governs Force Fidelity

    Across six activities and 129 human morphologies, ImpedanceMimic outperforms the other action spaces in imitating both a motion and its contact forces (Table 1, Fig. 3). On seen subjects, it has the lowest joint-angle error and the highest survival in every activity, and it leads on nearly every additional kinematic, force and center-of-pressure metric (Table 11, Fig. 10). Its force accuracy approaches that of GaitDynamics, a dedicated kinematics-to-force regressor that serves as a reference, even though ImpedanceMimic must also produce the motion itself by driving each participant’s body model under full physics, whereas the regressor reads the forces directly off the recorded kinematics. Fixed-PD has the second-lowest joint-angle error but the largest vertical-force RMSE of the three action-space baselines in standing, flexion and jumping (Table 11), activities spent largely in double support, where the motion does not fix how the force is split between the feet. Intuitively, the legs share the load like springs in parallel, and Fixed-PD can shift the load only through position offsets that the policy needs to hold the pose, whereas ImpedanceMimic stiffens the loaded joints without compromising kinematic tracking. The action-space bounds constrain fixed gains further in other activities (App. A.3.5). In running, the nominal stiffness misses Bound 1 on up to half of the knee and ankle contact frames, against under a tenth for the learned stiffness (Fig. 9), and in swing the nominal ankle damping violates Bound 2 on every frame, and capping it raises the vertical-force correlation (Table 20). Torque has a vertical-force accuracy similar to ImpedanceMimic’s, its slim lead in correlation (0.82 against 0.80) coming mostly from standing, where the force stays near body weight. Overall, however, it has twice the joint-angle error and is less accurate on horizontal forces (Table 11), as a torque held over the 10 ms policy step cannot correct deviations the way a PD law does at every 2 ms physics step. Acting at the physics rate leaves this error unchanged (4.55^∘ against 4.48^∘, Table 22), since a torque policy must learn the feedback the PD law computes from the joint state [(Peng & Van De Panne, 2017)].Muscle produces the smoothest torques and near-best forces in walking and running, but the lowest survival, particularly in flexion and jumping, likely because its activation dynamics (App. A.2.3) leave too little margin to recover from rapid load changes.

    Learning the gains triples the action dimension, from 15 to 45, without changing the network size or the simulation throughput. The wider action space does not slow learning, in line with reports that variable impedance raises the learning rate in contact-rich manipulation [(Martín-Martín et al., 2019; Bogdanovic et al., 2020)]. ImpedanceMimic, Fixed-PD and Torque each take about 1.3 GPU-hours per run on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000, against 1.8 for Muscle (Table 18), and ImpedanceMimic converges fastest, approaching its plateau within 0.5×10⁹ steps (Fig. 13).

    These results agree with the kinematic comparison of [Peng & Van De Panne (2017)], who found PD targets comparable to the best action space on every motion, torques among the worst and muscle activations the slowest to learn, and attributed the advantage of PD to its local feedback. Scoring the contact forces as well shows that fixed gains keep the pose at the cost of the force, and that learned impedance, which keeps the local feedback of PD while adapting it to the state, leads on both.

    4.2 Zero-Shot Transfer Across Human and Robot Embodiments

    ImpedanceMimic transfers zero-shot to new human and robot bodies without any anthropometric input (Table 1, Fig. 4). On the 22 held-out participants, who span 49–93 kg and 1.50–1.82 m, it retains the survival and joint-angle error of its seen-split counterpart with little loss of force accuracy. Fixed-PD keeps its survival and joint-angle error, and with them its force deficit. Torque keeps its vertical-force accuracy but loses survival, mostly in the non-cyclic activities, as does Muscle.

    The inertia prior expresses the controller in the units of each body. With base gains proportional to the joint-space inertia (Eq. 7), a given gain multiple yields the same closed-loop natural frequency and damping ratio on every body, and the PD feedback corrects the remaining differences at every physics step, which Torque, normalized by the same inertia, cannot. Removing the scaling leaves survival intact but multiplies torque jerk by 2.7 on unseen subjects (Table 27), since the damping limit of Bound 2 moves with the inertia of each body while unscaled gains do not.

    The same policies drive a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid without retraining, on held-out clips retargeted to the robot, with gain priors from its own inertia (Fig. 4a, App. A.3.3). It is lighter and shorter (33 kg, 1.32 m) than all 107 training participants. Without force plates, its reference forces come from the estimator’s physics prior on its center-of-mass acceleration. ImpedanceMimic is best on every activity-mean metric among the action spaces (Table 13, Fig. 4b–d), with its survival falling from 98.1 to 82.1 % against losses of about 35 points for Fixed-PD (56.9 %) and Torque (44.0 %).

    4.3 Learned Impedance Encodes Motor State

    The learned impedance follows motor state, stiffening loaded joints and releasing the ankle before the foot unloads. We segment held-out clips of seen subjects into movement cycles and characterize each cycle by hip, knee and ankle stiffness and damping, normalized by the subject’s nominal gains (Figs. 10 and 5a,b, App. A.3.6). Two patterns recur across activities, one for each action-space bound. Stiffness follows the torque demanded by the contact force, as Bound 1 requires. Within a walking stride, ankle stiffness rises from 0.6× nominal at heel strike to 1.5× at push-off, where ankle torque peaks, and across all six activities, its contact mean increases linearly with the cycle’s peak vertical force (r=0.93, Fig. 5c). Ankle damping is released before unloading, peaking 128–196 ms before toe-off or take-off in walking, running and jumping, and falling to about a third of nominal by toe-off (Fig. 5b). At lift-off, the ankle drives only the foot, which lowers Bound 2 below the peak contact damping (App. A.3.5). Because the gains lag by 50 ms (Eq. 6), damping must fall beforehand and then stays below Bound 2 on 99.99 % of swing frames (App. A.3.6).

    The learned gains partly match human ankle impedance (App. A.3.6). Ankle stiffness rises over contact, though less steeply than measured by [Rouse et al. (2014)], and holds 0.4 of the toppling stiffness in quiet standing, against 0.9 in humans [(Loram & Lakie, 2002)]. The damping release matches human data in timing [(Lee & Hogan, 2015)] but not in magnitude, which Bound 2 caps.

    Across activities, these schedules form a low-dimensional code of motor state. In a principal component analysis of the standardized, cycle-normalized gain trajectories, two components carry 57 % of the variance (Fig. 11a). The first encodes activity, which accounts for 89 % of its variance, and the second encodes activity and subject (Figs. 5d and 11b). Projected onto these components, cycles of the 22 unseen subjects fall on the same activity clusters (App. A.3.6), so new bodies reuse the code learned in training. A logistic regression on the first ten principal components, cross-validated across subjects, recovers the activity of a single cycle with a macro recall of 92.5 % (Fig. 11c). The activity can thus be read from the gains of one cycle alone, without kinematics or forces, making learned impedance a decodable latent of motor state. A fixed waveform per activity would form the same clusters, but replacing the learned gains with their subject-mean, phase-indexed schedule and retraining the offsets lowers survival below that of fixed gains (88.5 against 93.0 %, App. A.3.5), meaning the policy also adapts the gains to the state within each cycle.

    This shared code carries over to activities withheld from training, where ImpedanceMimic generalizes best (Table 1, bottom block). Trained on five activities and evaluated zero-shot on the sixth, it has the lowest joint-angle error in every fold and the highest survival in all but standing, losing 7 points of survival relative to training on all six, against 16 to 23 for the baselines.

    ImpedanceMimic loses force accuracy mainly when walking is withheld, keeping the pose but dropping to a vertical-force correlation of 0.66, against 0.98 when walking is trained (Tables 1 and 15). On these clips, the damping waveform of the policy trained without walking correlates with that of the policy trained on walking (r=0.99), including the release before toe-off and the swing level, but reaches only 66 % of the peak damping and 46 % of the push-off stiffening (App. A.3.6). This split between timing and magnitude is consistent with the two bounds, since the release is set by Bound 2, which depends only on foot inertia, the same in every activity, whereas the push-off stiffening is set by Bound 1, which depends on the torque each activity demands.

    4.4 Open Benchmark: Ablations, Sensitivity and Robustness

    We compare ImpedanceMimic with the existing imitation controllers PHC [(Luo et al., 2023)] and SimPoE [(Yuan et al., 2021)], each under the PD integration of its original implementation (Table 2, App. A.5). PHC, with our full reward in place of its own, still reaches 8.7 to 13.3^∘ of joint-angle error and trails nominal Fixed-PD and ImpedanceMimic under implicit damping in vertical-force correlation. SimPoE survives nearly as often as the best controllers but tracks joint angles and vertical forces less accurately than ImpedanceMimic. Its survival, however, depends on a residual root wrench that no joint or contact produces and that balances it instead of its feet (Table 19); without it, its survival drops to 85, 80 and 56 % (Tables 20 and 21). Retraining Fixed-PD and ImpedanceMimic under stable PD [(Tan et al., 2011)] and implicit damping [(Todorov et al., 2012)] separates the integration scheme from the learned gains. With the same gain priors, ImpedanceMimic leads Fixed-PD in joint-angle error and every force correlation on every benchmark (Table 2), survives more often in all but one cell (96.3 against 96.6 % on seen subjects at doubled stable priors), and its explicit-PD force correlations exceed those of Fixed-PD under any scheme. The lead carries to the Unitree G1, where the learned gains keep the highest survival under every scheme and gain level, by 1.4 to 25.2 points (Table 14). Doubled priors lower the joint-angle error of Fixed-PD under every scheme and reach their lowest values for ImpedanceMimic under stable PD, yet never raise the vertical-force correlation of either method, as the integrator lifts Bound 2 but leaves Bound 1 and the split of the load in double support to the gains. At nominal priors under stable PD, ImpedanceMimic trails doubled fixed gains in survival, a gap concentrated in flexion (85.1 against 99.0 % seen) that doubled priors close (98.4 %) and that the policy closes by itself under explicit PD (97.7 against 91.3 %). The learned gains modulate around the prior and do not replace the choice of its scale.

    Beyond the three benchmarks, we examine what drives the fidelity and robustness of ImpedanceMimic (App. A.5). To isolate the contribution of force supervision, we retrain every action space without the GRF reward (Fig. 6a–c, Table 26). In every action space, joint-angle error decreases while vertical-force correlation drops, so closer kinematic tracking does not recover the forces. Without this reward, ImpedanceMimic surpasses Torque in force correlation, recovering more force from kinematic tracking alone than any other action space.

    We perform ablations of ImpedanceMimic, from the inertia-scaled gains and reward terms to the force estimate and training-only signals (Fig. 6d, Table 28). Removing the inertia scaling has the largest effect, quadrupling torque jerk and lowering every force correlation. The estimated GRF improves force correlation, and the measured GRF adds little beyond it (Table 27). Force fidelity requires no privileged information, as removing the auxiliary GRF head or the asymmetric critic, which use measured forces only in training, leaves all metrics within seed variation. The log-ranges sₚ and s_d of Eq. 3 bound how far stiffness and damping depart from their nominal values, and the activation lag T_act of Eq. 6 limits how fast they change. Varying each has little effect on survival, but fidelity depends far more on the damping than on the stiffness range (Table 25), as Bound 2 binds at the ankle in every swing phase and Bound 1 mainly in running and lateral cutting (App. A.3.5). Restricting damping to within 10 % of nominal multiplies torque jerk sixfold and lowers the vertical-force correlation four times as much as the same restriction on stiffness. An activation lag of up to 50 ms is neutral, whereas 200 ms triples torque jerk, as the gains trail the contact events. Finally, we evaluate the four action spaces without retraining under eleven test-time perturbations, where ImpedanceMimic keeps the lowest joint-angle error throughout and the highest survival under all but the largest contact spheres (Table 23). Under a 20 ms observation delay, ImpedanceMimic retains 93.5 % survival, as its PD law acts on the current state at every simulation step, whereas Torque, whose corrections pass through the delayed policy, falls to 3.3 %. Fixed-PD closes the same loop with fixed gains yet falls to 65.6 %, a collapse largely of explicit PD (89.1 and 84.4 % under stable PD and implicit damping, against 91.6 and 91.4 % for ImpedanceMimic, Table 24).

    5 Discussion and Conclusion

    We introduced ImpedanceMimic, a motion-imitation policy that outputs per-joint stiffness, damping and setpoint offsets, supervised by force measurements withheld at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic is the best force-accurate motion imitation controller, at no additional training cost. It outperforms the Torque and Muscle action spaces, as well as the existing imitation controllers PHC and SimPoE, and its advantage over fixed gains holds under every PD integration scheme. Its gains, learned as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, transfer zero-shot to unseen humans and a simulated humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a decodable representation of motor state, stiffening with load and releasing damping before the foot unloads, an anticipatory behavior the policy reproduces even in activities withheld from training.

    Our results further highlight the role of physical simulation in recovering physically realizable forces. GaitDynamics, a regressor that leads in vertical-force correlation, loads the ground on 30 % of lateral-cutting and 39 % of jump flight frames, against 11 % and 17 % for ImpedanceMimic (a tracking error in contact timing, not a physical inconsistency), and places the center of pressure outside the foot on 6 % and 17 % of their loaded frames, against at most 0.2 % for ImpedanceMimic (App. A.3.7). Yet simulation alone does not guarantee consistency with the dynamics of the body, as is the case for SimPoE, where a residual external wrench supplies more than half of the mediolateral force and with it much of the balance (Table 19). Without such a wrench, balance rests on the foot-contact model, as our robustness tests show (App. A.5). Together with the subject models provided by the datasets, which lack the arms humans use to recover balance [(Bruijn et al., 2010)], and the low coverage of non-cyclic activities (16 % of the training clips, Table 5), this likely explains why every method performs worse in lateral cutting, flexion and jumping. For a controller that acts only through its joints, the action-space bounds explain why fixed gains cannot reconcile force authority in contact with stability in swing. With stiff gains, a stable integrator recovers the kinematic accuracy of learned impedance but not its force accuracy, as only a load-dependent stiffness redistributes the load between the feet in double support. Learned impedance sets damping independently of stiffness, releasing the ankle damping ahead of toe-off while the stiffness peaks at push-off (Fig. 5). On hardware, joint-level motor drivers evaluate the PD law at kilohertz rates without the mass matrix that stable PD requires, and their shorter step h raises Bound 2, leaving the learned damping conservative. They would, however, expose the policy to effects that our simulation omits, including actuator bandwidth, stiction and torque limits (App. A.3.3). Powered lower-limb prostheses already modulate joint impedance with gait phase, using gains tuned by hand for each user [(Sup et al., 2008)], and a learned, state-dependent impedance could replace this tuning once its force estimate is causal, as the estimator and the reference lookahead currently draw on up to 400 ms of future motion.

    Acknowledgments

    This work has been made possible in part by a gift from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Foundation to establish the Kempner Institute for the Study of Natural and Artificial Intelligence at Harvard University.

    AI use statement

    In this work, we used generative AI tools for literature research, for polishing author-written text, and as a coding assistant, including for LaTeX table formatting. All research ideas, the experimental design, and the analysis are our own. We therefore did not use generative AI for ideation or for the generation of research artifacts such as figures, data, or proofs.

    We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: we read every paper we cite in its original published form, and we reviewed every line of AI-assisted code. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

    Reproducibility statement

    Code is released openly at https://impedancemimic.github.io/ImpedanceMimic/. Experimental data used in this work is open-sourced at https://addbiomechanics.org/.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    A Appendix
